"I really think this is a time to put safety and mission first," he said. Asked about OpenAI's recent decision to hold back a new model, Altman said it fell short on some of the evaluations the company uses to gauge safety and alignment, rather than pointing to a specific serious incident. The model was "a little bit worse on a few of the evals" OpenAI uses, Altman said, characterizing the decision as an "abundance of caution." "There's not a big scary thing in this case," he said. He described withholding or reworking models that do not meet OpenAI's standards as part of the normal development process. More broadly, Altman said alignment, safety, monitoring and security need to remain "way ahead of capabilities" as models improve. He described that approach as "pacing" progress. Altman also pushed back on the idea that AI safety can be solved entirely through engineering. "We still have discovery about how to align these models," he said, arguing that the industry faces a scientific problem alongside the engineering work required to make AI systems safer. On liability, Altman said he expects a multi-level framework to emerge depending on whether a failure originates in the model, how a developer uses it, or intentional misuse by an end user. He compared the possible structure to the automotive industry, where responsibility can fall on different parties depending on what went wrong. Altman also expressed cautious optimism about discussions in Washington and international coordination, while acknowledging that previous expectations for policy progress had not always materialized. sources.title: OpenAI IPO will not happen in 2026 amid AI safety fears, Sam Altman says - The Guardian
passages: OpenAI will not go public in 2026, Sam Altman said in a Fortune interview published on Saturday, citing safety concerns over artificial intelligence .
When asked by Fortune whether 2026 is off the table in favor of 2027, Altman said: “I would say not 2026.
Yeah, we got a lot of stuff to do, like meeting this moment of what is going to be required for safety and alignment, and how the industry and governments can work together.”
“I actually think that, given everything happening with safety, right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public, and we don’t feel pressure on that,” Altman, OpenAI’s CEO, told Fortune .
Altman also suggested that OpenAI and other leading AI companies may be close to announcing an agreement to slow AI development and work together to address safety risks, Fortune reported.
The New York Times in June reported that the San Francisco-based OpenAI was considering whether to hold off on a potentially trillion-dollar IPO until next year.

extraction.body: OpenAI’s decision comes after dire warnings about rapidly progressing technology and lawmakers’ calls for new rules OpenAI’s decision comes after dire warnings about rapidly progressing technology and lawmakers’ calls for new rules OpenAI will not go public in 2026, Sam Altman said in a Fortune interview published on Saturday, citing safety concerns over artificial intelligence . “I actually think that, given everything happening with safety, right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public, and we don’t feel pressure on that,” Altman, OpenAI’s CEO, told Fortune . Growing numbers of US lawmakers ​are calling for new rules to govern AI systems after dire warnings from two researchers from OpenAI rival Anthropic that rapidly progressing artificial intelligence could lead to the extinction of the human race ‌in the not-too-distant future. The warnings follow cases of AI agents going rogue to hack external systems and AI ​safety researchers quitting their companies concerned about the technology’s risks. Politicians, both Democrats and Republicans, have responded with alarm and calls for more action. The New York Times in June reported that the San Francisco-based OpenAI was considering whether to hold off on a potentially trillion-dollar IPO until next year. At the time, shares in Elon Musk’s SpaceX IPO were tumbling after a surge that sent that company’s valuation to $1.8tn. When asked by Fortune whether 2026 is off the table in favor of 2027, Altman said: “I would say not 2026. Yeah, we got a lot of stuff to do, like meeting this moment of what is going to be required for safety and alignment, and how the industry and governments can work together.” Altman also suggested that OpenAI and other leading AI companies may be close to announcing an agreement to slow AI development and work together to address safety risks, Fortune reported. Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s CEO, on Saturday urged AI companies to take a more deliberate approach to development. “We must slow the ‌pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Amodei wrote in an essay shared on social media. Altman later posted that he agreed with the sentiment. “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier,” Altman wrote in a response to Amodei’s post on the X platform. “This has been a primary topic of discussions we’ve had at OpenAI in recent weeks.” Safety concerns have not slowed down Anthropic’s own IPO plans so far. Anthropic is expected to begin marketing its initial public offering in mid-October at the earliest and complete the listing days before the US midterm elections in November, people familiar with the matter told Reuters this month.

sources.title: Sam Altman says OpenAI won’t go public until its models are safe
passages: OpenAI, alongside its rivals, called for regulation and “pacing the frontier.” And earlier this month, Altman said in an interview that the company would likely not go public this year.
CEO Sam Altman says it won’t happen until the company can make better promises about model safety, with no firm timeline in sight.

But he expressed concerns that going public could create the potential to “disappoint Wall Street supporters in the names of safety or whatever else,” and that doing it during a “shift to very capable models and a new kind of safety requirement seems ill-advised.” He said OpenAI would prioritize safety to “confidently scale to the next stage of AI without people debating what percent chance we’re going to do all these bad things,” rather than “barrel, all guns blazing, towards an IPO.” “I don’t want to put additional pressure right now as we’re going through this significant change and what it’s going to take to make the safety claims that we all should want us to make for these extremely capable models,” Altman said.
For months, people have wondered when OpenAI will go public.
OpenAI rival Anthropic officially filed to go public in June, with its IPO likely to happen in November, reportedly after the US midterm elections.
In July, news broke that an unreleased OpenAI model had hacked into a rival AI lab, Hugging Face, without OpenAI’s knowledge.
More cybersecurity incidents soon came to light at OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Google.

CEO Sam Altman says it won’t happen until the company can make better promises about model safety, with no firm timeline in sight. “We intend to continue with AI progress … but as the models have had this surge forward in capability, and we see more of that ahead of us, we have got to be able to make confident safety claims,” Altman said Tuesday during a Q&A with reporters after his DevDay keynote. At the same time, he said, waiting too long for an IPO would be “bad for the world.” Altman’s comments come after months of controversy about whether or not OpenAI and its rivals can control their own creations. In July, news broke that an unreleased OpenAI model had hacked into a rival AI lab, Hugging Face, without OpenAI’s knowledge. More cybersecurity incidents soon came to light at OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Google. A high-profile resignation letter from an Anthropic employee sparked a public discussion about how risky these systems are for society at large. OpenAI rival Anthropic officially filed to go public in June, with its IPO likely to happen in November, reportedly after the US midterm elections. Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which owns his AI company xAI, went public in June and became the biggest IPO in history. “I think it’s great when companies are public,” Altman said, adding, “I think it’s also kind of bad for the world if OpenAI waits too long to go public.”

sources.title: OpenAI IPO Delayed Until AI Safety Goals Met, Altman Says
passages: Speaking to reporters after his DevDay keynote Tuesday, CEO Sam Altman made it crystal clear that the company's much-anticipated public offering won't happen until OpenAI can make rock-solid promises about AI safety - and there's no timeline for when that might be.

"We intend to continue with AI progress, but as the models have had this surge forward in capability, and we see more of that ahead of us, we have got to be able to make confident safety claims," Altman told the press gathering.
Altman's IPO delay represents a watershed moment for the AI industry, where safety considerations are finally getting equal weight with growth ambitions.
The announcement puts OpenAI's highly anticipated IPO on indefinite hold as the AI leader grapples with mounting pressure over model safety and capability concerns.
Where companies like Meta and Google went public first and figured out safety concerns later, OpenAI appears to be flipping that script entirely.
Internal benchmarks suggest OpenAI's next-generation models will represent another significant leap in capabilities, potentially raising new safety questions that current protocols can't address.

Private market valuations for AI companies have been built on assumptions of near-term public offerings, and OpenAI's safety-first approach could signal a broader shift in how the market values AI companies versus their potential risks.
But Altman's DevDay comments suggest OpenAI is taking a fundamentally different approach than its tech predecessors.
The real test will be whether OpenAI can maintain its competitive edge while developing the safety frameworks that will ultimately determine when - or if - it goes public.

extraction.body: OpenAI won't go public until the company can make "confident safety claims" about its AI models, CEO Sam Altman declared Tuesday at the company's DevDay conference. The announcement puts OpenAI's highly anticipated IPO on indefinite hold as the AI leader grapples with mounting pressure over model safety and capability concerns. Altman's comments signal a major shift in how tech companies are weighing safety considerations against investor demands. OpenAI just threw a wrench into Wall Street's AI investment plans. Speaking to reporters after his DevDay keynote Tuesday, CEO Sam Altman made it crystal clear that the company's much-anticipated public offering won't happen until OpenAI can make rock-solid promises about AI safety - and there's no timeline for when that might be. "We intend to continue with AI progress, but as the models have had this surge forward in capability, and we see more of that ahead of us, we have got to be able to make confident safety claims," Altman told the press gathering. The statement represents a dramatic departure from typical Silicon Valley IPO timelines, where companies race to go public while investor appetite runs hot. OpenAI has been riding an unprecedented wave of success since ChatGPT's launch, with the company reportedly valued at over $150 billion in recent private funding rounds. Investment bankers have been circling for months, and industry watchers expected an IPO announcement within the next 12-18 months. But Altman's DevDay comments suggest OpenAI is taking a fundamentally different approach than its tech predecessors. Where companies like Meta and Google went public first and figured out safety concerns later, OpenAI appears to be flipping that script entirely. The decision comes as AI safety has moved from academic concern to boardroom priority. Regulators worldwide are scrambling to establish frameworks for AI oversight, while researchers warn about increasingly capable models outpacing safety measures. Just last month, several AI safety organizations published reports highlighting gaps between current safety protocols and the rapid advancement of large language models. "The models have had this surge forward in capability," Altman acknowledged, referencing the exponential improvements in AI performance that have caught even industry insiders off guard. Internal benchmarks suggest OpenAI's next-generation models will represent another significant leap in capabilities, potentially raising new safety questions that current protocols can't address. The announcement puts OpenAI in an unusual position among tech giants. While competitors like Anthropic and Google continue racing toward more powerful models, OpenAI is essentially hitting the brakes on its biggest potential payday to ensure its technology won't pose unforeseen risks. But Altman also warned against the opposite extreme. Waiting too long for an IPO would be "bad for the world," he said, suggesting the company recognizes the broader implications of keeping advanced AI development locked within private walls. The comment hints at ongoing internal debates about balancing safety with accessibility and innovation speed. Private market valuations for AI companies have been built on assumptions of near-term public offerings, and OpenAI's safety-first approach could signal a broader shift in how the market values AI companies versus their potential risks. The ripple effects extend beyond OpenAI itself. Other AI companies now face pressure to demonstrate their own safety protocols before going public, while investors must weigh whether safety-conscious approaches represent responsible leadership or competitive disadvantage in the global AI race. Altman's IPO delay represents a watershed moment for the AI industry, where safety considerations are finally getting equal weight with growth ambitions. While the decision might frustrate investors eager for OpenAI exposure, it could establish a new standard for responsible AI development that other companies will be forced to follow. The real test will be whether OpenAI can maintain its competitive edge while developing the safety frameworks that will ultimately determine when - or if - it goes public.

When asked by Fortune whether 2026 is off the table in favor of 2027, Altman said: “I would say not 2026.

sources.title: OpenAI IPO will not happen in 2026 amid AI safety fears, Sam Altman says - The Guardian
passages: OpenAI will not go public in 2026, Sam Altman said in a Fortune interview published on Saturday, citing safety concerns over artificial intelligence .
When asked by Fortune whether 2026 is off the table in favor of 2027, Altman said: “I would say not 2026.
Yeah, we got a lot of stuff to do, like meeting this moment of what is going to be required for safety and alignment, and how the industry and governments can work together.”
“I actually think that, given everything happening with safety, right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public, and we don’t feel pressure on that,” Altman, OpenAI’s CEO, told Fortune .
Altman also suggested that OpenAI and other leading AI companies may be close to announcing an agreement to slow AI development and work together to address safety risks, Fortune reported.
The New York Times in June reported that the San Francisco-based OpenAI was considering whether to hold off on a potentially trillion-dollar IPO until next year.

Growing numbers of US lawmakers ​are calling for new rules to govern AI systems after dire warnings from two researchers from OpenAI rival Anthropic that rapidly progressing artificial intelligence could lead to the extinction of the human race ‌in the not-too-distant future. The warnings follow cases of AI agents going rogue to hack external systems and AI ​safety researchers quitting their companies concerned about the technology’s risks. Politicians, both Democrats and Republicans, have responded with alarm and calls for more action. The New York Times in June reported that the San Francisco-based OpenAI was considering whether to hold off on a potentially trillion-dollar IPO until next year. At the time, shares in Elon Musk’s SpaceX IPO were tumbling after a surge that sent that company’s valuation to $1.8tn. When asked by Fortune whether 2026 is off the table in favor of 2027, Altman said: “I would say not 2026. Yeah, we got a lot of stuff to do, like meeting this moment of what is going to be required for safety and alignment, and how the industry and governments can work together.” Altman also suggested that OpenAI and other leading AI companies may be close to announcing an agreement to slow AI development and work together to address safety risks, Fortune reported. Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s CEO, on Saturday urged AI companies to take a more deliberate approach to development. “We must slow the ‌pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Amodei wrote in an essay shared on social media. Altman later posted that he agreed with the sentiment. “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier,” Altman wrote in a response to Amodei’s post on the X platform. “This has been a primary topic of discussions we’ve had at OpenAI in recent weeks.” Safety concerns have not slowed down Anthropic’s own IPO plans so far. Anthropic is expected to begin marketing its initial public offering in mid-October at the earliest and complete the listing days before the US midterm elections in November, people familiar with the matter told Reuters this month.

sources.title: Sam Altman says OpenAI won’t go public until its models are safe
passages: OpenAI, alongside its rivals, called for regulation and “pacing the frontier.” And earlier this month, Altman said in an interview that the company would likely not go public this year.
CEO Sam Altman says it won’t happen until the company can make better promises about model safety, with no firm timeline in sight.

But he expressed concerns that going public could create the potential to “disappoint Wall Street supporters in the names of safety or whatever else,” and that doing it during a “shift to very capable models and a new kind of safety requirement seems ill-advised.” He said OpenAI would prioritize safety to “confidently scale to the next stage of AI without people debating what percent chance we’re going to do all these bad things,” rather than “barrel, all guns blazing, towards an IPO.” “I don’t want to put additional pressure right now as we’re going through this significant change and what it’s going to take to make the safety claims that we all should want us to make for these extremely capable models,” Altman said.
For months, people have wondered when OpenAI will go public.
OpenAI rival Anthropic officially filed to go public in June, with its IPO likely to happen in November, reportedly after the US midterm elections.
In July, news broke that an unreleased OpenAI model had hacked into a rival AI lab, Hugging Face, without OpenAI’s knowledge.
More cybersecurity incidents soon came to light at OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Google.

extraction.body: For months, people have wondered when OpenAI will go public. CEO Sam Altman says it won’t happen until the company can make better promises about model safety, with no firm timeline in sight. “We intend to continue with AI progress … but as the models have had this surge forward in capability, and we see more of that ahead of us, we have got to be able to make confident safety claims,” Altman said Tuesday during a Q&A with reporters after his DevDay keynote. At the same time, he said, waiting too long for an IPO would be “bad for the world.” Altman’s comments come after months of controversy about whether or not OpenAI and its rivals can control their own creations. In July, news broke that an unreleased OpenAI model had hacked into a rival AI lab, Hugging Face, without OpenAI’s knowledge. More cybersecurity incidents soon came to light at OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Google. A high-profile resignation letter from an Anthropic employee sparked a public discussion about how risky these systems are for society at large. At DevDay, Altman was circumspect about what “pacing the frontier” actually meant, refraining from calling it an outright slowdown. “Pacing to us means that we push safety and alignment ahead of capabilities,” Altman said. OpenAI rival Anthropic officially filed to go public in June, with its IPO likely to happen in November, reportedly after the US midterm elections. Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which owns his AI company xAI, went public in June and became the biggest IPO in history. “I think it’s great when companies are public,” Altman said, adding, “I think it’s also kind of bad for the world if OpenAI waits too long to go public.”

sources.title: OpenAI IPO Delayed Until AI Safety Goals Met, Altman Says
passages: Speaking to reporters after his DevDay keynote Tuesday, CEO Sam Altman made it crystal clear that the company's much-anticipated public offering won't happen until OpenAI can make rock-solid promises about AI safety - and there's no timeline for when that might be.

"We intend to continue with AI progress, but as the models have had this surge forward in capability, and we see more of that ahead of us, we have got to be able to make confident safety claims," Altman told the press gathering.
Altman's IPO delay represents a watershed moment for the AI industry, where safety considerations are finally getting equal weight with growth ambitions.
The announcement puts OpenAI's highly anticipated IPO on indefinite hold as the AI leader grapples with mounting pressure over model safety and capability concerns.
Where companies like Meta and Google went public first and figured out safety concerns later, OpenAI appears to be flipping that script entirely.
Internal benchmarks suggest OpenAI's next-generation models will represent another significant leap in capabilities, potentially raising new safety questions that current protocols can't address.

Private market valuations for AI companies have been built on assumptions of near-term public offerings, and OpenAI's safety-first approach could signal a broader shift in how the market values AI companies versus their potential risks.
But Altman's DevDay comments suggest OpenAI is taking a fundamentally different approach than its tech predecessors.
The real test will be whether OpenAI can maintain its competitive edge while developing the safety frameworks that will ultimately determine when - or if - it goes public.

extraction.body: OpenAI won't go public until the company can make "confident safety claims" about its AI models, CEO Sam Altman declared Tuesday at the company's DevDay conference. The announcement puts OpenAI's highly anticipated IPO on indefinite hold as the AI leader grapples with mounting pressure over model safety and capability concerns. Altman's comments signal a major shift in how tech companies are weighing safety considerations against investor demands. OpenAI just threw a wrench into Wall Street's AI investment plans. Speaking to reporters after his DevDay keynote Tuesday, CEO Sam Altman made it crystal clear that the company's much-anticipated public offering won't happen until OpenAI can make rock-solid promises about AI safety - and there's no timeline for when that might be. "We intend to continue with AI progress, but as the models have had this surge forward in capability, and we see more of that ahead of us, we have got to be able to make confident safety claims," Altman told the press gathering. The statement represents a dramatic departure from typical Silicon Valley IPO timelines, where companies race to go public while investor appetite runs hot. OpenAI has been riding an unprecedented wave of success since ChatGPT's launch, with the company reportedly valued at over $150 billion in recent private funding rounds. Investment bankers have been circling for months, and industry watchers expected an IPO announcement within the next 12-18 months. But Altman's DevDay comments suggest OpenAI is taking a fundamentally different approach than its tech predecessors. Where companies like Meta and Google went public first and figured out safety concerns later, OpenAI appears to be flipping that script entirely. The decision comes as AI safety has moved from academic concern to boardroom priority. Regulators worldwide are scrambling to establish frameworks for AI oversight, while researchers warn about increasingly capable models outpacing safety measures. Just last month, several AI safety organizations published reports highlighting gaps between current safety protocols and the rapid advancement of large language models. "The models have had this surge forward in capability," Altman acknowledged, referencing the exponential improvements in AI performance that have caught even industry insiders off guard. Internal benchmarks suggest OpenAI's next-generation models will represent another significant leap in capabilities, potentially raising new safety questions that current protocols can't address. The announcement puts OpenAI in an unusual position among tech giants. While competitors like Anthropic and Google continue racing toward more powerful models, OpenAI is essentially hitting the brakes on its biggest potential payday to ensure its technology won't pose unforeseen risks. But Altman also warned against the opposite extreme. Waiting too long for an IPO would be "bad for the world," he said, suggesting the company recognizes the broader implications of keeping advanced AI development locked within private walls. The comment hints at ongoing internal debates about balancing safety with accessibility and innovation speed. Private market valuations for AI companies have been built on assumptions of near-term public offerings, and OpenAI's safety-first approach could signal a broader shift in how the market values AI companies versus their potential risks. The ripple effects extend beyond OpenAI itself. Other AI companies now face pressure to demonstrate their own safety protocols before going public, while investors must weigh whether safety-conscious approaches represent responsible leadership or competitive disadvantage in the global AI race. Altman's IPO delay represents a watershed moment for the AI industry, where safety considerations are finally getting equal weight with growth ambitions. While the decision might frustrate investors eager for OpenAI exposure, it could establish a new standard for responsible AI development that other companies will be forced to follow. The real test will be whether OpenAI can maintain its competitive edge while developing the safety frameworks that will ultimately determine when - or if - it goes public.

extraction.body: DevDay is here for OpenAI, and that means the company is sharing a whole bunch of news about its latest work on models and the services built around them. While we just heard that GPT-6.1 Astra is getting sent back to the bench for misbehaving, progress continues on the rest of OpenAI’s headlining models, and this afternoon we’re getting the scoop on the first member of that 6.1-series to actually make its public debut, with the launch of GPT‑6.1 Sol. While we only just got GPT-6 Sol , OpenAI is not a company to rest on its laurels, and today is pushing right on forward with the evolution of GPT-6.1 Sol . Even though Astra remains the more capable model, with these 6.1 improvements, OpenAI reports that Sol is rapidly approaching Astra in “intelligence,” nearly matching the flagship model in performance across multiple metrics. In coding, GPT-6.1 Sol is neck-and-neck with 6 Astra, and also performs competitively at answering professional questions and working with documents — all at around one-fifth the cost of Astra. This general trend continues across evaluations like computer usage and scientific research, with GPT-6.1 Sol either directly outperforming previous models, or offering comparable performance at increased speed or with decreased expense. Accuracy is the elephant in the room with far too many AI models, and even some of the best will still confidently report incorrect information. Compared to GPT-6 Sol, 6.1 pushes lower-effort response rates containing factual errors down from 11.4% to 7.7%. And once again, 6.1 Sol manages to perform comparably to 6 Astra here, albeit it for pennies on the dollar. Unlike the obstreperous GPT-6.1 Astra model that was caught deceiving researchers, Sol didn’t raise any red flags during safety evaluations, so hopefully we don’t have much to worry about there. extraction.body: OpenAI has introduced GPT-6.1 Sol, giving developers and ChatGPT users a cheaper model that comes close to the performance of its more powerful GPT-6 Astra model. The company says GPT-6.1 Sol improves on GPT-6 Sol in areas including coding, computer use and professional work, while costing roughly one-fifth as much as Astra based on standard API input and output token prices. For developers, GPT-6.1 Sol costs $2 USD per million input tokens, $0.10 USD per million cached input tokens and $10 USD per million output tokens. OpenAI says cached inputs cost 95 per cent less than regular inputs and half as much as cached inputs with GPT-6 Sol. OpenAI also published benchmark results showing where the new model has improved. On DeepSWE v1.1, which measures software engineering performance, GPT-6.1 Sol matched GPT-6 Astra while costing about one-fifth as much and scored 6.4 percentage points higher than GPT-6 Sol. The model also scored higher than Opus 5.5 with fallbacks on GDP.pdf, a benchmark based on professional PDF tasks, while costing less than half as much per task. On AutomationBench, GPT-6.1 Sol finished 2.2 percentage points ahead of Opus 5.5 at roughly one-third of the cost. OpenAI says computer use has improved as well. GPT-6.1 Sol scored seven percentage points higher than GPT-6 Sol on OSWorld 2.0 and came within 2.1 points of GPT-6 Astra while costing roughly one-seventh as much. On Terminal-Bench Science, GPT-6.1 Sol more than doubled GPT-6 Sol’s score. Its average cost was $5.47 USD per task, compared with $23.21 USD for Opus 5.5 and $23.80 USD for GPT-6 Astra. OpenAI also says the model makes fewer factual mistakes. At low reasoning effort, 7.7 per cent of tested GPT-6.1 Sol responses contained a factual error, down from 11.4 per cent with GPT-6 Sol. GPT-6.1 Sol is available starting today to Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Edu users through ChatGPT Work and Codex, although it is not yet available in regular ChatGPT conversations. Developers can access it through the OpenAI API under the name gpt-6.1-sol. The model arrives alongside OpenAI’s new Dots AI agents , which the company also announced today. Dots are designed to work continuously on assigned tasks using their own cloud computers. OpenAI says a GPT-6.1 Sol Ultrafast version is also coming to Codex in the next few days, offering up to eight times faster token generation.

extraction.body: At OpenAI’s DevDay event on Tuesday, the company showed off GPT-6.1 Sol, a mere week after it launched GPT-6 Sol . OpenAI says the new model delivers nearly the same level of intelligence as GPT-6 Astra for agentic coding, computer use, and professional work, at one-fifth the standard input and output token prices. Notably, the company is not launching GPT-6.1 Astra, as was originally expected. The Wall Street Journal reported this week that OpenAI scrapped the release over safety concerns raised by researchers during internal testing after the model showed higher levels of deception and a tendency to move forward with tasks without asking the user for permission. OpenAI says GPT-6.1 Sol delivers significant improvements over its predecessor GPT-6 Sol across complex tasks, including programming and debugging, understanding documents, and executing multistep workflows. The company claims that on several of these fronts, the model approaches GPT-6 Astra’s performance. OpenAI also says the new model improves factual accuracy when given difficult prompts. Its largest gain over GPT-6 Sol on this front appears at low reasoning effort, where the share of responses containing a factual error drops from 11.4% to 7.7%. Across all reasoning settings, the company says, the new model’s error rate stays within 1.9% of GPT-6 Astra. Additionally, the company says GPT-6.1 Sol is more up front about its limitations and more reliable when it comes to honoring user intent and safety constraints. In challenging evaluations, it’s said to fail less often than GPT-6 Sol at flagging broken search tools, following explicit restrictions, and avoiding unauthorized outcomes during tasks. OpenAI claims it observed no attempts to circumvent the automated safety reviewer, consistent with GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6 Sol. GPT-6.1 Sol is available starting today to all Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu users in ChatGPT Work and Codex. OpenAI notes that the model is not yet available in Chat. extraction.body: OpenAI has introduced GPT-6.1 Sol, giving developers and ChatGPT users a cheaper model that comes close to the performance of its more powerful GPT-6 Astra model. The company says GPT-6.1 Sol improves on GPT-6 Sol in areas including coding, computer use and professional work, while costing roughly one-fifth as much as Astra based on standard API input and output token prices. For developers, GPT-6.1 Sol costs $2 USD per million input tokens, $0.10 USD per million cached input tokens and $10 USD per million output tokens. OpenAI says cached inputs cost 95 per cent less than regular inputs and half as much as cached inputs with GPT-6 Sol. OpenAI also published benchmark results showing where the new model has improved. On DeepSWE v1.1, which measures software engineering performance, GPT-6.1 Sol matched GPT-6 Astra while costing about one-fifth as much and scored 6.4 percentage points higher than GPT-6 Sol. The model also scored higher than Opus 5.5 with fallbacks on GDP.pdf, a benchmark based on professional PDF tasks, while costing less than half as much per task. On AutomationBench, GPT-6.1 Sol finished 2.2 percentage points ahead of Opus 5.5 at roughly one-third of the cost. OpenAI says computer use has improved as well. GPT-6.1 Sol scored seven percentage points higher than GPT-6 Sol on OSWorld 2.0 and came within 2.1 points of GPT-6 Astra while costing roughly one-seventh as much. On Terminal-Bench Science, GPT-6.1 Sol more than doubled GPT-6 Sol’s score. Its average cost was $5.47 USD per task, compared with $23.21 USD for Opus 5.5 and $23.80 USD for GPT-6 Astra. OpenAI also says the model makes fewer factual mistakes. At low reasoning effort, 7.7 per cent of tested GPT-6.1 Sol responses contained a factual error, down from 11.4 per cent with GPT-6 Sol. GPT-6.1 Sol is available starting today to Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Edu users through ChatGPT Work and Codex, although it is not yet available in regular ChatGPT conversations. Developers can access it through the OpenAI API under the name gpt-6.1-sol. The model arrives alongside OpenAI’s new Dots AI agents , which the company also announced today. Dots are designed to work continuously on assigned tasks using their own cloud computers. OpenAI says a GPT-6.1 Sol Ultrafast version is also coming to Codex in the next few days, offering up to eight times faster token generation.

extraction.body: The creator of ICEBlock, the app used to track local sightings of ICE agents and other law-enforcement authorities, has asked Apple to rescind its decision to drop the app from its online store. Joshua Aaron, the free app's creator, also blasted the Trump administration for pressuring Apple to ban the app over fears it could be used to harm U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents. "This is not about me, or ICEBlock," Aaron said in an interview on Friday with CNBC. "This is about our fundamental constitutional rights in this country being stripped away by this administration, and the powers that be who are capitulating to their requests," he said. "I'm incredibly disappointed with the decision that Apple made," Aaron said. "In almost every interview that I did, I was asked if I was afraid that Apple might take the app down, and my answer was always to defend Apple and say, you know, look, when this app was first submitted, it went through a heavy review process with both Apple's legal and senior officials in App Review." Aaron, who said that he is consulting an attorney about the situation, directly asked Apple to allow him to appeal its decision Thursday to drop the app, which became available last spring. He shared a screengrab of the message he sent Apple after the company notified him of the move. "There is no objectionable content in the app," Aaron wrote in that message, which noted Apple's review process. "There have been no changes to the content provided or the features in the app," he wrote. "Please immediately rescind this removal and put it back on the App Store." Aaron, in his interview with CNBC, compared ICEBlock to apps like Waze and others that allow drivers to report sightings of law enforcement officers on public roads so they can warn each other about and avoid getting speeding tickets. CNBC has requested comment from Apple on Aaron's remarks. "We created the App Store to be a safe and trusted place to discover apps," Apple said in a statement to NBC News on Thursday. "Based on information we've received from law enforcement about the safety risks associated with ICEBlock , we have removed it and similar apps from the App Store," the company said. Google on Friday joined Apple in removing from its online store other apps that can be used to anonymously report sightings of ICE agents and other authorities. Google's store had not carried ICEBlock, which exploded in popularity over the summer after Trump administration officials criticized it. "ICEBlock was never available on Google Play, but we removed similar apps for violations of our policies," a Google spokesperson told NBC News. The spokesperson said Google was not contacted by the Justice Department about its offering of such apps. Apple's dropping of ICEBlock came after direct pressure from Attorney General Pam Bondi , and amid controversy over the Trump administration's aggressive enforcement of immigration law with ICE agents and other authorities. The FBI said last week that a gunman whose attack on a Dallas ICE facility led to the deaths of two detained immigrants and the wounding of a third detainee had recently searched apps tracking the presence of ICE agents. The gunman, Joshua Jahn, intended to kill ICE agents in the attack, which ended with him fatally shooting himself, authorities said. Bondi, in a statement that the Justice Department sent CNBC on Friday, said, "We reached out to Apple [Thursday] demanding they remove the ICEBlock app from their App Store — and Apple did so." "ICEBlock is designed to put ICE agents at risk just for doing their jobs, and violence against law enforcement is an intolerable red line that cannot be crossed," Bondi said. "This Department of Justice will continue making every effort to protect our brave federal law enforcement officers, who risk their lives every day to keep Americans safe." Trump administration border czar Tom Homan, in an interview Thursday night with Fox News' Sean Hannity, said, "They're gonna investigate these people who put these apps up — because it puts law enforcement at great risk." ICEBlock became the top social networking app in Apple's App Store shortly after White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt condemned the app during a June 30 briefing. CNN that same day had published an article on the app that quoted Aaron as saying that he developed ICEBlock after seeing the Trump administration's deportation efforts escalate. "When I saw what was happening in this country, I wanted to do something to fight back," Aaron said at the time, suggesting that the immigration enforcement efforts were reminiscent of Nazi Germany. extraction.body: Nearly a year after pulling ICEBlock and similar apps from the App Store, Apple explained its decision to a sitting congressman in a July 2026 letter: real-time location data on ICE officers, the company argues, could function as a tracking users map for violence. Apple's App Store removal decisions are under congressional scrutiny following the October 2025 takedown of ICEBlock and similar ICE-tracking applications. Apple's explanation centers on the risk that precise location data could endanger not only federal officers but also protesters, detainees, and bystanders nearby. Precise location information about ICE personnel could expose the positions of protesters, detainees, and nearby civilians, Apple told Rep. Jamie Raskin in its July 2026 letter, according to CNN. The company described that combination as a potential roadmap for targeted violence. Apple said it observed a notable increase in ICE operations and threats against ICE personnel during the period surrounding the October 2025 removals. The company also pointed to safety concerns raised by then-Attorney General Pam Bondi following a September 2025 shooting at an ICE facility in Dallas, according to CNN and AppleInsider. Separately, Apple told ICEBlock creator Joshua Aaron that the app violated App Store rules concerning objectionable, defamatory, discriminatory, or mean-spirited content, according to Uniladtech. Rep. Raskin is pressing Apple to justify its removal decision independently, arguing the available evidence does not connect ICEBlock to the Dallas shooting. Raskin's position is that Apple's rationale deserves independent scrutiny. According to CNN, he said there was no publicly established evidence linking ICEBlock to the Dallas shooting and asked Apple to conduct a new, independent policy review. His investigation covers both Apple's and Google's app stores and examines potential effects on constitutionally protected speech. The scope reflects a broader unresolved concern: whether the removal was an independent platform decision or one shaped by pressure from federal officials. The ICEBlock app's own website states the removal followed pressure from the Trump administration, a self-published characterization that Apple has not adopted in its public statements, according to iceblock.app. Apple has publicly framed its action as a response to safety information received from law enforcement. Neither Apple's account nor Raskin's position has been established conclusively by available reporting. The ICEBlock dispute surfaces a largely opaque process that determines which politically significant tools survive on the world's most-used mobile software marketplace. Apple's platform decisions can remove access to politically significant tools without a transparent public process. For users whose only software gateway is the App Store, that power carries real civic weight. The ICEBlock case puts that dynamic in sharp relief. One company, acting on information provided by government officials, can determine which civic and political applications remain broadly available , a dynamic echoed by other cases involving a surveillance app built to target dissidents. How much evidence does Apple require before flagging a location-based app as a safety threat? And how clearly does it explain that standard to developers and users? Those thresholds, largely undisclosed right now, shape what kinds of community-reporting tools can exist on the platform at all. A congressional inquiry that compels more disclosure could reshape how Apple documents and explains future sensitive-app reviews. That shift would bring accountability to a process that currently operates without meaningful public visibility. extraction.body: Apple says its decision to remove ICEBlock and similar platforms from the app store last year was prompted by concerns — including those raised by the Trump administration — about agent safety following a fatal shooting that left two detainees dead at a Dallas Immigration and Customs Enforcement office. Apple’s explanation came in a July letter to Rep. Jamie Raskin, a Maryland Democrat and ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, who earlier this year launched an investigation into the Justice Department’s role in the removal of the apps from Apple’s and Google’s app stores and the impact on constitutionally protected speech. Raskin said the move suggests that Apple may be “working with the government to violate its customers’ First Amendment rights to record and report on the activities of their own government” in a response letter sent Monday to Apple’s senior director of government affairs, Timothy Powderly. Raskin added that there’s “no evidence” such apps were used to conduct the Dallas shooting and directed the company to conduct a new, independent review as to whether the apps violate Apple’s policies. The letters shed new light on the removal of the ICE tracking apps. The apps had sparked intense backlash from Trump administration officials, who claimed they put agents’ safety at risk. But the apps’ creators and proponents argued the apps were simply a way for users to avoid contact with law enforcement and bore little difference in how Apple and Google maps let users alert others to police speed traps. ICEBlock let users add a pin on a map when they saw agents operating in their area; other users within a five-mile radius would then receive a push alert notifying them of the sighting. Similar apps cropped up around the same time. ICEBlock creator Joshua Aaron sued Trump administration officials in December, claiming the government abused its power and infringed on his free speech by pushing Apple to remove the app. Aaron has called the claim that ICEBlock was designed to harm law enforcement officers “patently false.” The officials, including then-Attorney General Pam Bondi, have moved to dismiss the case, denying they were directly responsible for the app’s removal and therefore rejecting the First Amendment violation claim. Raskin’s inquiry could reignite a fraught political issue for Apple that began under previous CEO Tim Cook, at a time when new CEO John Ternus is attempting to focus the company’s efforts on AI and hardware innovation. Apple did not immediately respond to CNN’s request for comment. The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, has stood by its claim that ICE tracking apps endanger agents. “Our law officers are facing an over 1,600% increase in assaults, a 3,300% increase in vehicle attacks, and an 8,000% increase in death threats,” a spokesperson for DHS said in a statement Monday. “Further, these apps are a method to interfere with law enforcement activities and harbor illegal aliens.” CNN has also reached out to the Justice Department for comment. Safety risk or First Amendment-protected speech? Apple said in its letter to Raskin that it approved ICEBlock for the app store in April 2025, after Aaron addressed “certain user privacy concerns” identified during its initial review process. The company says it was “attentive” to news coverage and backlash to the app in the subsequent months. Following the September 2025 Dallas ICE facility shooting, Bondi “expressed serious concerns to Apple that ICEBlock posed a threat to the safety of federal officers,” the company wrote. A 29-year-old gunman who opened fire at the facility killed two detainees and wounded another before taking his own life. The letter also points to reports on statements from officials such as FBI Director Kash Patel, who claimed at the time that the shooter had searched for apps that tracked ICE agents’ locations. And Apple noted a “significant increase in ICE activity and threats against ICE” at the time, which it said endangered both agents and detainees — and all of which the company says prompted a new review of the app. Ultimately, Apple determined ICE tracking apps violated its guidelines because they provided “precise location information about ICE officers (and, as a result, other individuals who may be in proximity to ICE agents, such as protestors or detainees), thus providing a potential roadmap for targeted violence and creating a significant risk of harm,” the company said in its letter. Apple “does not take decisions about removing apps from the App Store lightly, but acts when it must — especially when there are serious concerns that an app is creating safety risks,” it said in the letter, which is signed by Powderly. But Raskin raised questions about that justification in his Monday response to the company. Raskin noted that while the shooter may have searched for ICE tracking apps, “he did not need a tracking app to locate the fixed position of a government building” and “is reported to have found the address using an app that comes standard on Apple devices.” “There appears to be no direct connection between the Dallas incident and the apps you removed,” Raskin wrote. He also pointed to navigation apps still available within Apple’s app store that also track the real-time location of law enforcement officers. Raskin requested that Apple send a full list of the apps it removed following concerns from the Justice Department and conduct an independent review of those removal decisions. “Monitoring the actions of federal immigration authorities who have been deployed to (users’) neighborhoods … is a core First Amendment right and not a crime,” Raskin wrote.

extraction.body: The creator of ICEBlock, the app used to track local sightings of ICE agents and other law-enforcement authorities, has asked Apple to rescind its decision to drop the app from its online store. Joshua Aaron, the free app's creator, also blasted the Trump administration for pressuring Apple to ban the app over fears it could be used to harm U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents. "This is not about me, or ICEBlock," Aaron said in an interview on Friday with CNBC. "This is about our fundamental constitutional rights in this country being stripped away by this administration, and the powers that be who are capitulating to their requests," he said. "I'm incredibly disappointed with the decision that Apple made," Aaron said. "In almost every interview that I did, I was asked if I was afraid that Apple might take the app down, and my answer was always to defend Apple and say, you know, look, when this app was first submitted, it went through a heavy review process with both Apple's legal and senior officials in App Review." Aaron, who said that he is consulting an attorney about the situation, directly asked Apple to allow him to appeal its decision Thursday to drop the app, which became available last spring. He shared a screengrab of the message he sent Apple after the company notified him of the move. "There is no objectionable content in the app," Aaron wrote in that message, which noted Apple's review process. "There have been no changes to the content provided or the features in the app," he wrote. "Please immediately rescind this removal and put it back on the App Store." Aaron, in his interview with CNBC, compared ICEBlock to apps like Waze and others that allow drivers to report sightings of law enforcement officers on public roads so they can warn each other about and avoid getting speeding tickets. CNBC has requested comment from Apple on Aaron's remarks. "We created the App Store to be a safe and trusted place to discover apps," Apple said in a statement to NBC News on Thursday. "Based on information we've received from law enforcement about the safety risks associated with ICEBlock , we have removed it and similar apps from the App Store," the company said. Google on Friday joined Apple in removing from its online store other apps that can be used to anonymously report sightings of ICE agents and other authorities. Google's store had not carried ICEBlock, which exploded in popularity over the summer after Trump administration officials criticized it. "ICEBlock was never available on Google Play, but we removed similar apps for violations of our policies," a Google spokesperson told NBC News. The spokesperson said Google was not contacted by the Justice Department about its offering of such apps. Apple's dropping of ICEBlock came after direct pressure from Attorney General Pam Bondi , and amid controversy over the Trump administration's aggressive enforcement of immigration law with ICE agents and other authorities. The FBI said last week that a gunman whose attack on a Dallas ICE facility led to the deaths of two detained immigrants and the wounding of a third detainee had recently searched apps tracking the presence of ICE agents. The gunman, Joshua Jahn, intended to kill ICE agents in the attack, which ended with him fatally shooting himself, authorities said. Bondi, in a statement that the Justice Department sent CNBC on Friday, said, "We reached out to Apple [Thursday] demanding they remove the ICEBlock app from their App Store — and Apple did so." "ICEBlock is designed to put ICE agents at risk just for doing their jobs, and violence against law enforcement is an intolerable red line that cannot be crossed," Bondi said. "This Department of Justice will continue making every effort to protect our brave federal law enforcement officers, who risk their lives every day to keep Americans safe." Trump administration border czar Tom Homan, in an interview Thursday night with Fox News' Sean Hannity, said, "They're gonna investigate these people who put these apps up — because it puts law enforcement at great risk." ICEBlock became the top social networking app in Apple's App Store shortly after White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt condemned the app during a June 30 briefing. CNN that same day had published an article on the app that quoted Aaron as saying that he developed ICEBlock after seeing the Trump administration's deportation efforts escalate. "When I saw what was happening in this country, I wanted to do something to fight back," Aaron said at the time, suggesting that the immigration enforcement efforts were reminiscent of Nazi Germany. "We're literally watching history repeat itself." ICEBlock has been downloaded more than 1 million times since it was introduced this year, according to data provided to NBC News by the app tracking firm Appfigures. The app hit a high of nearly 114,000 downloads in a single day on July 1, a day after the CNN article about the app sparked criticism from the Trump administration. ICE's acting director, Todd Lyons , on June 30 said, "Advertising an app that basically paints a target on federal law enforcement officers' backs is sickening." "My officers and agents are already facing a 500% increase in assaults, and going on live television to announce an app that lets anyone zero in on their locations is like inviting violence against them with a national megaphone," Lyons said. But Aaron, in an NBC interview days later , called the Trump administration's criticism of ICEBlock "another right-wing fearmongering scare tactic."

extraction.body: Nearly a year after pulling ICEBlock and similar apps from the App Store, Apple explained its decision to a sitting congressman in a July 2026 letter: real-time location data on ICE officers, the company argues, could function as a tracking users map for violence. Apple's App Store removal decisions are under congressional scrutiny following the October 2025 takedown of ICEBlock and similar ICE-tracking applications. Apple's explanation centers on the risk that precise location data could endanger not only federal officers but also protesters, detainees, and bystanders nearby. Precise location information about ICE personnel could expose the positions of protesters, detainees, and nearby civilians, Apple told Rep. Jamie Raskin in its July 2026 letter, according to CNN. The company described that combination as a potential roadmap for targeted violence. Apple said it observed a notable increase in ICE operations and threats against ICE personnel during the period surrounding the October 2025 removals. The company also pointed to safety concerns raised by then-Attorney General Pam Bondi following a September 2025 shooting at an ICE facility in Dallas, according to CNN and AppleInsider. Separately, Apple told ICEBlock creator Joshua Aaron that the app violated App Store rules concerning objectionable, defamatory, discriminatory, or mean-spirited content, according to Uniladtech. Rep. Raskin is pressing Apple to justify its removal decision independently, arguing the available evidence does not connect ICEBlock to the Dallas shooting. Raskin's position is that Apple's rationale deserves independent scrutiny. According to CNN, he said there was no publicly established evidence linking ICEBlock to the Dallas shooting and asked Apple to conduct a new, independent policy review. His investigation covers both Apple's and Google's app stores and examines potential effects on constitutionally protected speech. The scope reflects a broader unresolved concern: whether the removal was an independent platform decision or one shaped by pressure from federal officials. The ICEBlock app's own website states the removal followed pressure from the Trump administration, a self-published characterization that Apple has not adopted in its public statements, according to iceblock.app. Apple has publicly framed its action as a response to safety information received from law enforcement. Neither Apple's account nor Raskin's position has been established conclusively by available reporting. The ICEBlock dispute surfaces a largely opaque process that determines which politically significant tools survive on the world's most-used mobile software marketplace. Apple's platform decisions can remove access to politically significant tools without a transparent public process. For users whose only software gateway is the App Store, that power carries real civic weight. The ICEBlock case puts that dynamic in sharp relief. One company, acting on information provided by government officials, can determine which civic and political applications remain broadly available , a dynamic echoed by other cases involving a surveillance app built to target dissidents. How much evidence does Apple require before flagging a location-based app as a safety threat? And how clearly does it explain that standard to developers and users? Those thresholds, largely undisclosed right now, shape what kinds of community-reporting tools can exist on the platform at all. A congressional inquiry that compels more disclosure could reshape how Apple documents and explains future sensitive-app reviews. That shift would bring accountability to a process that currently operates without meaningful public visibility. passages: Nearly a year after pulling ICEBlock and similar apps from the App Store, Apple explained its decision to a sitting congressman in a July 2026 letter: real-time location data on ICE officers, the company argues, could function as a tracking users map for violence.
Apple's App Store removal decisions are under congressional scrutiny following the October 2025 takedown of ICEBlock and similar ICE-tracking applications.
Apple's explanation centers on the risk that precise location data could endanger not only federal officers but also protesters, detainees, and bystanders nearby.

Precise location information about ICE personnel could expose the positions of protesters, detainees, and nearby civilians, Apple told Rep. Jamie Raskin in its July 2026 letter, according to CNN. The company described that combination as a potential roadmap for targeted violence.

Apple said it observed a notable increase in ICE operations and threats against ICE personnel during the period surrounding the October 2025 removals. The company also pointed to safety concerns raised by then-Attorney General Pam Bondi following a September 2025 shooting at an ICE facility in Dallas, according to CNN and AppleInsider.
Separately, Apple told ICEBlock creator Joshua Aaron that the app violated App Store rules concerning objectionable, defamatory, discriminatory, or mean-spirited content, according to Uniladtech.
Rep. Raskin is pressing Apple to justify its removal decision independently, arguing the available evidence does not connect ICEBlock to the Dallas shooting.

Raskin's position is that Apple's rationale deserves independent scrutiny. According to CNN, he said there was no publicly established evidence linking ICEBlock to the Dallas shooting and asked Apple to conduct a new, independent policy review.

His investigation covers both Apple's and Google's app stores and examines potential effects on constitutionally protected speech. The scope reflects a broader unresolved concern: whether the removal was an independent platform decision or one shaped by pressure from federal officials.

The ICEBlock app's own website states the removal followed pressure from the Trump administration, a self-published characterization that Apple has not adopted in its public statements, according to iceblock.app. Apple has publicly framed its action as a response to safety information received from law enforcement.
Neither Apple's account nor Raskin's position has been established conclusively by available reporting.
The ICEBlock dispute surfaces a largely opaque process that determines which politically significant tools survive on the world's most-used mobile software marketplace.

Apple's platform decisions can remove access to politically significant tools without a transparent public process. For users whose only software gateway is the App Store, that power carries real civic weight.

The ICEBlock case puts that dynamic in sharp relief. One company, acting on information provided by government officials, can determine which civic and political applications remain broadly available , a dynamic echoed by other cases involving a surveillance app built to target dissidents.

How much evidence does Apple require before flagging a location-based app as a safety threat? And how clearly does it explain that standard to developers and users? Those thresholds, largely undisclosed right now, shape what kinds of community-reporting tools can exist on the platform at all.

A congressional inquiry that compels more disclosure could reshape how Apple documents and explains future sensitive-app reviews. That shift would bring accountability to a process that currently operates without meaningful public visibility.

extraction.body: Apple says its decision to remove ICEBlock and similar platforms from the app store last year was prompted by concerns — including those raised by the Trump administration — about agent safety following a fatal shooting that left two detainees dead at a Dallas Immigration and Customs Enforcement office. Apple’s explanation came in a July letter to Rep. Jamie Raskin, a Maryland Democrat and ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, who earlier this year launched an investigation into the Justice Department’s role in the removal of the apps from Apple’s and Google’s app stores and the impact on constitutionally protected speech. Raskin said the move suggests that Apple may be “working with the government to violate its customers’ First Amendment rights to record and report on the activities of their own government” in a response letter sent Monday to Apple’s senior director of government affairs, Timothy Powderly. Raskin added that there’s “no evidence” such apps were used to conduct the Dallas shooting and directed the company to conduct a new, independent review as to whether the apps violate Apple’s policies. The letters shed new light on the removal of the ICE tracking apps. The apps had sparked intense backlash from Trump administration officials, who claimed they put agents’ safety at risk. But the apps’ creators and proponents argued the apps were simply a way for users to avoid contact with law enforcement and bore little difference in how Apple and Google maps let users alert others to police speed traps. ICEBlock let users add a pin on a map when they saw agents operating in their area; other users within a five-mile radius would then receive a push alert notifying them of the sighting. Similar apps cropped up around the same time. ICEBlock creator Joshua Aaron sued Trump administration officials in December, claiming the government abused its power and infringed on his free speech by pushing Apple to remove the app. Aaron has called the claim that ICEBlock was designed to harm law enforcement officers “patently false.” The officials, including then-Attorney General Pam Bondi, have moved to dismiss the case, denying they were directly responsible for the app’s removal and therefore rejecting the First Amendment violation claim. Raskin’s inquiry could reignite a fraught political issue for Apple that began under previous CEO Tim Cook, at a time when new CEO John Ternus is attempting to focus the company’s efforts on AI and hardware innovation. Apple did not immediately respond to CNN’s request for comment. The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, has stood by its claim that ICE tracking apps endanger agents. “Our law officers are facing an over 1,600% increase in assaults, a 3,300% increase in vehicle attacks, and an 8,000% increase in death threats,” a spokesperson for DHS said in a statement Monday. “Further, these apps are a method to interfere with law enforcement activities and harbor illegal aliens.” CNN has also reached out to the Justice Department for comment. Safety risk or First Amendment-protected speech? Apple said in its letter to Raskin that it approved ICEBlock for the app store in April 2025, after Aaron addressed “certain user privacy concerns” identified during its initial review process. The company says it was “attentive” to news coverage and backlash to the app in the subsequent months. Following the September 2025 Dallas ICE facility shooting, Bondi “expressed serious concerns to Apple that ICEBlock posed a threat to the safety of federal officers,” the company wrote. A 29-year-old gunman who opened fire at the facility killed two detainees and wounded another before taking his own life. The letter also points to reports on statements from officials such as FBI Director Kash Patel, who claimed at the time that the shooter had searched for apps that tracked ICE agents’ locations. And Apple noted a “significant increase in ICE activity and threats against ICE” at the time, which it said endangered both agents and detainees — and all of which the company says prompted a new review of the app. Ultimately, Apple determined ICE tracking apps violated its guidelines because they provided “precise location information about ICE officers (and, as a result, other individuals who may be in proximity to ICE agents, such as protestors or detainees), thus providing a potential roadmap for targeted violence and creating a significant risk of harm,” the company said in its letter. Apple “does not take decisions about removing apps from the App Store lightly, but acts when it must — especially when there are serious concerns that an app is creating safety risks,” it said in the letter, which is signed by Powderly. But Raskin raised questions about that justification in his Monday response to the company. Raskin noted that while the shooter may have searched for ICE tracking apps, “he did not need a tracking app to locate the fixed position of a government building” and “is reported to have found the address using an app that comes standard on Apple devices.” “There appears to be no direct connection between the Dallas incident and the apps you removed,” Raskin wrote. He also pointed to navigation apps still available within Apple’s app store that also track the real-time location of law enforcement officers. passages: Apple says its decision to remove ICEBlock and similar platforms from the app store last year was prompted by concerns — including those raised by the Trump administration — about agent safety following a fatal shooting that left two detainees dead at a Dallas Immigration and Customs Enforcement office.
Apple’s explanation came in a July letter to Rep.

Jamie Raskin, a Maryland Democrat and ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, who earlier this year launched an investigation into the Justice Department’s role in the removal of the apps from Apple’s and Google’s app stores and the impact on constitutionally protected speech.

Raskin said the move suggests that Apple may be “working with the government to violate its customers’ First Amendment rights to record and report on the activities of their own government” in a response letter sent Monday to Apple’s senior director of government affairs, Timothy Powderly.

Raskin added that there’s “no evidence” such apps were used to conduct the Dallas shooting and directed the company to conduct a new, independent review as to whether the apps violate Apple’s policies.
The letters shed new light on the removal of the ICE tracking apps.
The apps had sparked intense backlash from Trump administration officials, who claimed they put agents’ safety at risk.

But the apps’ creators and proponents argued the apps were simply a way for users to avoid contact with law enforcement and bore little difference in how Apple and Google maps let users alert others to police speed traps.
ICEBlock let users add a pin on a map when they saw agents operating in their area; other users within a five-mile radius would then receive a push alert notifying them of the sighting.
Similar apps cropped up around the same time.
ICEBlock creator Joshua Aaron sued Trump administration officials in December, claiming the government abused its power and infringed on his free speech by pushing Apple to remove the app.

Aaron has called the claim that ICEBlock was designed to harm law enforcement officers “patently false.” The officials, including then-Attorney General Pam Bondi, have moved to dismiss the case, denying they were directly responsible for the app’s removal and therefore rejecting the First Amendment violation claim.

Raskin’s inquiry could reignite a fraught political issue for Apple that began under previous CEO Tim Cook, at a time when new CEO John Ternus is attempting to focus the company’s efforts on AI and hardware innovation.
Apple did not immediately respond to CNN’s request for comment.
The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, has stood by its claim that ICE tracking apps endanger agents.
“Our law officers are facing an over 1,600% increase in assaults, a 3,300% increase in vehicle attacks, and an 8,000% increase in death threats,” a spokesperson for DHS said in a statement Monday.
“Further, these apps are a method to interfere with law enforcement activities and harbor illegal aliens.” CNN has also reached out to the Justice Department for comment.
Safety risk or First Amendment-protected speech?
Apple said in its letter to Raskin that it approved ICEBlock for the app store in April 2025, after Aaron addressed “certain user privacy concerns” identified during its initial review process.
The company says it was “attentive” to news coverage and backlash to the app in the subsequent months.
Following the September 2025 Dallas ICE facility shooting, Bondi “expressed serious concerns to Apple that ICEBlock posed a threat to the safety of federal officers,” the company wrote.
A 29-year-old gunman who opened fire at the facility killed two detainees and wounded another before taking his own life.
The letter also points to reports on statements from officials such as FBI Director Kash Patel, who claimed at the time that the shooter had searched for apps that tracked ICE agents’ locations.

And Apple noted a “significant increase in ICE activity and threats against ICE” at the time, which it said endangered both agents and detainees — and all of which the company says prompted a new review of the app.

Ultimately, Apple determined ICE tracking apps violated its guidelines because they provided “precise location information about ICE officers (and, as a result, other individuals who may be in proximity to ICE agents, such as protestors or detainees), thus providing a potential roadmap for targeted violence and creating a significant risk of harm,” the company said in its letter.

Apple “does not take decisions about removing apps from the App Store lightly, but acts when it must — especially when there are serious concerns that an app is creating safety risks,” it said in the letter, which is signed by Powderly.
But Raskin raised questions about that justification in his Monday response to the company.

Raskin noted that while the shooter may have searched for ICE tracking apps, “he did not need a tracking app to locate the fixed position of a government building” and “is reported to have found the address using an app that comes standard on Apple devices.” “There appears to be no direct connection between the Dallas incident and the apps you removed,” Raskin wrote.
He also pointed to navigation apps still available within Apple’s app store that also track the real-time location of law enforcement officers.
Raskin requested that Apple send a full list of the apps it removed following concerns from the Justice Department and conduct an independent review of those removal decisions.
“Monitoring the actions of federal immigration authorities who have been deployed to (users’) neighborhoods … is a core First Amendment right and not a crime,” Raskin wrote.

CBP routinely runs ads discouraging illegal immigration.
These spots instead feature Trump heavily, tout his tax cuts , attack communism and recycle language from his 2024 campaign.

extraction.body: Taxpayer money from U.S. Customs and Border Protection funded the pro-Trump television ads that have drawn bipartisan scrutiny just weeks before November's midterm election , The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday. President Donald Trump personally pushed for the ads and was involved in creating them, the Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter. The revelation puts a CBP, part of the Department of Homeland Security, behind a campaign that looks far different from its traditional public messaging. CBP routinely runs ads discouraging illegal immigration. These spots instead feature Trump heavily, tout his tax cuts , attack communism and recycle language from his 2024 campaign. One ad declares that "America will never be a communist country" as images of Trump fill the screen. Another revives his "final battle" message from the 2024 race and attacks the political establishment and news media. The ads have already aired thousands of times nationally and locally. CNBC previously reported that more than $1.2 million had been spent airing two of the spots, according to AdImpact, which tracks political advertising spending. Democrats and at least one Republican senator have questioned whether taxpayer dollars should be used for ads centered so heavily on Trump. Some Democrats in Congress are now calling for investigations into whether money appropriated for border protection is being used to promote the president's political message. "It appears DHS has dedicated $20 million to this outrageous scheme," Sens. Patty Murray , D-Wash., and Chris Murphy , D-Conn., wrote in a letter to DHS on Tuesday, saying the department tapped money provided to CBP through Republicans' " One Big Beautiful Bill Act ." Federal contracting records show CBP awarded $20 million to Maryland-based advertising firm LMD Agency on Sept. 20 for a "National Media Campaign." The one-year contract was fully funded at the time of the award. The award came one day after the Office of Management and Budget approved the release of $20 million to CBP under a "Commemorative Events" funding line. The public contract record does not specify what the "National Media Campaign" entails or establish that LMD worked on the Trump ads. LMD has previously performed advertising work for agencies within the Department of Homeland Security, federal procurement records show. LMD did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on whether its $20 million contract is connected to the ads, whether it is playing a role in the ad campaign or whether additional advertisements or media buys are planned. CBP did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the ads or the procurement contract. Blowback to the ads also spread to federal regulators Tuesday. Watchdog group Public Citizen filed a complaint with the Federal Communications Commission and Federal Trade Commission urging broadcasters to stop airing the ads, while separately asking the Government Accountability Office and Office of Special Counsel last Friday to investigate alleged violations of federal propaganda restrictions and the Hatch Act, which restricts the involvement of federal government employees in political campaigns. The White House defended the campaign Tuesday, calling the spots public service announcements. “These public service announcements are about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad,” a White House spokesperson told CNBC. “The ad is educational and unapologetically patriotic.
