extraction.body: The Department of Homeland Security has tapped $20 million to pay for the campaign-style ads glorifying President Trump that have drawn widespread criticism from Republicans and Democrats as a blatant misuse of taxpayer dollars that probably runs afoul of anti-propaganda law. “Don’t let the Fake News get away with their lies about our epic Public Service Announcements that have been running on tv,” White House communications director Steven Cheung posted Sunday on X. But the Republican administration's ads have attracted mounting criticism, including from members of Trump’s party. “It shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) told reporters. “It would not have been something that I would have done," said Sen. Multiple legal experts said the ads appear to run afoul of federal statutes, including a law against congressionally appropriated funds being used for “publicity or propaganda” and a law that limits the partisan political activities of government employees. They said the new ads, which are airing on network and cable TV and streaming, differ from other administrations’ PSAs because they aren’t designed to help Americans access any specific program. The first ad in the campaign, which began airing Wednesday, features clips of Trump talking about defeating communism interspersed with onscreen text promoting the “largest tax cuts in history,” “reigniting American manufacturing” and a call to “defend law and order and police.” Later in the week, a second ad began running, showing scenic videos of Mt. Rushmore at night with quotes and clips from Trump’s Fourth of July weekend speech there honoring the country’s 250th anniversary. The latest of the ads, a spot that first aired over the weekend, is virtually identical to an ad for Trump’s Republican reelection campaign in 2024. It shows him walking down a hallway as his voice can be heard warning of a “final battle” against “globalists” and “warmongers.” All three ads end with a message that says: "Paid for by the U.S. “You watch all three ads, they’re sheer propaganda,” said Richard Painter, a former White House ethics advisor under Republican President George W. “This is increasingly looking like what authoritarian governments do to promote their leaders.” The heightened scrutiny comes as the Trump administration has increased spending on the ads and bought time on popular TV shows, including college football and National Football League programming. With both chambers of Congress led by Republicans, any oversight would probably have to come from Trump's allies, decreasing the likelihood of hearings or other accountability efforts before November's midterm elections. In a letter Tuesday to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, two top Democratic senators said that the money is being drawn from Trump's so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act and was supposed to go to U.S. "We should not have to remind you that using government funding to create or air political ads like the ones that have been running over the last few days is illegal and a shockingly corrupt misuse of taxpayer dollars," wrote Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut, the ranking Democrat on the subcommittee that handles Homeland Security funding. The senators, in their letter to Mullin, demanded answers within the next 48 hours about “how this president is literally stealing their tax dollars to air campaign ads celebrating himself.” They asked the secretary whether the department plans to use additional federal funds to air these ads or create new ones, and if so to share contracting information with the Congress. They also asked Mullin whether he had spoken to Trump about using the taxpayer funds for the ads. The political uproar over Trump's hagiographic ads has not abated as critics on the left and right raise alarms about the use of taxpayer funds, particularly so close to the midterm elections. Ad spend tops $2.5 million; criticism and legal scrutiny grow Sen. Thom Tillis, a Republican from North Carolina, compared Trump's ads to those used by authoritarian former leader Viktor Orban of Hungary. John Kennedy, a Republican from Louisiana, said on CBS' “Face the Nation” on Sunday that no public official should spend public money on private ads for themselves. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican who lost his primary to a Trump-backed challenger, had his own harsh words for the administration on Monday. “Don’t worry, using taxpayer dollars to run ominous campaign ads of the President has been done before and is completely legal … in banana republics,” he wrote on X. Data from the outside firm AdImpact shows more than $2.5 million was spent on the three ads over the last seven days. The senators said that Homeland Security has committed $20 million to the campaign. A person who was unauthorized to discuss the situation and granted anonymity confirmed the findings, which were first reported by the Wall Street Journal. Trump's ads use taxpayer dollars, probably skirting the law The unusual ad campaign comes as Republicans face an increasingly volatile midterm election season with their control of the House and Senate — and Trump's future agenda — all at risk. Democrats are gearing up for vast oversight of Trump and his administration if they seize power, and impeachment is not off the table. House Democrats said Trump's director of the Office of Management and Budget, Russell Vought, moved the money from Homeland Security to the ad campaign on Sept. The Homeland Security funds are part of a whopping $175 billion Congress gave the department in the Big Beautiful Bill as part of his immigration enforcement and deportation agenda. Democrats voted against that package, which Trump signed into law in the summer last year, in part because of its steep cuts to Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, known as SNAP. Henry Cuellar of Texas, the ranking Democrat on the Homeland Security subcommittee, said that after gutting $1 trillion from Medicaid and social services and “more than quadrupling funding for mass deportations, it turns out the Trump administration used Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill to pay for President Trump’s political ads.” They said when Democrats regain control, they "will work to uncover and reverse misuses of taxpayer money like this and hold those who abused their power accountable.” What's also striking about the administration's use of taxpayer dollars for the ads is that Trump's own political campaign committee MAGA Inc. is sitting on hundreds of millions of dollars of funding that could be used during the midterm season. Groups aligned with MAGA Inc. have started shelling out funds for the House and Senate races. In defending the campaign, the White House published a list of PSAs from recent Democratic and Republican administrations.

extraction.body: The Department of Homeland Security has tapped $20 million to pay for the campaign-style ads glorifying President Trump that have drawn widespread criticism from Republicans and Democrats as a blatant misuse of taxpayer dollars that probably runs afoul of anti-propaganda law. “Don’t let the Fake News get away with their lies about our epic Public Service Announcements that have been running on tv,” White House communications director Steven Cheung posted Sunday on X. But the Republican administration's ads have attracted mounting criticism, including from members of Trump’s party. “It shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) told reporters. “It would not have been something that I would have done," said Sen. Multiple legal experts said the ads appear to run afoul of federal statutes, including a law against congressionally appropriated funds being used for “publicity or propaganda” and a law that limits the partisan political activities of government employees. They said the new ads, which are airing on network and cable TV and streaming, differ from other administrations’ PSAs because they aren’t designed to help Americans access any specific program. The first ad in the campaign, which began airing Wednesday, features clips of Trump talking about defeating communism interspersed with onscreen text promoting the “largest tax cuts in history,” “reigniting American manufacturing” and a call to “defend law and order and police.” Later in the week, a second ad began running, showing scenic videos of Mt. Rushmore at night with quotes and clips from Trump’s Fourth of July weekend speech there honoring the country’s 250th anniversary. The latest of the ads, a spot that first aired over the weekend, is virtually identical to an ad for Trump’s Republican reelection campaign in 2024. It shows him walking down a hallway as his voice can be heard warning of a “final battle” against “globalists” and “warmongers.” All three ads end with a message that says: "Paid for by the U.S. “You watch all three ads, they’re sheer propaganda,” said Richard Painter, a former White House ethics advisor under Republican President George W. “This is increasingly looking like what authoritarian governments do to promote their leaders.” The heightened scrutiny comes as the Trump administration has increased spending on the ads and bought time on popular TV shows, including college football and National Football League programming. With both chambers of Congress led by Republicans, any oversight would probably have to come from Trump's allies, decreasing the likelihood of hearings or other accountability efforts before November's midterm elections. In a letter Tuesday to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, two top Democratic senators said that the money is being drawn from Trump's so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act and was supposed to go to U.S. "We should not have to remind you that using government funding to create or air political ads like the ones that have been running over the last few days is illegal and a shockingly corrupt misuse of taxpayer dollars," wrote Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut, the ranking Democrat on the subcommittee that handles Homeland Security funding. The senators, in their letter to Mullin, demanded answers within the next 48 hours about “how this president is literally stealing their tax dollars to air campaign ads celebrating himself.” They asked the secretary whether the department plans to use additional federal funds to air these ads or create new ones, and if so to share contracting information with the Congress. They also asked Mullin whether he had spoken to Trump about using the taxpayer funds for the ads. The political uproar over Trump's hagiographic ads has not abated as critics on the left and right raise alarms about the use of taxpayer funds, particularly so close to the midterm elections. Ad spend tops $2.5 million; criticism and legal scrutiny grow Sen. Thom Tillis, a Republican from North Carolina, compared Trump's ads to those used by authoritarian former leader Viktor Orban of Hungary. John Kennedy, a Republican from Louisiana, said on CBS' “Face the Nation” on Sunday that no public official should spend public money on private ads for themselves. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican who lost his primary to a Trump-backed challenger, had his own harsh words for the administration on Monday. “Don’t worry, using taxpayer dollars to run ominous campaign ads of the President has been done before and is completely legal … in banana republics,” he wrote on X. Data from the outside firm AdImpact shows more than $2.5 million was spent on the three ads over the last seven days. The senators said that Homeland Security has committed $20 million to the campaign. A person who was unauthorized to discuss the situation and granted anonymity confirmed the findings, which were first reported by the Wall Street Journal. Trump's ads use taxpayer dollars, probably skirting the law The unusual ad campaign comes as Republicans face an increasingly volatile midterm election season with their control of the House and Senate — and Trump's future agenda — all at risk. Democrats are gearing up for vast oversight of Trump and his administration if they seize power, and impeachment is not off the table. House Democrats said Trump's director of the Office of Management and Budget, Russell Vought, moved the money from Homeland Security to the ad campaign on Sept. The Homeland Security funds are part of a whopping $175 billion Congress gave the department in the Big Beautiful Bill as part of his immigration enforcement and deportation agenda. Democrats voted against that package, which Trump signed into law in the summer last year, in part because of its steep cuts to Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, known as SNAP. Henry Cuellar of Texas, the ranking Democrat on the Homeland Security subcommittee, said that after gutting $1 trillion from Medicaid and social services and “more than quadrupling funding for mass deportations, it turns out the Trump administration used Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill to pay for President Trump’s political ads.” They said when Democrats regain control, they "will work to uncover and reverse misuses of taxpayer money like this and hold those who abused their power accountable.” What's also striking about the administration's use of taxpayer dollars for the ads is that Trump's own political campaign committee MAGA Inc. is sitting on hundreds of millions of dollars of funding that could be used during the midterm season. Groups aligned with MAGA Inc. have started shelling out funds for the House and Senate races. In defending the campaign, the White House published a list of PSAs from recent Democratic and Republican administrations.

sources.title: Trump is rebranding ‘Artificial Intelligence’ as ‘Super Intelligence’. Here’s what will change
passages: By rebranding the domain to "Super Intelligence," the White House aims to project awe, authority, and undeniable dominance, aligning the technology's label with what Trump describes as an economic and strategic transformation bigger than the Industrial Revolution or the internet combined.

United States President Donald Trump has announced that the federal government will officially eliminate the term "Artificial Intelligence" (AI) from all official United States government documentation.

In characteristic fashion, Trump publicly outlined the qualification standard for the incoming official on social media: "Only High IQ individuals need apply!" The data centre infra push To power the massive cluster infrastructure required for "Super Intelligence," the administration has launched an aggressive push for power grid expansion and data centre construction.

The polling process went through several distinct iterations: The president floated options including "Superior Intelligence," "Extreme Intelligence," "Supreme Intelligence," and "Super Intelligence." Trump publicly dropped "Supreme Intelligence" after it lost traction in early voting.
"Whoever wins SI, wins" In his UN speech, Trump explicitly linked the terminology "Super Intelligence" (SI) to America's strategic competition with China.
He argued that "Artificial Intelligence" was "inaccurate and ineloquent," urging citizens to vote on alternative naming conventions.

Addressing local communities and municipal leaders who have expressed concern over energy consumption, land use, and noise pollution from hyperscale facilities, Trump warned that opposing data centres would leave regions "backwards and poor," concluding a public memo with the directive: "Let Data Reign." During a broadcasted onstage telephone conversation with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Trump hailed data centres as "the oil of the next 20, 25 years," asserting that abundant energy and compute capacity represent the primary wealth generators of the 21st century.

Addressing world leaders at the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York on Tuesday, Trump argued that the word "artificial" fundamentally diminishes the technology's true power, making it sound "fake" or synthetic rather than revolutionary.

The formation of the "AI Force" Days prior to his UN address, Trump announced the creation of an "AI Force" — a specialised military branch and administrative body built on the blueprint of the US Space Force created during his first presidential term.

Trump rejected these international frameworks outright, describing proposed global oversight as a "globalist scheme" that threatens to shackle American innovation while giving adversaries an open field.
Over the course of this month, the Trump administration unveiled several key initiatives designed to cement the nation's technological engine.
It's actually amazing," Trump told the UN assembly.

"From this point forward, all of United States documents, and hopefully the world's, will be changed to use the much more accurate term 'super' as opposed to 'artificial.' In other words, welcome to the new world of superintelligence — SI.

extraction.body: United States President Donald Trump has announced that the federal government will officially eliminate the term "Artificial Intelligence" (AI) from all official United States government documentation. In its place, the administration is mandating the adoption of "Super Intelligence" — or simply "SI". Addressing world leaders at the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York on Tuesday, Trump argued that the word "artificial" fundamentally diminishes the technology's true power, making it sound "fake" or synthetic rather than revolutionary. The moniker change is far more than a simple linguistic tweak. It signals a posture shift in Washington's national technology policy. The administration is aggressively accelerating domestic data centre deployment, rejecting international regulatory frameworks, forming an "AI Force" military branch, and framing advanced computing not as a speculative safety risk, but as an existential geopolitical race against China that America must win at all costs. "From this point forward, all of United States documents, and hopefully the world's, will be changed to use the much more accurate term 'super' as opposed to 'artificial.' In other words, welcome to the new world of superintelligence — SI. Why "Artificial" sounded "Fake" According to Trump, the primary flaw of the term "artificial intelligence" lies in its connotation. The word "artificial," he argued, implies something counterfeit, weak, or imitation. It's actually amazing," Trump told the UN assembly. By rebranding the domain to "Super Intelligence," the White House aims to project awe, authority, and undeniable dominance, aligning the technology's label with what Trump describes as an economic and strategic transformation bigger than the Industrial Revolution or the internet combined. Over the preceding weekend, Trump posted open polls on Truth Social and X, asking millions of followers to vote on a replacement name for AI. He argued that "Artificial Intelligence" was "inaccurate and ineloquent," urging citizens to vote on alternative naming conventions. The polling process went through several distinct iterations: The president floated options including "Superior Intelligence," "Extreme Intelligence," "Supreme Intelligence," and "Super Intelligence." Trump publicly dropped "Supreme Intelligence" after it lost traction in early voting. He noted with a touch of humour that voters were reacting negatively to "Supreme" due to its subconscious association with the US Supreme Court. The poll narrowed down to "Superior Intelligence" versus "Extreme Intelligence," with "Super Intelligence" emerging as the decisive executive selection ahead of his UN speech. While Trump acknowledged with candor during his speech — "Let's see if I have any power. Maybe I do, and maybe I don't, we're gonna find out pretty soon" — the directive stands as an official mandate for federal agency compliance. "Whoever wins SI, wins" In his UN speech, Trump explicitly linked the terminology "Super Intelligence" (SI) to America's strategic competition with China. The administration rejects the view of AI as a shared global resource requiring collective international stewardship, framing it instead as a zero-sum contest for global hegemony. "Whoever wins AI, you have to remember this... and now I say, whoever wins SI, whoever wins superintelligence, wins," Trump stated. The president asserted that the United States is currently leading China "by a lot" in frontier model capabilities, hardware design, and infrastructure deployment. Washington will maintain this gap by aggressively expanding domestic capabilities and clearing federal regulatory hurdles. UN Secretary-General António Guterres and UN Human Rights Chief Volker Türk have repeatedly advocated for global AI governance frameworks, mandatory safety audits, human rights safeguards, and international treaty standards. Trump rejected these international frameworks outright, describing proposed global oversight as a "globalist scheme" that threatens to shackle American innovation while giving adversaries an open field. The administration’s policy explicitly prioritises domestic acceleration over multinational consensus, signalling to foreign capitals that Washington will not sign binding international AI safety pacts that limit model scale or compute capacity. Behind the US AI policy overhaul The renaming to "Super Intelligence" is backed by major structural shifts within the US executive branch. Over the course of this month, the Trump administration unveiled several key initiatives designed to cement the nation's technological engine. The formation of the "AI Force" Days prior to his UN address, Trump announced the creation of an "AI Force" — a specialised military branch and administrative body built on the blueprint of the US Space Force created during his first presidential term. The AI Force will be tasked with defending American digital infrastructure, securing supply chains for advanced semiconductors, preventing intellectual property theft by foreign actors, and integrating advanced autonomous software directly into US defence doctrines. Search for a new "AI Czar" Alongside the AI Force, the White House announced an open search for a new "AI & Crypto Czar" to head federal tech strategy. This post was previously held by Silicon Valley venture capitalist David Sacks, who concluded his term as a special government employee earlier this year. In characteristic fashion, Trump publicly outlined the qualification standard for the incoming official on social media: "Only High IQ individuals need apply!" The data centre infra push To power the massive cluster infrastructure required for "Super Intelligence," the administration has launched an aggressive push for power grid expansion and data centre construction. Addressing local communities and municipal leaders who have expressed concern over energy consumption, land use, and noise pollution from hyperscale facilities, Trump warned that opposing data centres would leave regions "backwards and poor," concluding a public memo with the directive: "Let Data Reign." During a broadcasted onstage telephone conversation with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Trump hailed data centres as "the oil of the next 20, 25 years," asserting that abundant energy and compute capacity represent the primary wealth generators of the 21st century. How Trump dismissed an existential risk Trump's enthusiastic push for "Super Intelligence" stands in stark opposition to a growing chorus of warnings from AI safety researchers, whistleblowers, and tech executives. Notably, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and former research personnel who recently resigned from top labs issued public warnings regarding the catastrophic risks of losing human control over self-improving systems.

House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA), Vice President JD Vance, White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, and other Cabinet members were in attendance. The meeting took place as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has repeatedly called for congressional leaders to help slow down the development of AI due to fears that mankind may not be able to control it. Trump downplayed the fears in his brief remarks to reporters on Tuesday. “The one thing that we all have in common is we love our country, and we love the world, and we want to make sure it’s a safe place,” the president said. “And what we’re talking about today will make it a better place and a much safer place.” The president has insisted the U.S. must remain a leader in the AI race with China. “We have a very big lead, and we’re going to keep our lead, and it’s a very positive thing,” Trump said. “It’s an amazing industry. There are those that say it’s bigger than the industrial revolution.” TRUMP LAUNCHES AMERICA.GOV AI WEBSITE TO MAKE GOVERNMENT SERVICES MORE ACCESSIBLE Trump also pointed to the Justice Department and the FBI as key regulators of AI while answering reporter questions. Earlier on Tuesday, Trump signed an executive order directing all federal government agencies to integrate their public-facing services with America.gov.

coreStoryFacts.text: By rebranding the domain to "Super Intelligence," the White House aims to project awe, authority, and undeniable dominance, aligning the technology's label with what Trump describes as an economic and strategic transformation bigger than the Industrial Revolution or the internet combined.

United States President Donald Trump has announced that the federal government will officially eliminate the term "Artificial Intelligence" (AI) from all official United States government documentation.

In characteristic fashion, Trump publicly outlined the qualification standard for the incoming official on social media: "Only High IQ individuals need apply!" The data centre infra push To power the massive cluster infrastructure required for "Super Intelligence," the administration has launched an aggressive push for power grid expansion and data centre construction.

The polling process went through several distinct iterations: The president floated options including "Superior Intelligence," "Extreme Intelligence," "Supreme Intelligence," and "Super Intelligence." Trump publicly dropped "Supreme Intelligence" after it lost traction in early voting.
"Whoever wins SI, wins" In his UN speech, Trump explicitly linked the terminology "Super Intelligence" (SI) to America's strategic competition with China.
He argued that "Artificial Intelligence" was "inaccurate and ineloquent," urging citizens to vote on alternative naming conventions.

Addressing local communities and municipal leaders who have expressed concern over energy consumption, land use, and noise pollution from hyperscale facilities, Trump warned that opposing data centres would leave regions "backwards and poor," concluding a public memo with the directive: "Let Data Reign." During a broadcasted onstage telephone conversation with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Trump hailed data centres as "the oil of the next 20, 25 years," asserting that abundant energy and compute capacity represent the primary wealth generators of the 21st century.

Addressing world leaders at the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York on Tuesday, Trump argued that the word "artificial" fundamentally diminishes the technology's true power, making it sound "fake" or synthetic rather than revolutionary.

The formation of the "AI Force" Days prior to his UN address, Trump announced the creation of an "AI Force" — a specialised military branch and administrative body built on the blueprint of the US Space Force created during his first presidential term.

Trump rejected these international frameworks outright, describing proposed global oversight as a "globalist scheme" that threatens to shackle American innovation while giving adversaries an open field.
Over the course of this month, the Trump administration unveiled several key initiatives designed to cement the nation's technological engine.
It's actually amazing," Trump told the UN assembly.

"From this point forward, all of United States documents, and hopefully the world's, will be changed to use the much more accurate term 'super' as opposed to 'artificial.' In other words, welcome to the new world of superintelligence — SI.
President Donald Trump on Saturday announced he is forming an "AI Force" and plans to name an artificial intelligence czar soon.
"For this purpose, I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force, which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my First Term," Trump wrote on Truth Social .
"Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!" Trump described AI as an economic and strategic priority, predicting it could account for "possibly as much as 25%" of U.S. gross domestic product, or GDP.
Trump called concerns about artificial intelligence another in a list of what he described as "hoaxes" promoted by Democrats.

“We’re going to be signing a document today at about 5 o’clock, renaming artificial intelligence because it’s not artificial,” Trump said while flanked by tech billionaire Elon Musk , Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, and other AI leaders.

Trump also pointed to the Justice Department and the FBI as key regulators of AI while answering reporter questions.

extraction.body: United States President Donald Trump has announced that the federal government will officially eliminate the term "Artificial Intelligence" (AI) from all official United States government documentation. In its place, the administration is mandating the adoption of "Super Intelligence" — or simply "SI". Addressing world leaders at the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York on Tuesday, Trump argued that the word "artificial" fundamentally diminishes the technology's true power, making it sound "fake" or synthetic rather than revolutionary. The moniker change is far more than a simple linguistic tweak. It signals a posture shift in Washington's national technology policy. The administration is aggressively accelerating domestic data centre deployment, rejecting international regulatory frameworks, forming an "AI Force" military branch, and framing advanced computing not as a speculative safety risk, but as an existential geopolitical race against China that America must win at all costs. "From this point forward, all of United States documents, and hopefully the world's, will be changed to use the much more accurate term 'super' as opposed to 'artificial.' In other words, welcome to the new world of superintelligence — SI. Why "Artificial" sounded "Fake" According to Trump, the primary flaw of the term "artificial intelligence" lies in its connotation. The word "artificial," he argued, implies something counterfeit, weak, or imitation. It's actually amazing," Trump told the UN assembly. By rebranding the domain to "Super Intelligence," the White House aims to project awe, authority, and undeniable dominance, aligning the technology's label with what Trump describes as an economic and strategic transformation bigger than the Industrial Revolution or the internet combined. Over the preceding weekend, Trump posted open polls on Truth Social and X, asking millions of followers to vote on a replacement name for AI. He argued that "Artificial Intelligence" was "inaccurate and ineloquent," urging citizens to vote on alternative naming conventions. The polling process went through several distinct iterations: The president floated options including "Superior Intelligence," "Extreme Intelligence," "Supreme Intelligence," and "Super Intelligence." Trump publicly dropped "Supreme Intelligence" after it lost traction in early voting. He noted with a touch of humour that voters were reacting negatively to "Supreme" due to its subconscious association with the US Supreme Court. The poll narrowed down to "Superior Intelligence" versus "Extreme Intelligence," with "Super Intelligence" emerging as the decisive executive selection ahead of his UN speech. While Trump acknowledged with candor during his speech — "Let's see if I have any power. Maybe I do, and maybe I don't, we're gonna find out pretty soon" — the directive stands as an official mandate for federal agency compliance. "Whoever wins SI, wins" In his UN speech, Trump explicitly linked the terminology "Super Intelligence" (SI) to America's strategic competition with China. The administration rejects the view of AI as a shared global resource requiring collective international stewardship, framing it instead as a zero-sum contest for global hegemony. "Whoever wins AI, you have to remember this... and now I say, whoever wins SI, whoever wins superintelligence, wins," Trump stated. The president asserted that the United States is currently leading China "by a lot" in frontier model capabilities, hardware design, and infrastructure deployment. Washington will maintain this gap by aggressively expanding domestic capabilities and clearing federal regulatory hurdles. UN Secretary-General António Guterres and UN Human Rights Chief Volker Türk have repeatedly advocated for global AI governance frameworks, mandatory safety audits, human rights safeguards, and international treaty standards. Trump rejected these international frameworks outright, describing proposed global oversight as a "globalist scheme" that threatens to shackle American innovation while giving adversaries an open field. The administration’s policy explicitly prioritises domestic acceleration over multinational consensus, signalling to foreign capitals that Washington will not sign binding international AI safety pacts that limit model scale or compute capacity. Behind the US AI policy overhaul The renaming to "Super Intelligence" is backed by major structural shifts within the US executive branch. Over the course of this month, the Trump administration unveiled several key initiatives designed to cement the nation's technological engine. sources.title: Nvidia releases software platform to stop AI agents from misbehaving - cnbc.com
passages: Nvidia is rolling out a new software platform to allow AI developers to set safeguards for agents and prevent them from breaking out of containment.

The release on Monday of Nvidia's Open Agent Safety Platform comes after companies including OpenAI , Anthropic , Meta , and Google disclosed recent incidents in which their artificial intelligence models escaped their sandboxes and attempted to hack other companies and access their computer systems.
"Each security incident is unique, and we have to look at all of them in detail," said Justin Boitano, vice president of enterprise AI at Nvidia, the world's most valuable company.
"From what we know, Hugging Face reported over 17,000 agents attacking their infrastructure that went on for days and weeks."
One component of the platform is called Nvidia OpenShell, which runs on central processors and sets limits on agent capabilities.
Nvidia also announced Sentry, which monitors agents and runs on network chips, not CPUs or GPUs.
Some of the software is open source, and Nvidia is calling its platform a reference design, which means partners are intended to build products on top of it to bring it to market.
"You can't have agents roam around and drift around the company, and so you have to find a way to container it," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Monday.
Nvidia named Cisco , Microsoft , Oracle , CoreWeave , Dell , HPE , Lenovo, ARM and Intel as partners.
Nvidia is also working with Anthropic to integrate cloud managed agents with OpenShell.
Huang said the new platform is essentially "a browser for agents," providing a containment system that only allows access to things an agent needs to do its job.

Nvidia has been at the center of the generative AI boom since the launch of ChatGPT almost four years ago, as the chipmaker's graphics processing units are critical to the development of large language models and to the AI services offered by hyperscalers.

But Huang has more recently emerged as a key voice in the AI safety debate, arguing that many security concerns are engineering issues that can be solved through computer science and product development.
An Nvidia representative told reporters on a call on Sunday that its platform could have prevented OpenAI's Hugging Face incident in July.

President Donald Trump told reporters in front of the White House on Tuesday the artificial intelligence summit he just hosted with tech execs like Elon Musk and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg did not change his mind one bit — he does not want to regulate AI anytime soon.

Instead, Trump said he is depending on AI companies to continue with their “tremendous self-policing.” But he did float one possibility: a new government board to oversee the AI industry, which he said could include several of the CEOs he just lunched with.

“We’re also thinking about forming a committee of sorts, where we put, maybe ten people on that committee — it could be from that group — so the committee can watch over the whole enterprise,” Trump said.
Trump delivered the message while flanked by Nvidia boss Jensen Huang and House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA), as Musk crossed his arms and stood a few feet behind.

His comments came shortly after he wrapped up the meeting with Musk and a number of other tech bigwigs, including: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos , Palantir CEO Alex Karp , Google head honcho Sundar Pichai , Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella , and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei .
And one big name conspicuously absent: OpenAI chief Sam Altman .

Tuesday’s powwow comes after AI has been a hot topic lately, following Amodei’s warning “we must slow down the pace” of AI development to make sure it doesn’t go rogue and hurt humans. Musk and Altman — two rivals who rarely agree on anything in public — quickly endorsed his take.

Trump has went the other way and scoffed at the doomsday fears about AI, saying they are nothing more than a “HOAX.” He has said he’s not even a big fan of the term “artificial intelligence” — instead opting to call it “super intelligence.”

The president vowed he will not burden AI companies with new regulations, arguing it is imperative American companies stay ahead of China in the AI race; he said the best defense against AI going off the rails was having a a “STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT” like himself in the Oval Office.

Trump reiterated he believed the worst-case scenario projections about AI are a “hoax” on Tuesday — and that he believed Democrats are cynically pushing it, just like they pushed global warming on the masses.
“I think they would love to see it shut down,” Trump said.

passages: WASHINGTON — After privately huddling with nearly 20 tech titans at a White House lunch Tuesday, President Donald Trump continued to push back on calls for new safety regulations for artificial intelligence, saying there was agreement in the room that there should be “tremendous self-regulation” by companies.

Johnson, a close Trump ally, began pushing for an AI summit with some of the biggest names in tech shortly after whistleblower Jacob Coxon made international headlines by resigning from Claude maker Anthropic.
“But the self-regulation is very important,” he said.
During the lunch, Trump also addressed the proliferation of data centers, which are unpopular among voters but are being built to power AI companies.
Trump was introduced by self-help author and motivational speaker Tony Robbins.
“I’m seeing tremendous self-policing, and they understand that they have to self-police,” he told reporters.

So you’re going to see data centers are going to be very popular.” Trump has consistently argued against regulating AI, even as the dire warnings about humans’ potentially losing control over self-improving AI systems — known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI — grow louder and more frequent.

A White House official called the tool “a new front door for the federal government that will provide a one-stop shop for Americans looking for information and resources from the federal government that are currently spread over a maze of various agency websites.” The National Design Studio, the year-old agency launched by Trump and led by Airbnb co-founder Joe Gebbia, helped create the project.

“We’re launching today something that is really — it’s not just simply a website; it’s a restoration of America’s founding promise, and it’s a reinvention of your government for the 21st century and beyond,” Trump said.

Even before Tuesday’s lunch, Trump had dismissed the existential warnings, arguing that American tech companies need to continue to innovate and keep their foot on the gas to stay ahead of China in the AI arms race.

It is that this is a start and an accord that the whole industry could come to.” Trump, asked whether the accord was binding, replied: “I think it’s morally binding.” He later posted the text of the document on Truth Social.
Trump, who supports data centers, said tech leaders will work with local communities and help pay for costs like energy and education.
Trump hosted the lunch with House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La.
In an appearance Monday on Fox Business, Johnson praised Trump for convening the AI leaders in one room.

extraction.body: WASHINGTON — After privately huddling with nearly 20 tech titans at a White House lunch Tuesday, President Donald Trump continued to push back on calls for new safety regulations for artificial intelligence, saying there was agreement in the room that there should be “tremendous self-regulation” by companies. “There’s a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation, and we automatically have regulation with the Department of Justice, the FBI, all of that,” said Trump, flanked by tech and government leaders. “But the self-regulation is very important,” he said. Moments later, outside the White House, Trump was asked whether anything would persuade him to back tougher AI guardrails or a slowdown of the industry. “I’m seeing tremendous self-policing, and they understand that they have to self-police,” he told reporters. In recent weeks, tech executives on the AI frontier — including Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman — have sounded the alarm about the potential dangers of AI, calling for greater government oversight and global cooperation in regulating the technology. Even before Tuesday’s lunch, Trump had dismissed the existential warnings, arguing that American tech companies need to continue to innovate and keep their foot on the gas to stay ahead of China in the AI arms race. The doomsday scenarios were a “hoax,” he said. Tuesday’s gathering included a who’s who of the tech world, including Amodei, SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su, Palantir CEO Alex Karp and OpenAI President Greg Brockman. Trump hosted the lunch with House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La. Vice President JD Vance, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles also attended. The day’s events included Trump saying he would sign an executive order renaming artificial intelligence as “super intelligence.” The White House later released a document about the signed order. Meanwhile, Johnson said after the meeting that people at the lunch had signed a “White House Accord on Super Intelligence.” Zuckerberg described the document as “a set of principles and commitments around building robust internal controls and detecting if there are any issues with the technology, coupled with multiple layers of auditing and controls, starting with internal risk review, external auditors and evaluators.” Companies agreed that their boards of directors would independently review the auditors’ reports, Zuckerberg said. “I think that these are good steps forward,” he told reporters. It is that this is a start and an accord that the whole industry could come to.” Trump, asked whether the accord was binding, replied: “I think it’s morally binding.” He later posted the text of the document on Truth Social. During the lunch, Trump also addressed the proliferation of data centers, which are unpopular among voters but are being built to power AI companies. Trump, who supports data centers, said tech leaders will work with local communities and help pay for costs like energy and education. They love our country, and they’re going to work with local communities for the data centers, in particular, and they’re going to work to make the community happy,” Trump told reporters. So you’re going to see data centers are going to be very popular.” Trump has consistently argued against regulating AI, even as the dire warnings about humans’ potentially losing control over self-improving AI systems — known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI — grow louder and more frequent. That’s the group that wins, and we’re leading now over China by a lot and everyone else, and we’re going to keep it that way,” Trump said in his address last week to the United Nations General Assembly. “I’m not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution — many say bigger than the Industrial Revolution or the internet itself — and we will be very careful,” he said. Johnson, a close Trump ally, began pushing for an AI summit with some of the biggest names in tech shortly after whistleblower Jacob Coxon made international headlines by resigning from Claude maker Anthropic. Coxon warned that the people building those systems believe they could “kill us all by the end of the decade.” Johnson has made it clear he doesn’t believe Washington should take a heavy-handed approach to regulating AI, arguing that existing laws and regulations can be applied to AI companies and suggesting that they should be held legally liable if their products caused harm. In an appearance Monday on Fox Business, Johnson praised Trump for convening the AI leaders in one room. “They have a corporate responsibility, as every corporation does, to create safe products, right? And there’s product liabilities laws that apply and a labyrinth of federal regulations on all this stuff already. House members aren’t expected back in Washington until after the Nov. “We do not need to jump in and hyperregulate this, because we’ll lose the race to China,” Johnson said on Fox Business. “The innovation is important to continue, but we have to strike the right balance.” Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., didn’t attend the AI lunch, but he privately met with Amodei in the Capitol on Monday evening. “I hope it’s productive,” Thune said ahead of Tuesday’s summit. Before the White House lunch, Trump gathered with Vance, Cabinet members and a handful of tech leaders a few blocks away at the Andrew W. Mellon Auditorium to unveil America.gov, a website that features an AI-powered web portal and chatbot and aims to improve Americans’ experiences accessing federal resources. A White House official called the tool “a new front door for the federal government that will provide a one-stop shop for Americans looking for information and resources from the federal government that are currently spread over a maze of various agency websites.” The National Design Studio, the year-old agency launched by Trump and led by Airbnb co-founder Joe Gebbia, helped create the project. Trump was introduced by self-help author and motivational speaker Tony Robbins. “We’re launching today something that is really — it’s not just simply a website; it’s a restoration of America’s founding promise, and it’s a reinvention of your government for the 21st century and beyond,” Trump said. “Instead of forcing citizens to search through the endless maze of tens of thousands of terrible government websites and rules ... you’ll now have one front door for every single question,” he said.

Moments later, outside the White House, Trump was asked whether anything would persuade him to back tougher AI guardrails or a slowdown of the industry. “I’m seeing tremendous self-policing, and they understand that they have to self-police,” he told reporters. In recent weeks, tech executives on the AI frontier — including Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman — have sounded the alarm about the potential dangers of AI, calling for greater government oversight and global cooperation in regulating the technology. Even before Tuesday’s lunch, Trump had dismissed the existential warnings, arguing that American tech companies need to continue to innovate and keep their foot on the gas to stay ahead of China in the AI arms race. The doomsday scenarios were a “hoax,” he said. passages: Key Takeaways Reform as Survival Strategy, Not Substance: Iraq’s anti-corruption crackdown and militia disarmament deadline function less as coherent reform and more as a survival strategy for the Coordination Framework, aimed at satisfying Washington without confronting Iran-aligned power centers.

Compliance is already fractured: parliamentary-linked factions show partial willingness, while hardline, US-designated groups refuse outright, pointing toward an ambiguous outcome rather than real resolution.
A cosmetic disarmament process risks renewed attacks on US and Gulf targets and could trigger a fresh cycle of strikes on Iraqi soil.
Domestically, a weak coalition’s reliance on foreign-facing reform narratives, amid rising intra-Shia competition, threatens government stability.

Internationally, how Washington reads Baghdad’s actions will shape sanctions policy and test whether Iraq can maintain sovereignty between the US and Iran — or become the next flashpoint between them.

Al-Zaidi, a political newcomer, emerged as the compromise candidate because his good ties with rival Framework leaders meant he triggered no vetoes from al-Sudani, al-Maliki, or Chief Justice Faiq Zidan.

1 In parallel, Baghdad has set a September 30 deadline for all armed factions to surrender weapons to state control, timed explicitly to coincide with the withdrawal of the US-led anti-ISIS coalition.

Tom Barrack met Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi in Baghdad on June 16, 2026, where the two stressed the “complete disarmament and disbandment” of militia groups as part of a shared vision for the new government.

The visit, Barrack’s first to Iraq in his envoy role, also took him to Erbil for talks with Kurdish leaders, including KRG Prime Minister Masrour Barzani, on advancing trade and energy investment and supporting the federal government.

The al-Zaidi Washington visit should be used to establish concrete, monitorable benchmarks, such as verified weapons handover and PMF payroll transparency, rather than accepting rhetorical commitments as sufficient.

This should also include clarity on what happens to fighters and weapons after surrender, whether through integration into the Iraqi Security Forces, formal demobilization, or structured payout schemes, since the absence of such a pathway is likely to undermine compliance in practice.

Crucially, al-Zaidi visited Iran shortly after as per a predetermined schedule, signaling an attempt to satisfy both patrons at once, the clearest expression of Iraq’s “managed pragmatism.” This balancing act plays out against renewed US-Iran hostilities and threats of resumed militia attacks just as disarmament is being pushed.

Washington needs to proactively support the Iraqi government’s efforts to curb Iranian influence, including by strengthening Iraq’s armed forces to assume the security role currently filled by militias, and by ensuring that promised US investments actually materialize and remain insulated from Iranian pressure.

It is the outcome of two decades of institutional erosion, sectarian bargaining, and external patronage, layered slowly enough that each step seemed manageable even as the cumulative effect reshaped the state itself.
Reversing that trajectory will not be accomplished through a single disarmament deadline, a single high-profile visit, or a single change of government.
It will require the same patience, consistency, and long-term investment that allowed the problem to take root in the first place.

Those seeking a sovereign, stable Iraq, in Baghdad and in Washington alike, should measure progress not by the speed of announcements, but by the durability of the institutions being rebuilt in their place.
Analysts note the real test begins now that he’s back in Baghdad, with any gains remaining “opportunities rather than guarantees.” 9

Iraqi authorities restricted the July 2026 funeral procession of Ayatollah Khamenei through Najaf and Karbala, opposing the participation of senior IRGC commanders, including Quds Force chief Esmail Qaani, to avoid the ceremonies being read as a display of Iran’s political and military influence in Iraq.

5 In a further signal of distance, Grand Ayatollah Ali Sistani, Iraq’s most influential Shia religious authority, declined to recite funeral prayers over Khamenei’s body, with his representative in Iran also notably absent from Tehran’s ceremonies.
Three dynamics stand out for decision-makers:
This engagement should be paired with close monitoring of cross-border security risks, particularly given prior incidents linking Iraq-based groups to attacks on Gulf infrastructure.

Independent verification mechanisms for both the anti-corruption and disarmament processes are needed, given the credibility gap that regional analysts have identified between government messaging and actual enforcement patterns.

Iraq’s anti-corruption crackdown and September 30 militia disarmament deadline function more as survival tactics for a fragile coalition than as substantive reform — signaling cooperation to Washington while leaving powerful Iran-aligned factions untouched. Compliance is already fractured: parliamentary-linked factions show partial willingness, while hardline, US-designated groups refuse outright, pointing toward an ambiguous outcome rather than real resolution. A cosmetic disarmament process risks renewed attacks on US and Gulf targets and could trigger a fresh cycle of strikes on Iraqi soil. Domestically, a weak coalition’s reliance on foreign-facing reform narratives, amid rising intra-Shia competition, threatens government stability. Internationally, how Washington reads Baghdad’s actions will shape sanctions policy and test whether Iraq can maintain sovereignty between the US and Iran — or become the next flashpoint between them. Since Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi formed Iraq’s government in May 2026, Baghdad has pursued a set of simultaneous initiatives that, taken together, function less as a coherent reform agenda than as a survival strategy for the ruling Coordination Framework. Iraq’s November 2025 elections saw high turnout despite Muqtada al-Sadr’s boycott but produced a fragmented parliament in which no Shia Coordination Framework leader could command consensus for prime minister. Al-Zaidi, a political newcomer, emerged as the compromise candidate because his good ties with rival Framework leaders meant he triggered no vetoes from al-Sudani, al-Maliki, or Chief Justice Faiq Zidan. The government has launched a nationwide anti-corruption campaign, sealing Baghdad’s Green Zone and detaining dozens of officials and lawmakers, including a wave of 47 arrests in late June and a further round of detentions days later. 1 In parallel, Baghdad has set a September 30 deadline for all armed factions to surrender weapons to state control, timed explicitly to coincide with the withdrawal of the US-led anti-ISIS coalition. 2 Both initiatives are unfolding against the backdrop of the 2026 US-Israel-Iran war and its aftermath, during which Iran-aligned Iraqi factions, operating under the banner of the “Islamic Resistance of Iraq,” claimed repeated drone attacks on US interests. The anti-corruption drive and the disarmament deadline are formally presented by the government as independent, technocratic acts of state-building. This policy brief argues for a different assessment to ensure an accurate implementation of the process. One assessment infers that the campaign may be serving the Coordination Framework’s interest in demonstrating cooperation to Washington while it has not yet touched any high-level Iran-linked interests or proxies, and that the operation may gradually slow down following the September 30 deadline as international monitoring and attention decrease. Hence, a structured mechanism to ensure consistent monitoring and follow-ups on the process is vital. On disarmament, response among Iran-aligned militias has been uneven: some factions with parliamentary representation, including Asaib Ahl al-Haq, have signaled willingness to place weapons under state control and the Coordination Framework itself issued a statement backing initiatives toward a state monopoly on arms, while more hardline Iran-associated groups such as Kataib Hezbollah and Harakat Hezbollah al-Nujaba have publicly rejected surrendering weapons, citing continued foreign (particularly US) military presence as justification. 3 This justification of “foreign military presence” is self-contradictory from groups that are also ideologically and militarily connected to Iran (a foreign neighboring country). Regionally, Baghdad seeks to avoid binary alignment, in contrast to the early years following the US invasion of Iraq in 2003, when Iran’s increasing influence in Iraq exploited the fragile Iraq-GCC relations. Washington has simultaneously deepened engagement with Baghdad through a high-level visit by the US Special Presidential Envoy for Iraq and Syria Tom Barrack, with disarmament and containment of Iranian influence as explicit agenda items. 4 Iraqi authorities restricted the July 2026 funeral procession of Ayatollah Khamenei through Najaf and Karbala, opposing the participation of senior IRGC commanders, including Quds Force chief Esmail Qaani, to avoid the ceremonies being read as a display of Iran’s political and military influence in Iraq. 5 In a further signal of distance, Grand Ayatollah Ali Sistani, Iraq’s most influential Shia religious authority, declined to recite funeral prayers over Khamenei’s body, with his representative in Iran also notably absent from Tehran’s ceremonies. 6 Though never publicly confirmed by the government, the move reflects Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s effort to honor the funeral’s religious weight for Iraq’s Shia population while avoiding overt Iranian military symbolism ahead of his scheduled Washington visit, illustrating the balancing act central to the Coordination Framework’s “managed pragmatism” toward Tehran and Washington alike. Tom Barrack met Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi in Baghdad on June 16, 2026, where the two stressed the “complete disarmament and disbandment” of militia groups as part of a shared vision for the new government. The visit, Barrack’s first to Iraq in his envoy role, also took him to Erbil for talks with Kurdish leaders, including KRG Prime Minister Masrour Barzani, on advancing trade and energy investment and supporting the federal government. The meeting came against the backdrop of heightened US-Iran tensions in Iraq, underscoring Washington’s push to rein in Iran-aligned armed factions as a condition for deeper bilateral cooperation. 7 Some analysts argue Washington’s Iraq policy is reverting to a pre-1990 logic, treating Baghdad as a strategic buffer against Iran. Iraqi researcher Haider Saeed of the Arab Center for Research and Policy Studies has raised this comparison in an Al Jazeera Arabic commentary, noting that the current push to disarm Iran-aligned militias and anchor Iraq to US interests echoes the earlier era before Iraq’s 1990 invasion of Kuwait triggered Desert Storm and a decade of sanctions. 8 Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s July 13–19 Washington trip, his first foreign visit since taking office and the first official Iraqi PM visit to the US since 2003, produced a warm reception from Trump, dozens of economic deals, and energy cooperation commitments, but experts call it more political theatre than a concrete breakthrough. Al-Zaidi pledged to disarm Iran-aligned militias and see US forces withdraw by September 30, a timeline widely seen as unrealistic given Iran’s entrenchment in Iraq’s security and political system. Analysts note the real test begins now that he’s back in Baghdad, with any gains remaining “opportunities rather than guarantees.” 9 Crucially, al-Zaidi visited Iran shortly after as per a predetermined schedule, signaling an attempt to satisfy both patrons at once, the clearest expression of Iraq’s “managed pragmatism.” This balancing act plays out against renewed US-Iran hostilities and threats of resumed militia attacks just as disarmament is being pushed. 10 For Iraq to sustain this balancing act without collapsing into open confrontation between Washington and Tehran, or being blamed for a failed disarmament process, the burden cannot rest on Baghdad alone. Washington needs to proactively support the Iraqi government’s efforts to curb Iranian influence, including by strengthening Iraq’s armed forces to assume the security role currently filled by militias, and by ensuring that promised US investments actually materialize and remain insulated from Iranian pressure. Without follow-through on both fronts, Iran retains an easy indirect lever, slowing or sabotaging economic cooperation as leverage against disarmament, while al-Zaidi is left absorbing the political cost of a policy Washington pushed but did not adequately back. The July 29, 2026 US-Saudi joint strikes on PMF sites across seven Iraqi provinces, launched in response to drone attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure that Riyadh blamed on Iran-backed militias, forced Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi to cancel his planned Riyadh visit, a symbolic rupture that lays bare how conditional and reversible Gulf-Iraq alignment against Iranian influence still is. 11 That Zaidi’s foreign itinerary had taken him to Iran and then Turkey, just before Riyadh was to be his fourth stop, is itself telling: it suggests a leader still hedging across rival patrons rather than one who has settled into a clear camp, even as he has pledged to demobilize the PMF, a force US officials characterize as operating outside government command and often in coordination with Iran. Trump’s own claim that the strikes were coordinated with Baghdad reads less as a diplomatic aside than an attempt to publicly implicate Zaidi in a policy his domestic base would never openly endorse. 12 Read against Baghdad’s declared priority of restoring state control over weapons, a push that runs headlong into resistance from armed factions wielding real military, economic, and political capital inside state institutions, the episode looks less like an isolated security incident and more like a preview of the confrontation Zaidi’s disarmament agenda was always going to provoke. 13 The scale of the domestic backlash is itself a useful gauge of how combustible the disarmament file has become: Iraqi lawmakers openly called for military retaliation against Saudi Arabia and the US, with one invoking the “dark record” of Washington and Riyadh in language clearly aimed at outflanking Zaidi from a more hardline, anti-Western position. 14 That the rupture was patched over so quickly, with Riyadh renewing its invitation and the Islamic Resistance shelving a threatened response, likely reflects mutual interest in avoiding further escalation rather than any genuine resolution of the underlying dispute, since the core tension persists undiminished. GCC states want disarmament delivered on a fixed calendar, while Zaidi has to pursue it without detonating a backlash from coordination-framework elites whose own political survival is bound up with the very factions he is meant to dismantle, all under a public mood now openly hostile to both Iranian overreach and US-Saudi unilateralism on Iraqi soil. 15 The developments in Baghdad are of direct relevance to Washington’s Iraq policy, Gulf regional security planning, and broader efforts to manage Iran’s post-war regional posture. Three dynamics stand out for decision-makers: The Iraqi government’s anti-corruption enforcement and disarmament announcements function primarily as instruments of legitimacy-building — externally toward Washington and internally toward a domestic public fatigued by past, largely symbolic, anti-corruption drives. Policymakers assessing these commitments should therefore distinguish between visible enforcement actions and genuine structural shifts in the distribution of coercive and financial power. This assessment is complicated by the fact that the PMF and affiliated factions are not a unitary actor: political and economic incentives are producing divergent responses, ranging from selective compliance by parliamentary-linked factions to open refusal by internationally designated groups. A uniform expectation for “compliance” by the September 30 deadline therefore risks obscuring meaningful variation in outcomes across these factions. This dynamic is reinforced by domestic political fragility, which increases the value of a foreign-facing reform narrative. The government was formed with several cabinet posts, including defense and interior, left unfilled, and now faces cleric Muqtada al-Sadr’s public alignment with the anti-corruption campaign, raising the prospect of intensified intra-Shia political competition. A weak coalition operating under these conditions has strong incentives to lean on externally oriented reform messaging to consolidate its domestic standing. If anti-corruption arrests continue to bypass the most powerful Iran-aligned political and militia figures, the campaign risks being read, both domestically and internationally, as an instrument of intra-coalition score-settling rather than a genuine governance reform, weakening the government’s negotiating position with Washington. Relatedly, the most probable outcome by the September 30 deadline will be a bifurcated result: parliamentary-linked factions surrendering heavy weapons or nominal PMF affiliation while retaining their organizational structure and funding access, alongside continued refusal by hardline, US-designated factions. Such an outcome would satisfy neither Washington’s more maximalist objectives nor eliminate the risk of renewed attacks on US or Gulf-linked targets, and, most importantly, would fail to resolve Iraq’s broader problem with the rise of non-state armed groups. This partial compliance carries its own escalatory risk: continued attacks by non-compliant factions could trigger renewed US or Israeli strikes on Iraqi soil, as occurred during the earlier phase of the regional war, forcing the Coordination Framework government to manage domestic backlash while its stated disarmament commitments are exposed as unenforceable. Compounding these external pressures, Sadrist endorsement of the anti-corruption campaign, combined with public defenses of the Coordination Framework by senior Coordination Framework-aligned figures, signals rising internal contestation that could destabilize the governing coalition irrespective of any external pressure from Washington. Voluntary steps by parliamentary-linked factions to detach from the PMF and place their weapons under state oversight could, if paired with credible political and economic guarantees, produce a durable, if partial, recalibration of militia influence without triggering violent confrontation. This incremental approach could be reinforced by Sadrist public backing of the anti-corruption campaign: if channeled constructively rather than confrontationally, this support could broaden the government’s domestic coalition and create space for deeper reforms beyond the current pattern of selective enforcement. Underpinning both possibilities is Baghdad’s parallel engagement with Washington and Tehran. Provided this hedging strategy does not collapse into open contradiction, it allows Iraq to avoid becoming a frontline in a renewed US-Iran confrontation — a stabilizing outcome not just for Iraq, but for the wider Gulf region. The September 30 deadline will most likely produce a mixed and ambiguous outcome rather than a clear resolution, with continued negotiation over what “disarmament” and “state control” actually entail in practice. In parallel, the anti-corruption campaign will likely continue in a manner calibrated to avoid direct confrontation with entrenched Iran-aligned interests, unless internal political competition, most notably Sadrist pressure, forces an expansion of its scope. Al-Zaidi’s Washington visit will function as a key signaling moment in this trajectory: the degree to which Washington accepts Baghdad’s actions as sufficient progress, rather than demanding further steps, will shape whether sanctions pressure on Iraqi officials and factions intensifies or eases through year-end. Underlying all of this, Iran is likely to continue permitting limited, face-saving cooperation on disarmament rhetoric while resisting any measures that would materially degrade the operational capacity of its most capable Iraqi proxies. Policymakers should calibrate expectations around the September 30 deadline to account for the fragmented militia landscape, avoiding the treatment of declarative commitments by parliamentary-linked factions as equivalent to enforceable, verifiable disarmament of hardline, designated groups. This calls for maintaining differentiated pressure, using targeted sanctions and financial network disruption against non-compliant factions, rather than blanket conditionality that could weaken the Coordination Framework government’s domestic standing without producing commensurate security gains. The al-Zaidi Washington visit should be used to establish concrete, monitorable benchmarks, such as verified weapons handover and PMF payroll transparency, rather than accepting rhetorical commitments as sufficient. This should also include clarity on what happens to fighters and weapons after surrender, whether through integration into the Iraqi Security Forces, formal demobilization, or structured payout schemes, since the absence of such a pathway is likely to undermine compliance in practice. Washington should also consider gradually loosening its oversight of Iraq’s oil revenue account at the New York Federal Reserve as a tangible goodwill gesture that reinforces its stated commitment to a “strong, sovereign, and united” Iraq, rather than leaving this Bremer-era financial mechanism as a standing contradiction to its sovereignty rhetoric. There should also be continued incremental engagement with Baghdad by Washington on economic and security cooperation to reinforce Iraq’s incentive to maintain distance from full alignment with Tehran, while remaining attentive to the risk that Iran-aligned factions retain influence over Iraqi security policy. This engagement should be paired with close monitoring of cross-border security risks, particularly given prior incidents linking Iraq-based groups to attacks on Gulf infrastructure. Independent verification mechanisms for both the anti-corruption and disarmament processes are needed, given the credibility gap that regional analysts have identified between government messaging and actual enforcement patterns. This should extend to encouraging greater transparency around PMF financing and command structures, as such transparency is a precondition for assessing whether disarmament announcements reflect substantive change or merely a renegotiated term of coexistence between the state and armed factions. Any such verification mechanism must be managed by the government in coordination with international institutions to ensure a multilateral perspective in the monitoring process. Expanding the anti-corruption campaign to visibly include Iran-aligned political and militia-linked figures, as well as figures associated with other regional actors, would substantially strengthen the government’s credibility both domestically and with international partners, reducing the risk that the initiative is perceived primarily as an instrument of factional consolidation. Alongside this, establishing clear, published criteria for what constitutes compliance with the disarmament deadline would reduce the ambiguity that hardline factions might otherwise exploit to delay or dilute enforcement. The rise of armed factions and their gradual absorption into Iraq’s political fabric was not the product of a single crisis or a single election cycle. It is the outcome of two decades of institutional erosion, sectarian bargaining, and external patronage, layered slowly enough that each step seemed manageable even as the cumulative effect reshaped the state itself. Reversing that trajectory will not be accomplished through a single disarmament deadline, a single high-profile visit, or a single change of government. It will require the same patience, consistency, and long-term investment that allowed the problem to take root in the first place. Iraq’s Coordination Framework, and any government that succeeds it, will continue to navigate between Washington and Tehran not because its leaders lack conviction, but because the structures compelling that balancing act were built over years and will not dissolve in months. Those seeking a sovereign, stable Iraq, in Baghdad and in Washington alike, should measure progress not by the speed of announcements, but by the durability of the institutions being rebuilt in their place.
