Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s July 13–19 Washington trip, his first foreign visit since taking office and the first official Iraqi PM visit to the US since 2003, produced a warm reception from Trump, dozens of economic deals, and energy cooperation commitments, but experts call it more political theatre than a concrete breakthrough. Al-Zaidi pledged to disarm Iran-aligned militias and see US forces withdraw by September 30, a timeline widely seen as unrealistic given Iran’s entrenchment in Iraq’s security and political system. Analysts note the real test begins now that he’s back in Baghdad, with any gains remaining “opportunities rather than guarantees.” 9

Crucially, al-Zaidi visited Iran shortly after as per a predetermined schedule, signaling an attempt to satisfy both patrons at once, the clearest expression of Iraq’s “managed pragmatism.” This balancing act plays out against renewed US-Iran hostilities and threats of resumed militia attacks just as disarmament is being pushed. 10

For Iraq to sustain this balancing act without collapsing into open confrontation between Washington and Tehran, or being blamed for a failed disarmament process, the burden cannot rest on Baghdad alone. Washington needs to proactively support the Iraqi government’s efforts to curb Iranian influence, including by strengthening Iraq’s armed forces to assume the security role currently filled by militias, and by ensuring that promised US investments actually materialize and remain insulated from Iranian pressure. Without follow-through on both fronts, Iran retains an easy indirect lever, slowing or sabotaging economic cooperation as leverage against disarmament, while al-Zaidi is left absorbing the political cost of a policy Washington pushed but did not adequately back.

The July 29, 2026 US-Saudi joint strikes on PMF sites across seven Iraqi provinces, launched in response to drone attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure that Riyadh blamed on Iran-backed militias, forced Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi to cancel his planned Riyadh visit, a symbolic rupture that lays bare how conditional and reversible Gulf-Iraq alignment against Iranian influence still is. 11 That Zaidi’s foreign itinerary had taken him to Iran and then Turkey, just before Riyadh was to be his fourth stop, is itself telling: it suggests a leader still hedging across rival patrons rather than one who has settled into a clear camp, even as he has pledged to demobilize the PMF, a force US officials characterize as operating outside government command and often in coordination with Iran. Trump’s own claim that the strikes were coordinated with Baghdad reads less as a diplomatic aside than an attempt to publicly implicate Zaidi in a policy his domestic base would never openly endorse. 12 Read against Baghdad’s declared priority of restoring state control over weapons, a push that runs headlong into resistance from armed factions wielding real military, economic, and political capital inside state institutions, the episode looks less like an isolated security incident and more like a preview of the confrontation Zaidi’s disarmament agenda was always going to provoke. 13

The scale of the domestic backlash is itself a useful gauge of how combustible the disarmament file has become: Iraqi lawmakers openly called for military retaliation against Saudi Arabia and the US, with one invoking the “dark record” of Washington and Riyadh in language clearly aimed at outflanking Zaidi from a more hardline, anti-Western position. 14 That the rupture was patched over so quickly, with Riyadh renewing its invitation and the Islamic Resistance shelving a threatened response, likely reflects mutual interest in avoiding further escalation rather than any genuine resolution of the underlying dispute, since the core tension persists undiminished. GCC states want disarmament delivered on a fixed calendar, while Zaidi has to pursue it without detonating a backlash from coordination-framework elites whose own political survival is bound up with the very factions he is meant to dismantle, all under a public mood now openly hostile to both Iranian overreach and US-Saudi unilateralism on Iraqi soil. 15

The developments in Baghdad are of direct relevance to Washington’s Iraq policy, Gulf regional security planning, and broader efforts to manage Iran’s post-war regional posture. Three dynamics stand out for decision-makers:

The Iraqi government’s anti-corruption enforcement and disarmament announcements function primarily as instruments of legitimacy-building — externally toward Washington and internally toward a domestic public fatigued by past, largely symbolic, anti-corruption drives. Policymakers assessing these commitments should therefore distinguish between visible enforcement actions and genuine structural shifts in the distribution of coercive and financial power. This assessment is complicated by the fact that the PMF and affiliated factions are not a unitary actor: political and economic incentives are producing divergent responses, ranging from selective compliance by parliamentary-linked factions to open refusal by internationally designated groups. A uniform expectation for “compliance” by the September 30 deadline therefore risks obscuring meaningful variation in outcomes across these factions.

This dynamic is reinforced by domestic political fragility, which increases the value of a foreign-facing reform narrative. The government was formed with several cabinet posts, including defense and interior, left unfilled, and now faces cleric Muqtada al-Sadr’s public alignment with the anti-corruption campaign, raising the prospect of intensified intra-Shia political competition. A weak coalition operating under these conditions has strong incentives to lean on externally oriented reform messaging to consolidate its domestic standing.

If anti-corruption arrests continue to bypass the most powerful Iran-aligned political and militia figures, the campaign risks being read, both domestically and internationally, as an instrument of intra-coalition score-settling rather than a genuine governance reform, weakening the government’s negotiating position with Washington. Relatedly, the most probable outcome by the September 30 deadline will be a bifurcated result: parliamentary-linked factions surrendering heavy weapons or nominal PMF affiliation while retaining their organizational structure and funding access, alongside continued refusal by hardline, US-designated factions. Such an outcome would satisfy neither Washington’s more maximalist objectives nor eliminate the risk of renewed attacks on US or Gulf-linked targets, and, most importantly, would fail to resolve Iraq’s broader problem with the rise of non-state armed groups.

This partial compliance carries its own escalatory risk: continued attacks by non-compliant factions could trigger renewed US or Israeli strikes on Iraqi soil, as occurred during the earlier phase of the regional war, forcing the Coordination Framework government to manage domestic backlash while its stated disarmament commitments are exposed as unenforceable. Compounding these external pressures, Sadrist endorsement of the anti-corruption campaign, combined with public defenses of the Coordination Framework by senior Coordination Framework-aligned figures, signals rising internal contestation that could destabilize the governing coalition irrespective of any external pressure from Washington.

Voluntary steps by parliamentary-linked factions to detach from the PMF and place their weapons under state oversight could, if paired with credible political and economic guarantees, produce a durable, if partial, recalibration of militia influence without triggering violent confrontation. This incremental approach could be reinforced by Sadrist public backing of the anti-corruption campaign: if channeled constructively rather than confrontationally, this support could broaden the government’s domestic coalition and create space for deeper reforms beyond the current pattern of selective enforcement.

Underpinning both possibilities is Baghdad’s parallel engagement with Washington and Tehran. Provided this hedging strategy does not collapse into open contradiction, it allows Iraq to avoid becoming a frontline in a renewed US-Iran confrontation — a stabilizing outcome not just for Iraq, but for the wider Gulf region.

The September 30 deadline will most likely produce a mixed and ambiguous outcome rather than a clear resolution, with continued negotiation over what “disarmament” and “state control” actually entail in practice. In parallel, the anti-corruption campaign will likely continue in a manner calibrated to avoid direct confrontation with entrenched Iran-aligned interests, unless internal political competition, most notably Sadrist pressure, forces an expansion of its scope.

Al-Zaidi’s Washington visit will function as a key signaling moment in this trajectory: the degree to which Washington accepts Baghdad’s actions as sufficient progress, rather than demanding further steps, will shape whether sanctions pressure on Iraqi officials and factions intensifies or eases through year-end. Underlying all of this, Iran is likely to continue permitting limited, face-saving cooperation on disarmament rhetoric while resisting any measures that would materially degrade the operational capacity of its most capable Iraqi proxies.

Policymakers should calibrate expectations around the September 30 deadline to account for the fragmented militia landscape, avoiding the treatment of declarative commitments by parliamentary-linked factions as equivalent to enforceable, verifiable disarmament of hardline, designated groups. This calls for maintaining differentiated pressure, using targeted sanctions and financial network disruption against non-compliant factions, rather than blanket conditionality that could weaken the Coordination Framework government’s domestic standing without producing commensurate security gains. The al-Zaidi Washington visit should be used to establish concrete, monitorable benchmarks, such as verified weapons handover and PMF payroll transparency, rather than accepting rhetorical commitments as sufficient. This should also include clarity on what happens to fighters and weapons after surrender, whether through integration into the Iraqi Security Forces, formal demobilization, or structured payout schemes, since the absence of such a pathway is likely to undermine compliance in practice. Washington should also consider gradually loosening its oversight of Iraq’s oil revenue account at the New York Federal Reserve as a tangible goodwill gesture that reinforces its stated commitment to a “strong, sovereign, and united” Iraq, rather than leaving this Bremer-era financial mechanism as a standing contradiction to its sovereignty rhetoric.

There should also be continued incremental engagement with Baghdad by Washington on economic and security cooperation to reinforce Iraq’s incentive to maintain distance from full alignment with Tehran, while remaining attentive to the risk that Iran-aligned factions retain influence over Iraqi security policy. This engagement should be paired with close monitoring of cross-border security risks, particularly given prior incidents linking Iraq-based groups to attacks on Gulf infrastructure.

Independent verification mechanisms for both the anti-corruption and disarmament processes are needed, given the credibility gap that regional analysts have identified between government messaging and actual enforcement patterns. This should extend to encouraging greater transparency around PMF financing and command structures, as such transparency is a precondition for assessing whether disarmament announcements reflect substantive change or merely a renegotiated term of coexistence between the state and armed factions. Any such verification mechanism must be managed by the government in coordination with international institutions to ensure a multilateral perspective in the monitoring process.

Expanding the anti-corruption campaign to visibly include Iran-aligned political and militia-linked figures, as well as figures associated with other regional actors, would substantially strengthen the government’s credibility both domestically and with international partners, reducing the risk that the initiative is perceived primarily as an instrument of factional consolidation. Alongside this, establishing clear, published criteria for what constitutes compliance with the disarmament deadline would reduce the ambiguity that hardline factions might otherwise exploit to delay or dilute enforcement.

The rise of armed factions and their gradual absorption into Iraq’s political fabric was not the product of a single crisis or a single election cycle. It is the outcome of two decades of institutional erosion, sectarian bargaining, and external patronage, layered slowly enough that each step seemed manageable even as the cumulative effect reshaped the state itself. Reversing that trajectory will not be accomplished through a single disarmament deadline, a single high-profile visit, or a single change of government. It will require the same patience, consistency, and long-term investment that allowed the problem to take root in the first place. Iraq’s Coordination Framework, and any government that succeeds it, will continue to navigate between Washington and Tehran not because its leaders lack conviction, but because the structures compelling that balancing act were built over years and will not dissolve in months. Those seeking a sovereign, stable Iraq, in Baghdad and in Washington alike, should measure progress not by the speed of announcements, but by the durability of the institutions being rebuilt in their place.

extraction.body: Iraq marks national ‘Sovereignty Days’ as US troops depart, but must navigate risks of new security landscape. Iraq is set to hold four “Sovereignty Days”, a national holiday marking the complete withdrawal of US troops from the country and underscoring the deep symbolism of the exit after more than two decades of foreign intervention. Wednesday’s withdrawal deadline affirmed the exodus of a few hundred remaining US soldiers in the country, who have served in advisory roles in a coalition operation against ISIL (ISIS) first launched in 2015. While the exit plan predates Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, it fits into his wider vision of reasserting Iraqi state authority. That encompasses accelerating efforts to disarm all militias in the country by June 2027, including several powerful pro-Iran groups who have launched attacks throughout the region amid the US-Israeli war with Iran. Speaking at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) last week, al-Zaidi said his government was “striving to ensure that the state is the ultimate decision-maker in matters of peace and war, and that weapons and tools of power remain in the hands of its constitutional institutions”. He added, “With the end of the international coalition’s mission in Iraq, we are moving our relationship with our strategic partners to a new phase, moving from military cooperation to economic and development cooperation in service of our common interests.” Indeed, the US withdrawal appears to be part of a strategy by al-Zaidi to “politically weaken” influential militias , including those linked to Iran, according to Douglas Silliman, the former US ambassador to Iraq and Kuwait. Those militias have long pointed to the presence of the US military, and other foreign actors like Turkiye, as a pillar justification for maintaining their own weapons stores and chains of command. Some have already indicated they will refuse to hand over their arms. “It’s going to be a very difficult series of decisions,” Silliman said. “Both for the militias and for Prime Minister al-Zaidi and his defence team.” How the Iraqi government navigates the end of the US-led coalition’s deployment, dubbed “Operation Inherent Resolve”, will have wide-ranging implications for the future security of Iraq. The country has remained relatively stable in recent years following the 2017 territorial defeat of ISIL, despite being enveloped by conflict and insecurity on its borders. That stability has generally persisted since the US began its troop withdrawal in 2020 under US President Donald Trump, with the remaining military personnel consolidating at an airbase in Erbil, in northern Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdish region, at the end of 2025. Still, Renad Mansour, director of the Iraq Initiative at Chatham House, said militias aligned with Iran’s “axis of resistance” in the region ultimately remain “in full-on war mode, working with the IRGC [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] in the region. And so they will continue to target US and US interests.” While al-Zaidi has promised continued integration and cooperation with the US and other Western allies, there is likely disquiet behind the rhetoric, Mansour assessed, with some seeing the US’s erstwhile presence in the country as having served as a bulwark against a wider policy pivot. “The anxiety from the Iraqi government now is that the US might not need Iraq any more, or might, in the worst case, view Iraq as a pariah state, too close to Iran, and therefore another target,” he said. The targeting could eventually come in the form of sanctions or in an escalation of US and Israeli strikes on Iraqi territory, Mansour said. Mohammad Salih, a non-resident senior fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute and an expert on Iraq, also agreed that enthusiasm for the US troop withdrawal was likely more subdued within some segments of the Iraqi government than public statements – and national holidays – suggest. Salih assessed an underlying wariness to change the security status quo at a time of regional upheaval, pointing to the continued threat from ISIL sleeper cells, shifting cross-border dynamics in a post-Assad Syria, as well as the US-Israel war with Iran. “The official rhetoric tries to signal that Iraq is more or less fine, that it can take care of itself, and that it seeks stronger commercial and diplomatic ties with the US – that there is no need for the US military presence,” he said. “But in reality, there is a great deal of concern that Iraq could be the next theatre of some major regional development,” he told Al Jazeera. The operational implications of the end to the US-led anti-ISIL mission remain difficult to assess. In the wake of the withdrawal, the two countries appear to be reverting to a 2008 Strategic Framework and Security Agreement, signed under the administration of US President George W Bush, Salih said. The deal pledges continued, if non-binding, US security support for Iraq. Neither the Iraqi government nor the Pentagon have given a clear picture of what shape security cooperation could take going forward, particularly when it comes to the intelligence and logistical support that buoyed ISIL’s territorial defeat. However, a regional source with knowledge of the situation told Al Jazeera the relationship is “likely to become less centred on a visible military footprint and more focused on intelligence, training, technical support, capacity-building and institutional cooperation”. The source called the change a “test of whether a relationship built for a period of military intervention can evolve into a more conventional partnership between sovereign states”. “There are real capabilities and real experience in the Iraqi security forces. People I talk to in the military are quite confident that they can take on most threats against the sovereignty of Iraq,” former Ambassador Silliman said. But while the Iraqi parliament approved a partial cabinet in May, several key security roles, including minister of defence, remain unfilled. The Iraqi government also continues to lack a substantial air defence capability of its own, which could prove a major weakness if the domestic security situation were to spiral, Silliman said. “This is one area where there will be vulnerabilities because it is clear that the pro-Iran militias have been willing to use drones and rockets and missiles against Iraqi targets inside Iraq, and as of right now, the Iraqi military doesn’t really have a way to defend against that,” he said. Kurdish officials have been among the most vocal critics of the US withdrawal, pointing to a barrage of attacks on Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdish region by Iran and Iran-aligned militias thwarted by US anti-missile and anti-drone weapons this year. To be sure, the withdrawal of the remaining US troops is only one step in a larger, years-long effort to transform the US-Iraqi relationship from military to economic. Following the 2003 invasion as part of the US-led “global war on terror”, the US had initially withdrawn troops in 2011, only to redeploy them amid the rise of ISIL. Speaking at the UNGA, al-Zaidi promised an economic “renaissance”, pledging to boost Iraq’s petrochemical industry and build new fossil fuel delivery routes beyond the Strait of Hormuz. The constriction of traffic in the strait amid the US-Israel war with Iran has had an outsized impact on Iraq, with its oil output dropping by as much as 60 percent in March. For his part, during a meeting at the White House in July, US PresidentTrump pledged “a lot of deals” to come with Iraq, pointing to the country’s vast oil reserves. Hamzeh Hadad, an adjunct fellow with the Middle East Security Program at the Centre for a New American Security, said there were no immediate signs the US planned a wholesale shift in its approach towards Iraq, which still houses the largest US embassy in the world in Baghdad and the largest consulate in Erbil. Lahib Higel, the deputy director of the MENA programme at the International Crisis Group, called on Washington to focus on cooperation, while avoiding “pressuring al-Zaidi into a military confrontation against pro-Iran groups that he is unlikely to win”. “A better approach would be for the US to preserve bilateral security cooperation and support his efforts to strengthen state institutions over time,” Higel said in a social media post. “Washington cannot dictate Baghdad’s relationship with Tehran, nor can Tehran dictate Iraq’s relationship with Washington,” she said. “What Iraq instead needs is the space to find its own balance.”

coreStoryFacts.text: Key Takeaways Reform as Survival Strategy, Not Substance: Iraq’s anti-corruption crackdown and militia disarmament deadline function less as coherent reform and more as a survival strategy for the Coordination Framework, aimed at satisfying Washington without confronting Iran-aligned power centers.

Compliance is already fractured: parliamentary-linked factions show partial willingness, while hardline, US-designated groups refuse outright, pointing toward an ambiguous outcome rather than real resolution.
A cosmetic disarmament process risks renewed attacks on US and Gulf targets and could trigger a fresh cycle of strikes on Iraqi soil.
Domestically, a weak coalition’s reliance on foreign-facing reform narratives, amid rising intra-Shia competition, threatens government stability.

Internationally, how Washington reads Baghdad’s actions will shape sanctions policy and test whether Iraq can maintain sovereignty between the US and Iran — or become the next flashpoint between them.

Al-Zaidi, a political newcomer, emerged as the compromise candidate because his good ties with rival Framework leaders meant he triggered no vetoes from al-Sudani, al-Maliki, or Chief Justice Faiq Zidan.

1 In parallel, Baghdad has set a September 30 deadline for all armed factions to surrender weapons to state control, timed explicitly to coincide with the withdrawal of the US-led anti-ISIS coalition.

Tom Barrack met Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi in Baghdad on June 16, 2026, where the two stressed the “complete disarmament and disbandment” of militia groups as part of a shared vision for the new government.

The visit, Barrack’s first to Iraq in his envoy role, also took him to Erbil for talks with Kurdish leaders, including KRG Prime Minister Masrour Barzani, on advancing trade and energy investment and supporting the federal government.

The al-Zaidi Washington visit should be used to establish concrete, monitorable benchmarks, such as verified weapons handover and PMF payroll transparency, rather than accepting rhetorical commitments as sufficient.

This should also include clarity on what happens to fighters and weapons after surrender, whether through integration into the Iraqi Security Forces, formal demobilization, or structured payout schemes, since the absence of such a pathway is likely to undermine compliance in practice.

Crucially, al-Zaidi visited Iran shortly after as per a predetermined schedule, signaling an attempt to satisfy both patrons at once, the clearest expression of Iraq’s “managed pragmatism.” This balancing act plays out against renewed US-Iran hostilities and threats of resumed militia attacks just as disarmament is being pushed.

Washington needs to proactively support the Iraqi government’s efforts to curb Iranian influence, including by strengthening Iraq’s armed forces to assume the security role currently filled by militias, and by ensuring that promised US investments actually materialize and remain insulated from Iranian pressure.

It is the outcome of two decades of institutional erosion, sectarian bargaining, and external patronage, layered slowly enough that each step seemed manageable even as the cumulative effect reshaped the state itself.
Reversing that trajectory will not be accomplished through a single disarmament deadline, a single high-profile visit, or a single change of government.
It will require the same patience, consistency, and long-term investment that allowed the problem to take root in the first place.

Those seeking a sovereign, stable Iraq, in Baghdad and in Washington alike, should measure progress not by the speed of announcements, but by the durability of the institutions being rebuilt in their place.
Analysts note the real test begins now that he’s back in Baghdad, with any gains remaining “opportunities rather than guarantees.” 9

Iraqi authorities restricted the July 2026 funeral procession of Ayatollah Khamenei through Najaf and Karbala, opposing the participation of senior IRGC commanders, including Quds Force chief Esmail Qaani, to avoid the ceremonies being read as a display of Iran’s political and military influence in Iraq.

5 In a further signal of distance, Grand Ayatollah Ali Sistani, Iraq’s most influential Shia religious authority, declined to recite funeral prayers over Khamenei’s body, with his representative in Iran also notably absent from Tehran’s ceremonies.
Three dynamics stand out for decision-makers:
This engagement should be paired with close monitoring of cross-border security risks, particularly given prior incidents linking Iraq-based groups to attacks on Gulf infrastructure.

Independent verification mechanisms for both the anti-corruption and disarmament processes are needed, given the credibility gap that regional analysts have identified between government messaging and actual enforcement patterns.
Iraq marks national ‘Sovereignty Days’ as US troops depart, but must navigate risks of new security landscape.

Three dynamics stand out for decision-makers: The Iraqi government’s anti-corruption enforcement and disarmament announcements function primarily as instruments of legitimacy-building — externally toward Washington and internally toward a domestic public fatigued by past, largely symbolic, anti-corruption drives. This assessment is complicated by the fact that the PMF and affiliated factions are not a unitary actor: political and economic incentives are producing divergent responses, ranging from selective compliance by parliamentary-linked factions to open refusal by internationally designated groups. A uniform expectation for “compliance” by the September 30 deadline therefore risks obscuring meaningful variation in outcomes across these factions. This dynamic is reinforced by domestic political fragility, which increases the value of a foreign-facing reform narrative. The government was formed with several cabinet posts, including defense and interior, left unfilled, and now faces cleric Muqtada al-Sadr’s public alignment with the anti-corruption campaign, raising the prospect of intensified intra-Shia political competition. A weak coalition operating under these conditions has strong incentives to lean on externally oriented reform messaging to consolidate its domestic standing. If anti-corruption arrests continue to bypass the most powerful Iran-aligned political and militia figures, the campaign risks being read, both domestically and internationally, as an instrument of intra-coalition score-settling rather than a genuine governance reform, weakening the government’s negotiating position with Washington. Relatedly, the most probable outcome by the September 30 deadline will be a bifurcated result: parliamentary-linked factions surrendering heavy weapons or nominal PMF affiliation while retaining their organizational structure and funding access, alongside continued refusal by hardline, US-designated factions. Such an outcome would satisfy neither Washington’s more maximalist objectives nor eliminate the risk of renewed attacks on US or Gulf-linked targets, and, most importantly, would fail to resolve Iraq’s broader problem with the rise of non-state armed groups. This partial compliance carries its own escalatory risk: continued attacks by non-compliant factions could trigger renewed US or Israeli strikes on Iraqi soil, as occurred during the earlier phase of the regional war, forcing the Coordination Framework government to manage domestic backlash while its stated disarmament commitments are exposed as unenforceable. Compounding these external pressures, Sadrist endorsement of the anti-corruption campaign, combined with public defenses of the Coordination Framework by senior Coordination Framework-aligned figures, signals rising internal contestation that could destabilize the governing coalition irrespective of any external pressure from Washington. Voluntary steps by parliamentary-linked factions to detach from the PMF and place their weapons under state oversight could, if paired with credible political and economic guarantees, produce a durable, if partial, recalibration of militia influence without triggering violent confrontation. This incremental approach could be reinforced by Sadrist public backing of the anti-corruption campaign: if channeled constructively rather than confrontationally, this support could broaden the government’s domestic coalition and create space for deeper reforms beyond the current pattern of selective enforcement. Underpinning both possibilities is Baghdad’s parallel engagement with Washington and Tehran. Provided this hedging strategy does not collapse into open contradiction, it allows Iraq to avoid becoming a frontline in a renewed US-Iran confrontation — a stabilizing outcome not just for Iraq, but for the wider Gulf region. The September 30 deadline will most likely produce a mixed and ambiguous outcome rather than a clear resolution, with continued negotiation over what “disarmament” and “state control” actually entail in practice. In parallel, the anti-corruption campaign will likely continue in a manner calibrated to avoid direct confrontation with entrenched Iran-aligned interests, unless internal political competition, most notably Sadrist pressure, forces an expansion of its scope. Al-Zaidi’s Washington visit will function as a key signaling moment in this trajectory: the degree to which Washington accepts Baghdad’s actions as sufficient progress, rather than demanding further steps, will shape whether sanctions pressure on Iraqi officials and factions intensifies or eases through year-end. Underlying all of this, Iran is likely to continue permitting limited, face-saving cooperation on disarmament rhetoric while resisting any measures that would materially degrade the operational capacity of its most capable Iraqi proxies. Policymakers should calibrate expectations around the September 30 deadline to account for the fragmented militia landscape, avoiding the treatment of declarative commitments by parliamentary-linked factions as equivalent to enforceable, verifiable disarmament of hardline, designated groups. This calls for maintaining differentiated pressure, using targeted sanctions and financial network disruption against non-compliant factions, rather than blanket conditionality that could weaken the Coordination Framework government’s domestic standing without producing commensurate security gains. The al-Zaidi Washington visit should be used to establish concrete, monitorable benchmarks, such as verified weapons handover and PMF payroll transparency, rather than accepting rhetorical commitments as sufficient. This should also include clarity on what happens to fighters and weapons after surrender, whether through integration into the Iraqi Security Forces, formal demobilization, or structured payout schemes, since the absence of such a pathway is likely to undermine compliance in practice. Washington should also consider gradually loosening its oversight of Iraq’s oil revenue account at the New York Federal Reserve as a tangible goodwill gesture that reinforces its stated commitment to a “strong, sovereign, and united” Iraq, rather than leaving this Bremer-era financial mechanism as a standing contradiction to its sovereignty rhetoric. There should also be continued incremental engagement with Baghdad by Washington on economic and security cooperation to reinforce Iraq’s incentive to maintain distance from full alignment with Tehran, while remaining attentive to the risk that Iran-aligned factions retain influence over Iraqi security policy. This engagement should be paired with close monitoring of cross-border security risks, particularly given prior incidents linking Iraq-based groups to attacks on Gulf infrastructure. Independent verification mechanisms for both the anti-corruption and disarmament processes are needed, given the credibility gap that regional analysts have identified between government messaging and actual enforcement patterns. This should extend to encouraging greater transparency around PMF financing and command structures, as such transparency is a precondition for assessing whether disarmament announcements reflect substantive change or merely a renegotiated term of coexistence between the state and armed factions. Any such verification mechanism must be managed by the government in coordination with international institutions to ensure a multilateral perspective in the monitoring process. Expanding the anti-corruption campaign to visibly include Iran-aligned political and militia-linked figures, as well as figures associated with other regional actors, would substantially strengthen the government’s credibility both domestically and with international partners, reducing the risk that the initiative is perceived primarily as an instrument of factional consolidation. Alongside this, establishing clear, published criteria for what constitutes compliance with the disarmament deadline would reduce the ambiguity that hardline factions might otherwise exploit to delay or dilute enforcement. The rise of armed factions and their gradual absorption into Iraq’s political fabric was not the product of a single crisis or a single election cycle. It is the outcome of two decades of institutional erosion, sectarian bargaining, and external patronage, layered slowly enough that each step seemed manageable even as the cumulative effect reshaped the state itself. Reversing that trajectory will not be accomplished through a single disarmament deadline, a single high-profile visit, or a single change of government. It will require the same patience, consistency, and long-term investment that allowed the problem to take root in the first place. Iraq’s Coordination Framework, and any government that succeeds it, will continue to navigate between Washington and Tehran not because its leaders lack conviction, but because the structures compelling that balancing act were built over years and will not dissolve in months. Those seeking a sovereign, stable Iraq, in Baghdad and in Washington alike, should measure progress not by the speed of announcements, but by the durability of the institutions being rebuilt in their place.

The scale of the domestic backlash is itself a useful gauge of how combustible the disarmament file has become: Iraqi lawmakers openly called for military retaliation against Saudi Arabia and the US, with one invoking the “dark record” of Washington and Riyadh in language clearly aimed at outflanking Zaidi from a more hardline, anti-Western position. 14 That the rupture was patched over so quickly, with Riyadh renewing its invitation and the Islamic Resistance shelving a threatened response, likely reflects mutual interest in avoiding further escalation rather than any genuine resolution of the underlying dispute, since the core tension persists undiminished. GCC states want disarmament delivered on a fixed calendar, while Zaidi has to pursue it without detonating a backlash from coordination-framework elites whose own political survival is bound up with the very factions he is meant to dismantle, all under a public mood now openly hostile to both Iranian overreach and US-Saudi unilateralism on Iraqi soil. 15

The developments in Baghdad are of direct relevance to Washington’s Iraq policy, Gulf regional security planning, and broader efforts to manage Iran’s post-war regional posture. Three dynamics stand out for decision-makers:

The Iraqi government’s anti-corruption enforcement and disarmament announcements function primarily as instruments of legitimacy-building — externally toward Washington and internally toward a domestic public fatigued by past, largely symbolic, anti-corruption drives. Policymakers assessing these commitments should therefore distinguish between visible enforcement actions and genuine structural shifts in the distribution of coercive and financial power. This assessment is complicated by the fact that the PMF and affiliated factions are not a unitary actor: political and economic incentives are producing divergent responses, ranging from selective compliance by parliamentary-linked factions to open refusal by internationally designated groups. A uniform expectation for “compliance” by the September 30 deadline therefore risks obscuring meaningful variation in outcomes across these factions.

This dynamic is reinforced by domestic political fragility, which increases the value of a foreign-facing reform narrative. The government was formed with several cabinet posts, including defense and interior, left unfilled, and now faces cleric Muqtada al-Sadr’s public alignment with the anti-corruption campaign, raising the prospect of intensified intra-Shia political competition. A weak coalition operating under these conditions has strong incentives to lean on externally oriented reform messaging to consolidate its domestic standing.

If anti-corruption arrests continue to bypass the most powerful Iran-aligned political and militia figures, the campaign risks being read, both domestically and internationally, as an instrument of intra-coalition score-settling rather than a genuine governance reform, weakening the government’s negotiating position with Washington. Relatedly, the most probable outcome by the September 30 deadline will be a bifurcated result: parliamentary-linked factions surrendering heavy weapons or nominal PMF affiliation while retaining their organizational structure and funding access, alongside continued refusal by hardline, US-designated factions. Such an outcome would satisfy neither Washington’s more maximalist objectives nor eliminate the risk of renewed attacks on US or Gulf-linked targets, and, most importantly, would fail to resolve Iraq’s broader problem with the rise of non-state armed groups.

This partial compliance carries its own escalatory risk: continued attacks by non-compliant factions could trigger renewed US or Israeli strikes on Iraqi soil, as occurred during the earlier phase of the regional war, forcing the Coordination Framework government to manage domestic backlash while its stated disarmament commitments are exposed as unenforceable. Compounding these external pressures, Sadrist endorsement of the anti-corruption campaign, combined with public defenses of the Coordination Framework by senior Coordination Framework-aligned figures, signals rising internal contestation that could destabilize the governing coalition irrespective of any external pressure from Washington.

Voluntary steps by parliamentary-linked factions to detach from the PMF and place their weapons under state oversight could, if paired with credible political and economic guarantees, produce a durable, if partial, recalibration of militia influence without triggering violent confrontation. This incremental approach could be reinforced by Sadrist public backing of the anti-corruption campaign: if channeled constructively rather than confrontationally, this support could broaden the government’s domestic coalition and create space for deeper reforms beyond the current pattern of selective enforcement.

Underpinning both possibilities is Baghdad’s parallel engagement with Washington and Tehran. Provided this hedging strategy does not collapse into open contradiction, it allows Iraq to avoid becoming a frontline in a renewed US-Iran confrontation — a stabilizing outcome not just for Iraq, but for the wider Gulf region.

The September 30 deadline will most likely produce a mixed and ambiguous outcome rather than a clear resolution, with continued negotiation over what “disarmament” and “state control” actually entail in practice. In parallel, the anti-corruption campaign will likely continue in a manner calibrated to avoid direct confrontation with entrenched Iran-aligned interests, unless internal political competition, most notably Sadrist pressure, forces an expansion of its scope.

Al-Zaidi’s Washington visit will function as a key signaling moment in this trajectory: the degree to which Washington accepts Baghdad’s actions as sufficient progress, rather than demanding further steps, will shape whether sanctions pressure on Iraqi officials and factions intensifies or eases through year-end. Underlying all of this, Iran is likely to continue permitting limited, face-saving cooperation on disarmament rhetoric while resisting any measures that would materially degrade the operational capacity of its most capable Iraqi proxies.

Policymakers should calibrate expectations around the September 30 deadline to account for the fragmented militia landscape, avoiding the treatment of declarative commitments by parliamentary-linked factions as equivalent to enforceable, verifiable disarmament of hardline, designated groups. This calls for maintaining differentiated pressure, using targeted sanctions and financial network disruption against non-compliant factions, rather than blanket conditionality that could weaken the Coordination Framework government’s domestic standing without producing commensurate security gains. The al-Zaidi Washington visit should be used to establish concrete, monitorable benchmarks, such as verified weapons handover and PMF payroll transparency, rather than accepting rhetorical commitments as sufficient. This should also include clarity on what happens to fighters and weapons after surrender, whether through integration into the Iraqi Security Forces, formal demobilization, or structured payout schemes, since the absence of such a pathway is likely to undermine compliance in practice. Washington should also consider gradually loosening its oversight of Iraq’s oil revenue account at the New York Federal Reserve as a tangible goodwill gesture that reinforces its stated commitment to a “strong, sovereign, and united” Iraq, rather than leaving this Bremer-era financial mechanism as a standing contradiction to its sovereignty rhetoric.

There should also be continued incremental engagement with Baghdad by Washington on economic and security cooperation to reinforce Iraq’s incentive to maintain distance from full alignment with Tehran, while remaining attentive to the risk that Iran-aligned factions retain influence over Iraqi security policy. This engagement should be paired with close monitoring of cross-border security risks, particularly given prior incidents linking Iraq-based groups to attacks on Gulf infrastructure.

Independent verification mechanisms for both the anti-corruption and disarmament processes are needed, given the credibility gap that regional analysts have identified between government messaging and actual enforcement patterns. This should extend to encouraging greater transparency around PMF financing and command structures, as such transparency is a precondition for assessing whether disarmament announcements reflect substantive change or merely a renegotiated term of coexistence between the state and armed factions. Any such verification mechanism must be managed by the government in coordination with international institutions to ensure a multilateral perspective in the monitoring process.

Expanding the anti-corruption campaign to visibly include Iran-aligned political and militia-linked figures, as well as figures associated with other regional actors, would substantially strengthen the government’s credibility both domestically and with international partners, reducing the risk that the initiative is perceived primarily as an instrument of factional consolidation. Alongside this, establishing clear, published criteria for what constitutes compliance with the disarmament deadline would reduce the ambiguity that hardline factions might otherwise exploit to delay or dilute enforcement.

The rise of armed factions and their gradual absorption into Iraq’s political fabric was not the product of a single crisis or a single election cycle. It is the outcome of two decades of institutional erosion, sectarian bargaining, and external patronage, layered slowly enough that each step seemed manageable even as the cumulative effect reshaped the state itself. Reversing that trajectory will not be accomplished through a single disarmament deadline, a single high-profile visit, or a single change of government. It will require the same patience, consistency, and long-term investment that allowed the problem to take root in the first place. Iraq’s Coordination Framework, and any government that succeeds it, will continue to navigate between Washington and Tehran not because its leaders lack conviction, but because the structures compelling that balancing act were built over years and will not dissolve in months. Those seeking a sovereign, stable Iraq, in Baghdad and in Washington alike, should measure progress not by the speed of announcements, but by the durability of the institutions being rebuilt in their place.

extraction.body: Iraq marks national ‘Sovereignty Days’ as US troops depart, but must navigate risks of new security landscape. Iraq is set to hold four “Sovereignty Days”, a national holiday marking the complete withdrawal of US troops from the country and underscoring the deep symbolism of the exit after more than two decades of foreign intervention. Wednesday’s withdrawal deadline affirmed the exodus of a few hundred remaining US soldiers in the country, who have served in advisory roles in a coalition operation against ISIL (ISIS) first launched in 2015. While the exit plan predates Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, it fits into his wider vision of reasserting Iraqi state authority. That encompasses accelerating efforts to disarm all militias in the country by June 2027, including several powerful pro-Iran groups who have launched attacks throughout the region amid the US-Israeli war with Iran. Speaking at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) last week, al-Zaidi said his government was “striving to ensure that the state is the ultimate decision-maker in matters of peace and war, and that weapons and tools of power remain in the hands of its constitutional institutions”. He added, “With the end of the international coalition’s mission in Iraq, we are moving our relationship with our strategic partners to a new phase, moving from military cooperation to economic and development cooperation in service of our common interests.” Indeed, the US withdrawal appears to be part of a strategy by al-Zaidi to “politically weaken” influential militias , including those linked to Iran, according to Douglas Silliman, the former US ambassador to Iraq and Kuwait. Those militias have long pointed to the presence of the US military, and other foreign actors like Turkiye, as a pillar justification for maintaining their own weapons stores and chains of command. Some have already indicated they will refuse to hand over their arms. “It’s going to be a very difficult series of decisions,” Silliman said. “Both for the militias and for Prime Minister al-Zaidi and his defence team.” How the Iraqi government navigates the end of the US-led coalition’s deployment, dubbed “Operation Inherent Resolve”, will have wide-ranging implications for the future security of Iraq. The country has remained relatively stable in recent years following the 2017 territorial defeat of ISIL, despite being enveloped by conflict and insecurity on its borders. That stability has generally persisted since the US began its troop withdrawal in 2020 under US President Donald Trump, with the remaining military personnel consolidating at an airbase in Erbil, in northern Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdish region, at the end of 2025. Still, Renad Mansour, director of the Iraq Initiative at Chatham House, said militias aligned with Iran’s “axis of resistance” in the region ultimately remain “in full-on war mode, working with the IRGC [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] in the region. And so they will continue to target US and US interests.” While al-Zaidi has promised continued integration and cooperation with the US and other Western allies, there is likely disquiet behind the rhetoric, Mansour assessed, with some seeing the US’s erstwhile presence in the country as having served as a bulwark against a wider policy pivot. “The anxiety from the Iraqi government now is that the US might not need Iraq any more, or might, in the worst case, view Iraq as a pariah state, too close to Iran, and therefore another target,” he said. The targeting could eventually come in the form of sanctions or in an escalation of US and Israeli strikes on Iraqi territory, Mansour said. Mohammad Salih, a non-resident senior fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute and an expert on Iraq, also agreed that enthusiasm for the US troop withdrawal was likely more subdued within some segments of the Iraqi government than public statements – and national holidays – suggest. Salih assessed an underlying wariness to change the security status quo at a time of regional upheaval, pointing to the continued threat from ISIL sleeper cells, shifting cross-border dynamics in a post-Assad Syria, as well as the US-Israel war with Iran. “The official rhetoric tries to signal that Iraq is more or less fine, that it can take care of itself, and that it seeks stronger commercial and diplomatic ties with the US – that there is no need for the US military presence,” he said. “But in reality, there is a great deal of concern that Iraq could be the next theatre of some major regional development,” he told Al Jazeera. The operational implications of the end to the US-led anti-ISIL mission remain difficult to assess. In the wake of the withdrawal, the two countries appear to be reverting to a 2008 Strategic Framework and Security Agreement, signed under the administration of US President George W Bush, Salih said. The deal pledges continued, if non-binding, US security support for Iraq. Neither the Iraqi government nor the Pentagon have given a clear picture of what shape security cooperation could take going forward, particularly when it comes to the intelligence and logistical support that buoyed ISIL’s territorial defeat. However, a regional source with knowledge of the situation told Al Jazeera the relationship is “likely to become less centred on a visible military footprint and more focused on intelligence, training, technical support, capacity-building and institutional cooperation”. The source called the change a “test of whether a relationship built for a period of military intervention can evolve into a more conventional partnership between sovereign states”. “There are real capabilities and real experience in the Iraqi security forces. People I talk to in the military are quite confident that they can take on most threats against the sovereignty of Iraq,” former Ambassador Silliman said. But while the Iraqi parliament approved a partial cabinet in May, several key security roles, including minister of defence, remain unfilled. The Iraqi government also continues to lack a substantial air defence capability of its own, which could prove a major weakness if the domestic security situation were to spiral, Silliman said. “This is one area where there will be vulnerabilities because it is clear that the pro-Iran militias have been willing to use drones and rockets and missiles against Iraqi targets inside Iraq, and as of right now, the Iraqi military doesn’t really have a way to defend against that,” he said. Kurdish officials have been among the most vocal critics of the US withdrawal, pointing to a barrage of attacks on Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdish region by Iran and Iran-aligned militias thwarted by US anti-missile and anti-drone weapons this year. To be sure, the withdrawal of the remaining US troops is only one step in a larger, years-long effort to transform the US-Iraqi relationship from military to economic. Following the 2003 invasion as part of the US-led “global war on terror”, the US had initially withdrawn troops in 2011, only to redeploy them amid the rise of ISIL. Speaking at the UNGA, al-Zaidi promised an economic “renaissance”, pledging to boost Iraq’s petrochemical industry and build new fossil fuel delivery routes beyond the Strait of Hormuz. The constriction of traffic in the strait amid the US-Israel war with Iran has had an outsized impact on Iraq, with its oil output dropping by as much as 60 percent in March. For his part, during a meeting at the White House in July, US PresidentTrump pledged “a lot of deals” to come with Iraq, pointing to the country’s vast oil reserves. Hamzeh Hadad, an adjunct fellow with the Middle East Security Program at the Centre for a New American Security, said there were no immediate signs the US planned a wholesale shift in its approach towards Iraq, which still houses the largest US embassy in the world in Baghdad and the largest consulate in Erbil. Lahib Higel, the deputy director of the MENA programme at the International Crisis Group, called on Washington to focus on cooperation, while avoiding “pressuring al-Zaidi into a military confrontation against pro-Iran groups that he is unlikely to win”. “A better approach would be for the US to preserve bilateral security cooperation and support his efforts to strengthen state institutions over time,” Higel said in a social media post. “Washington cannot dictate Baghdad’s relationship with Tehran, nor can Tehran dictate Iraq’s relationship with Washington,” she said. “What Iraq instead needs is the space to find its own balance.”

In the wake of the withdrawal, the two countries appear to be reverting to a 2008 Strategic Framework and Security Agreement, signed under the administration of US President George W Bush, Salih said.
The deal pledges continued, if non-binding, US security support for Iraq.
“There are real capabilities and real experience in the Iraqi security forces.
People I talk to in the military are quite confident that they can take on most threats against the sovereignty of Iraq,” former Ambassador Silliman said.

Hamzeh Hadad, an adjunct fellow with the Middle East Security Program at the Centre for a New American Security, said there were no immediate signs the US planned a wholesale shift in its approach towards Iraq, which still houses the largest US embassy in the world in Baghdad and the largest consulate in Erbil.

Indeed, the US withdrawal appears to be part of a strategy by al-Zaidi to “politically weaken” influential militias , including those linked to Iran, according to Douglas Silliman, the former US ambassador to Iraq and Kuwait.

“This is one area where there will be vulnerabilities because it is clear that the pro-Iran militias have been willing to use drones and rockets and missiles against Iraqi targets inside Iraq, and as of right now, the Iraqi military doesn’t really have a way to defend against that,” he said.
Speaking at the UNGA, al-Zaidi promised an economic “renaissance”, pledging to boost Iraq’s petrochemical industry and build new fossil fuel delivery routes beyond the Strait of Hormuz.
“Washington cannot dictate Baghdad’s relationship with Tehran, nor can Tehran dictate Iraq’s relationship with Washington,” she said.
“What Iraq instead needs is the space to find its own balance.”
For his part, during a meeting at the White House in July, US PresidentTrump pledged “a lot of deals” to come with Iraq, pointing to the country’s vast oil reserves.

extraction.body: Advancing U.S. security through partnerships and alliances with other nations was the topic discussed by two combatant command leaders at Saturday's Reagan National Defense Forum at the Ronald Reagan Presidential Library in Simi Valley, California. Navy Adm. John Aquilino, commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, and Army Gen. Laura Richardson, commander U.S. Southern Command, took part in a panel discussion at the forum, which offers the defense community a chance to discuss and debate how the United States can lead the world in an era of increasingly complex challenges and opportunities. Aquilino said in the Indo-Pacom area, there is no concern about the strength of U.S. alliances and partnerships. "Our value and the value of our partners is clear in this region," he said. Additionally, Aukus, a trilateral security pact among Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States was announced Sept. 15 for the Indo-Pacific region, where the United States and the United Kingdom will help Australia acquire nuclear-powered submarines. "Aukus is an additive security relationship that will be extremely helpful to keep that peace and prosperity in the region," he said, adding, "so I certainly welcome it. Australia has made a big step, and I think it will increase the security in the region. For the [solutions set] long term, it is our allies and partners coming together to demonstrate the adherence to international rules-based order for the stability in the region, and [we must] continue that so we are stronger when we're together." As an additive to the other security arrangements, Aquilino said. "[Aukus'] interoperability with the United States [and] all those allies and partners is beneficial. We value that interoperability. And as the security apparatus works together, it does make us stronger." Adm. John Aquilino Adm. John Aquilino delivers remarks during the change of command ceremony for U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, where he assumed command. Aquilino, who was previously the U.S. Pacific Fleet commander, acknowledged Indo-Pacom's critical role in providing regional peace and security. SHARE IMAGE: Download Image Image Details Photo By: Navy Mass Communication Specialist 2nd Class Anthony J. Rivera VIRIN: 210430-N-XC372-2389C Richardson talked about the importance of Colombia and Brazil in her area of responsibility, which have been two of the United States' biggest security partners in the southern region for a long time. "[Given] all of the challenges that we have — the cross-cutting threats [that] challenge our collective security across all domains … our allies and partners exponentially make us stronger," she said. "And so, I think we have to look at that, from that perspective of what they have to bring and what we have to bring. We have to look at it from their perspective and their lens. A lot of times we look only through … our lens." Richardson said U.S. allies want to partner and be teammates with the United States and want to do more, she noted, adding, "I think that we've got to capitalize upon that." Military exercises give the United States and its partner nations the opportunities to showcase professional militaries and help train partners, who become key exporters of security in the region, she emphasized. "So, we're not only just participating in an exercise to work toward another one — it actually trains [nations] to be better security partners in the region, as well." Army Gen. Laura Richardson Army Gen. Laura Richardson, commander of U.S. Southern Command, meets in Colombia with Colombian wounded warriors during a Nov. 18, 2021visit to the Centro de Rehabilitación Inclusiva, a military rehabilitation facility. Richardson visited Colombia Nov. 16-18 to meet with defense leaders to discuss security cooperation. Using the Rim of the Pacific Exercise as an example, the Indo-Pacom commander pointed out that the last time it was conducted, there were 27 nations with maritime forces, ground forces and air forces. "That's what's been going on for 80 years, so we need to continue down that path, and we welcome those other sets of security exercise relationships." He added Aukus is a small microcosm that applies to the entire rest of the security apparatus, "and we're here to support all of our allies and partners who would like to expand or increase their capability." Turning to China, Richardson said that nation's playbook for Africa is taking place in Latin America now. "It's been happening in Africa for years, and if we're not careful, what's happening in Latin America will in five or 10 years have the same impacts," she said. China's Belt and Road Initiative is a strategy initiated by the People's Republic of China that seeks to connect Asia with Africa and Europe by land and maritime networks with the aim of improving regional integration, increasing trade and stimulating economic growth. passages: IPAMS provided all participants with a unique opportunity to discuss the Indo-Pacific region’s security issues and to exchange ideas on issues of mutual concern.
Army Pacific, told reporters during a media roundtable.

The annual conference brought together senior landpower leaders from across the region to participate in open dialogue with their Indo-Pacific counterparts on a wide range of topics affecting the region, and provided a venue where attendees met face to face; fostering military-to-military cooperation on topics such as security cooperation, military deterrence, and regional stability.

“A constant message emerged for our panels, syndicates, and informal engagements: no army can address the challenges of our region alone, said Gibbons. “The synergy of our collective strength derives from our partnerships, our interoperability, and our shared commitment to regional stability.”
Since then, the regional security environment has dramatically changed and so too the innovative approaches nations must take to ensure their own regional security.
For five decades, this annual gathering underscores the collective resolve to maintain a stable Indo-Pacific, demonstrating that countries are most effective when they stand and act together.
Regional Armies discuss their differences and similarities
The 51st edition of IPAMS will take place in Singapore, where it will share the stage with the bi-annual Indo-Pacific Army Chiefs Conference (IPACC) and Senior Enlisted Leaders Forum (SELF).

Olivia Cowart) More Details Senior leaders from across the Pacific are welcomed during a Pōwhiri at the Te Taua Moana Navy Marae as part of the 50th Indo-Pacific Armies Management Seminar in Auckland, New Zealand, Sept. 23, 2026. The Pōwhiri is a formal Māori ceremony that represents unity, kotahitanga, and is used to welcome visitors onto the Marae. (U.S. Army photo by Sgt. Olivia Cowart) More Details The annual conference brought together senior landpower leaders from across the region to participate in open dialogue with their Indo-Pacific counterparts on a wide range of topics affecting the region, and provided a venue where attendees met face to face; fostering military-to-military cooperation on topics such as security cooperation, military deterrence, and regional stability. This year’s theme, “The Sum is Greater Than the Parts: Security and Deterrence in the Indo-Pacific,” captured the essence of why IPAMS matters now more than ever. “Across this region, land forces are the backbone of deterrence, security cooperation, and the connective tissue that binds nations together,” Lt. Gen. Joel Vowell, deputy commander, U.S. Army Pacific, told reporters during a media roundtable. “When our armies train, communicate, and plan collectively, we generate a deterrence effect that is far stronger than any individual nation could achieve alone. Our discussions this week reinforce that truth,” said Vowell. The world has changed and so too has the Indo-Pacific New Zealand co-hosted this event in 2013. Since then, the regional security environment has dramatically changed and so too the innovative approaches nations must take to ensure their own regional security. “Peace remains important, however in the past decade our region has responded to major natural disasters, a global pandemic, and heinous terrorist actions,” said Brig. Gen. Hamish Gibbons, New Zealand’s deputy chief of NZ Army. “Each event required integrated, whole-of-government responses and highlighted the adaptability and effectiveness of land forces.” U.S. general Vowell also told conference attendees “There are real risks in this region. We won’t be given every tool and support that we all asked for, and our potential adversaries are working on how best to keep us apart. To dilute our contributions, to stay our goals of interoperability, that is their success-keeping us fragmented. Don’t let it happen.” Regional Armies discuss their differences and similarities For 50 years, IPAMS’ objective has been to promote peace and stability in the Indo-Pacific region through mutual understanding, dialogue, and friendship. IPAMS provided all participants with a unique opportunity to discuss the Indo-Pacific region’s security issues and to exchange ideas on issues of mutual concern. These discussions help generate combined deterrence and strengthen the Indo-Pacific land power network that is crucial to regional stability. This took place during plenary sessions featuring distinguished guest speakers and lively discussions on the complexities of operating in various environments from peacekeeping, humanitarian assistance/disaster relief, leader development, military deterrence, and how to succeed in these perplexing situations. The seminar’s working group sessions are specifically designed to be challenging and enlightening while promoting frank and open discussion. They also provided an opportunity to advance the understanding of key issues while showing respect for each other’s role in promoting security and stability in a free and open Indo-Pacific. “A constant message emerged for our panels, syndicates, and informal engagements: no army can address the challenges of our region alone, said Gibbons. “The synergy of our collective strength derives from our partnerships, our interoperability, and our shared commitment to regional stability.” The discussions and agreements gained during the conference foster collaborative relationships and are imperative to the future growth, stability, and development of gathered armies. IPAMS is the preeminent event of the Indo-Pacific Participation at this event has grown from 9 nations at the first conference held in Honolulu, Hawaii, in 1977, to a high of 31 nations that gathered in Seoul, Republic of Korea in 2017. For five decades, this annual gathering underscores the collective resolve to maintain a stable Indo-Pacific, demonstrating that countries are most effective when they stand and act together. “By listening and getting to know each other, we build trust and confidence now and not at crisis. It’s impossible to build trust once you’ve crossed that line of departure, it’s hard,” said Vowell. “Better to have known each other, work with each other, habituate relationships, so it’s easier to pick up the phone working together, side by side, to solve problems.” Deepening our personal relationships and strengthening existing bonds builds the foundation for shared values, interests and commitments to the security and prosperity of the region. The region is vast and fraught with challenges With close to 40 nations comprising their make-up, the Indo-Pacific region covers more than half of the earth’s surface featuring 6 of the most populated countries in the world. The region is inclusive of over 3,000 languages and dialects and poses some of the most pressing security challenges ranging from skirmishes, drug trafficking, terrorism to natural disasters. Many of the participating countries lie within the “Ring of Fire,” the unsettling area where earthquakes, tsunamis, typhoons, floods and other threats to life and property are most common. 7 of the world’s 10 largest armies are in the region where border disputes and sovereignty concerns are headline events. As is customary to conclude every IPAMS, the conference flag was passed from this year’s host to next year’s host, signifying the responsibility of event planning and gathering of participating armies. The 51st edition of IPAMS will take place in Singapore, where it will share the stage with the bi-annual Indo-Pacific Army Chiefs Conference (IPACC) and Senior Enlisted Leaders Forum (SELF).

The region is inclusive of over 3,000 languages and dialects and poses some of the most pressing security challenges ranging from skirmishes, drug trafficking, terrorism to natural disasters. Many of the participating countries lie within the “Ring of Fire,” the unsettling area where earthquakes, tsunamis, typhoons, floods and other threats to life and property are most common.
7 of the world’s 10 largest armies are in the region where border disputes and sovereignty concerns are headline events.

As is customary to conclude every IPAMS, the conference flag was passed from this year’s host to next year’s host, signifying the responsibility of event planning and gathering of participating armies.
The 51st edition of IPAMS will take place in Singapore, where it will share the stage with the bi-annual Indo-Pacific Army Chiefs Conference (IPACC) and Senior Enlisted Leaders Forum (SELF).

extraction.body: Advancing U.S. security through partnerships and alliances with other nations was the topic discussed by two combatant command leaders at Saturday's Reagan National Defense Forum at the Ronald Reagan Presidential Library in Simi Valley, California. Navy Adm. John Aquilino, commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, and Army Gen. Laura Richardson, commander U.S. Southern Command, took part in a panel discussion at the forum, which offers the defense community a chance to discuss and debate how the United States can lead the world in an era of increasingly complex challenges and opportunities. Aquilino said in the Indo-Pacom area, there is no concern about the strength of U.S. alliances and partnerships. "Our value and the value of our partners is clear in this region," he said. Additionally, Aukus, a trilateral security pact among Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States was announced Sept. 15 for the Indo-Pacific region, where the United States and the United Kingdom will help Australia acquire nuclear-powered submarines. "Aukus is an additive security relationship that will be extremely helpful to keep that peace and prosperity in the region," he said, adding, "so I certainly welcome it. Australia has made a big step, and I think it will increase the security in the region. For the [solutions set] long term, it is our allies and partners coming together to demonstrate the adherence to international rules-based order for the stability in the region, and [we must] continue that so we are stronger when we're together." As an additive to the other security arrangements, Aquilino said. "[Aukus'] interoperability with the United States [and] all those allies and partners is beneficial. We value that interoperability. And as the security apparatus works together, it does make us stronger." Adm. John Aquilino Adm. John Aquilino delivers remarks during the change of command ceremony for U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, where he assumed command. Aquilino, who was previously the U.S. Pacific Fleet commander, acknowledged Indo-Pacom's critical role in providing regional peace and security. SHARE IMAGE: Download Image Image Details Photo By: Navy Mass Communication Specialist 2nd Class Anthony J. Rivera VIRIN: 210430-N-XC372-2389C Richardson talked about the importance of Colombia and Brazil in her area of responsibility, which have been two of the United States' biggest security partners in the southern region for a long time. "[Given] all of the challenges that we have — the cross-cutting threats [that] challenge our collective security across all domains … our allies and partners exponentially make us stronger," she said. "And so, I think we have to look at that, from that perspective of what they have to bring and what we have to bring. We have to look at it from their perspective and their lens. A lot of times we look only through … our lens." Richardson said U.S. allies want to partner and be teammates with the United States and want to do more, she noted, adding, "I think that we've got to capitalize upon that." Military exercises give the United States and its partner nations the opportunities to showcase professional militaries and help train partners, who become key exporters of security in the region, she emphasized. "So, we're not only just participating in an exercise to work toward another one — it actually trains [nations] to be better security partners in the region, as well." Army Gen. Laura Richardson Army Gen. Laura Richardson, commander of U.S. Southern Command, meets in Colombia with Colombian wounded warriors during a Nov. 18, 2021visit to the Centro de Rehabilitación Inclusiva, a military rehabilitation facility. Richardson visited Colombia Nov. 16-18 to meet with defense leaders to discuss security cooperation. SHARE IMAGE: Download Image Image Details Photo By: Michael Wimbish VIRIN: 211118-A-BS728-001C Indo-Pacom executes 120 military exercises annually with U.S. allies and partners, and the nation is looking to make those more minilateral or multilateral, Aquilino said. Using the Rim of the Pacific Exercise as an example, the Indo-Pacom commander pointed out that the last time it was conducted, there were 27 nations with maritime forces, ground forces and air forces. "That's what's been going on for 80 years, so we need to continue down that path, and we welcome those other sets of security exercise relationships." He added Aukus is a small microcosm that applies to the entire rest of the security apparatus, "and we're here to support all of our allies and partners who would like to expand or increase their capability." Turning to China, Richardson said that nation's playbook for Africa is taking place in Latin America now. "It's been happening in Africa for years, and if we're not careful, what's happening in Latin America will in five or 10 years have the same impacts," she said. China's Belt and Road Initiative is a strategy initiated by the People's Republic of China that seeks to connect Asia with Africa and Europe by land and maritime networks with the aim of improving regional integration, increasing trade and stimulating economic growth. Ceremony Handshake Chief of Staff of the Army Gen. James C. McConville, left, shakes hands with Gen. Laura Richardson during her promotion ceremony at Conmy Hall, Joint Base Myer-Henderson Hall, Arlington, Va., Oct. 18, 2021. Richardson succeeded Navy Adm. Craig S. Faller as the commander of U.S. Southern Command, Oct. 29, 2021. Army Sgt. Kevin M. Roy SHARE IMAGE: Download Image Image Details Photo By: Army Sgt. Kevin M. Roy VIRIN: 211018-A-ZR313-1019 "So if you're having a problem with your economy already, and then the Chinese come with the Belt and Road Initiative with projects and money, and they're ready to start, it looks very attractive to some of our countries that are having a hard time with their economies," she said. COVID-19 is still very prevalent in our partner nations and countries in Latin America, and they have suffered at the hands of COVID-19, Richardson said, adding, "In my mind, that has changed the geopolitical landscape for some of the countries as they continue to deal with COVID[-19]."
