The Pōwhiri is a formal Māori ceremony that represents unity, kotahitanga, and is used to welcome visitors onto the Marae. (U.S. Army photo by Sgt. Olivia Cowart) More Details Senior leaders from across the Pacific are welcomed during a Pōwhiri at the Te Taua Moana Navy Marae as part of the 50th Indo-Pacific Armies Management Seminar in Auckland, New Zealand, Sept. 23, 2026. The Pōwhiri is a formal Māori ceremony that represents unity, kotahitanga, and is used to welcome visitors onto the Marae. (U.S. Army photo by Sgt. Olivia Cowart) More Details The annual conference brought together senior landpower leaders from across the region to participate in open dialogue with their Indo-Pacific counterparts on a wide range of topics affecting the region, and provided a venue where attendees met face to face; fostering military-to-military cooperation on topics such as security cooperation, military deterrence, and regional stability. This year’s theme, “The Sum is Greater Than the Parts: Security and Deterrence in the Indo-Pacific,” captured the essence of why IPAMS matters now more than ever. “Across this region, land forces are the backbone of deterrence, security cooperation, and the connective tissue that binds nations together,” Lt. Gen. Joel Vowell, deputy commander, U.S. Army Pacific, told reporters during a media roundtable. “When our armies train, communicate, and plan collectively, we generate a deterrence effect that is far stronger than any individual nation could achieve alone. Our discussions this week reinforce that truth,” said Vowell. The world has changed and so too has the Indo-Pacific New Zealand co-hosted this event in 2013. Since then, the regional security environment has dramatically changed and so too the innovative approaches nations must take to ensure their own regional security. “Peace remains important, however in the past decade our region has responded to major natural disasters, a global pandemic, and heinous terrorist actions,” said Brig. Gen. Hamish Gibbons, New Zealand’s deputy chief of NZ Army. “Each event required integrated, whole-of-government responses and highlighted the adaptability and effectiveness of land forces.” U.S. general Vowell also told conference attendees “There are real risks in this region. We won’t be given every tool and support that we all asked for, and our potential adversaries are working on how best to keep us apart. To dilute our contributions, to stay our goals of interoperability, that is their success-keeping us fragmented. Don’t let it happen.” Regional Armies discuss their differences and similarities For 50 years, IPAMS’ objective has been to promote peace and stability in the Indo-Pacific region through mutual understanding, dialogue, and friendship. IPAMS provided all participants with a unique opportunity to discuss the Indo-Pacific region’s security issues and to exchange ideas on issues of mutual concern. These discussions help generate combined deterrence and strengthen the Indo-Pacific land power network that is crucial to regional stability. This took place during plenary sessions featuring distinguished guest speakers and lively discussions on the complexities of operating in various environments from peacekeeping, humanitarian assistance/disaster relief, leader development, military deterrence, and how to succeed in these perplexing situations. The seminar’s working group sessions are specifically designed to be challenging and enlightening while promoting frank and open discussion. They also provided an opportunity to advance the understanding of key issues while showing respect for each other’s role in promoting security and stability in a free and open Indo-Pacific. “A constant message emerged for our panels, syndicates, and informal engagements: no army can address the challenges of our region alone, said Gibbons. “The synergy of our collective strength derives from our partnerships, our interoperability, and our shared commitment to regional stability.” The discussions and agreements gained during the conference foster collaborative relationships and are imperative to the future growth, stability, and development of gathered armies. IPAMS is the preeminent event of the Indo-Pacific Participation at this event has grown from 9 nations at the first conference held in Honolulu, Hawaii, in 1977, to a high of 31 nations that gathered in Seoul, Republic of Korea in 2017. For five decades, this annual gathering underscores the collective resolve to maintain a stable Indo-Pacific, demonstrating that countries are most effective when they stand and act together. “By listening and getting to know each other, we build trust and confidence now and not at crisis. It’s impossible to build trust once you’ve crossed that line of departure, it’s hard,” said Vowell. “Better to have known each other, work with each other, habituate relationships, so it’s easier to pick up the phone working together, side by side, to solve problems.” Deepening our personal relationships and strengthening existing bonds builds the foundation for shared values, interests and commitments to the security and prosperity of the region. The region is vast and fraught with challenges With close to 40 nations comprising their make-up, the Indo-Pacific region covers more than half of the earth’s surface featuring 6 of the most populated countries in the world. The region is inclusive of over 3,000 languages and dialects and poses some of the most pressing security challenges ranging from skirmishes, drug trafficking, terrorism to natural disasters. Many of the participating countries lie within the “Ring of Fire,” the unsettling area where earthquakes, tsunamis, typhoons, floods and other threats to life and property are most common. 7 of the world’s 10 largest armies are in the region where border disputes and sovereignty concerns are headline events. As is customary to conclude every IPAMS, the conference flag was passed from this year’s host to next year’s host, signifying the responsibility of event planning and gathering of participating armies. The 51st edition of IPAMS will take place in Singapore, where it will share the stage with the bi-annual Indo-Pacific Army Chiefs Conference (IPACC) and Senior Enlisted Leaders Forum (SELF).

sources.title: Cardano vs Ethereum: Which Smart Contract Platform Wins by 2030? - Yahoo Finance
passages: Currently, Cardano trades at around 25 cents, while Ethereum is priced at approximately $2,711.
Both platforms support smart contracts—self-executing programs that automatically fulfill the terms of a contract once predetermined conditions are met.
However, they are in direct competition for developers and applications.
So, which smart contract platform is likely to win by 2030?
Cardano (CRYPTO:ADA) has surged by 76% over the past three months, while Ethereum (CRYPTO:ETH) has gained 71%.
However, Ethereum's overall network is valued at about 35 times more than Cardano's.
Ethereum for a potential investment by 2030, you're weighing a recent fast rally against a much larger and more established platform.
When you consider all factors, Ethereum appears to be in a stronger position heading into 2030.
In contrast, Cardano's recent rally mainly reflects a recovery from a significant drop.

To put it into perspective, if you had invested $1,000 in Cardano three months ago, your investment would be worth approximately $1,760 now, compared to about $1,710 for the same investment in Ethereum.
Despite its recent gains, Cardano is still trading about 92% lower than its peak price of around $3.10 in September 2021.
Meanwhile, Ethereum reached an all-time high of $4,946 on August 24, 2025, and is now trading about 45% below that level.
This indicates that Ethereum has retained more of its value over time.
Ethereum holds about 11.4% of the total cryptocurrency market value, whereas Cardano accounts for only about 0.3%.
Cardano has approximately 36.8 billion tokens in circulation, while Ethereum has around 122 million.

For Cardano to match Ethereum's value with its current supply, it would need to rise to about $9 per token—an increase of nearly 3,490% from its current price, which is nearly three times its 2021 high.
In terms of recent performance, Cardano has outpaced Ethereum in several key metrics.
In comparison, Ethereum has risen 9.2%, 40%, and 71% over the same periods.
However, Cardano could still outperform Ethereum during market rallies, as smaller coins can move more rapidly in either direction.
On the flip side, if Ethereum's market share declines due to competition from other networks or changes in fund inflows, its lead could diminish as well.

However, this performance gap is relatively narrow over the 90 days, with most of Cardano's gains concentrated in the recent month.
Ethereum generates ongoing fee revenue from stablecoins, tokenized assets, and lending apps, while ETFs add another layer of institutional demand.
The vast difference in network usage contributes significantly to this valuation gap.
While both networks use proof of stake, allowing holders to lock up coins to confirm transactions, they differ primarily in how they're utilized.

In 2026, Strategy has amassed an impressive 846,000 Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ), representing approximately 65% of the nearly 1.3 million Bitcoin held by public companies. Together, these companies own around 6.2% of the total 21 million Bitcoin that will ever exist, worth about $109 billion at a price of roughly $84,018 per coin.
So, besides Strategy, which other public companies hold significant Bitcoin? What advantages do investors gain by buying shares in these companies rather than buying Bitcoin directly?

The following ranking features U.S.-listed companies, based on their latest reported Bitcoin holdings. Keep in mind that companies frequently buy and sell their Bitcoin , so these figures can fluctuate quickly.

Strategy ( NASDAQ:MSTR | MSTR Price Prediction ) leads the pack with 846,000 Bitcoin, valued at about $71 billion, which makes up about 4% of all Bitcoin that will ever exist. While it started as MicroStrategy, the company now primarily focuses on acquiring more Bitcoin, recently purchasing an additional 950 coins in mid-September.

Twenty One Capital ( NYSE:XXI ) holds 43,514 Bitcoin, worth approximately $3.7 billion. Even though it has a significant amount, Strategy holds about 19 times as many coins. The firm was established with Bitcoin as its primary asset, meaning that its stock price is closely tied to Bitcoin’s market movements.

MARA Holdings ( NASDAQ:MARA ) owns 35,303 Bitcoin, valued at around $3 billion. It stands out as the only mining company in the top five. By operating data centers to secure the Bitcoin network, MARA can increase its holdings without additional purchases. However, it is also shifting some of its resources toward AI computing, which may diversify its revenue streams away from Bitcoin mining.

Bitcoin Standard Treasury Company possesses 30,021 Bitcoin, worth about $2.5 billion. This firm was designed specifically to buy and hold Bitcoin, meaning it relies heavily on Bitcoin’s performance for support—if the price drops, the company has little else to fall back on.

Strive ( NASDAQ:ASST ) holds 26,354 Bitcoin, valued at roughly $2.2 billion. Initially an asset management firm for clients, Strive refocused its business on Bitcoin investing. Recently, it acquired 1,355 coins at around $79,475 each, and it is on track to surpass Twenty One Capital for the second spot if it continues purchasing around 1,200 coins per week.

Although not in the top five, several other public companies also hold Bitcoin. Tokyo-listed Metaplanet owns 43,000 Bitcoin, ranking third globally but not listed in the U.S. Galaxy Digital ( NASDAQ:GLXY ) has 25,723 coins, just behind Strive.

Other companies with notable Bitcoin holdings include Bullish (23,300), SpaceX (18,712), Coinbase (16,492), Riot Platforms (15,680), Tesla (11,509), Trump Media (9,542), and Block (9,032). While their Bitcoin stacks range from about $760 million to $2 billion, these firms generate most of their income through business models beyond Bitcoin.
In contrast, GameStop holds only a single Bitcoin, currently valued at about $84,000, which represents a minor fraction for a retailer with significant sales revenue.

Investing in companies that hold Bitcoin comes with certain risks that holding Bitcoin directly does not. A buyer of Bitcoin shares also takes on the company’s operations, debts, and potential future share sales. If a company issues new shares at a price lower than the value of the Bitcoin behind each share, existing shareholders end up with less Bitcoin per share.

On the other hand, individuals who invest directly in Bitcoin or through a spot Bitcoin fund own only the cryptocurrency itself, without the added risks associated with a company’s business operations. This means a Bitcoin stock could gain value faster than the coin itself when investors are willing to pay a premium for the shares. Conversely, it could also lose value faster if that premium disappears.

In summary, Strategy, Twenty One Capital, MARA, Bitcoin Standard Treasury Company, and Strive are the top five US-listed companies holding the most Bitcoin. Together, they control about 981,000 Bitcoin, accounting for roughly 76% of all Bitcoin held by public companies.

Strategy stands out by a wide margin, and if Strive continues its buying spree, it may rise to second place by year-end. For those looking to invest in Bitcoin’s value, a spot fund may sidestep many of the risks tied to these companies’ operations, share sales, and debt issues.

Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ) has experienced an impressive 71% increase over the past 90 days, reaching around $2,711. Meanwhile, XRP ( CRYPTO:XRP ) has also seen gains, rising about 46% to $1.51 as of September 29, 2026. So, for investors deciding between XRP or Ethereum, Ethereum clearly leads in terms of recent performance.

However, both cryptocurrencies are still trading significantly lower than they were a year ago—Ethereum is down 35%, and XRP has fallen 47%. Since neither coin generates profits for comparison, analyzing price trends, distance from their all-time highs, and market value provides the best way to evaluate them. So, which is the smarter investment right now?

Ethereum is a platform that allows developers to create smart contracts, which are programs that execute automatically when specific conditions are met. Users pay in ETH to utilize these contracts. On the other hand, XRP is the token of the XRP Ledger, designed for quick and cost-effective international money transfers.

In the last two months, Ethereum and XRP have both experienced similar growth rates, each up about 40%. Ethereum built most of its lead over XRP in July, when it jumped about 22% from roughly $1,560 to $1,910. During the same period, XRP rose only about 4%.

Since then, both coins have surged at a comparable pace, with Ethereum leading slightly over the past month—up 9% compared to XRP’s 8%. Currently, Ethereum is facing resistance near $2,800 , about 3% above its current price.

Ethereum is currently trading about 45% below its all-time high of $4,946 from August 24, 2025, meaning it needs to rise about 82% to recover that peak. In contrast, XRP is about 59% below its record of $3.65 from July 2025, which translates to a required increase of about 142% to reach its previous high.

Supporters of XRP often point out that a deeper decline provides more opportunity for recovery. Nevertheless, a significant drop also suggests sellers have had more control over XRP for a longer period. So far in 2026, XRP has fallen around 18%, while Ethereum has only decreased by about 10%. Additionally, XRP has lost more over the past year.

While XRP’s price of $1.51 may seem attractive compared to Ethereum’s $2,711, a single coin’s price isn’t the whole story. Currently, approximately 62.9 billion XRP are in circulation, valued at roughly $95 billion. In comparison, around 122 million ETH are worth about $331 billion, which is about 3.5 times more than XRP.

This market-size difference shows up in daily trading volumes. Over a 24-hour period, about $15.8 billion worth of ETH is traded, while XRP sees around $3.6 billion. This higher trading volume means large Ethereum orders have less impact on its price than they do on XRP.

On the supply side, XRP has a maximum cap of 100 billion tokens, with about 37 billion yet to enter circulation, primarily from Ripple’s escrow . Conversely, Ethereum has no cap, as the network continuously creates new ETH to reward validators while also burning a portion of transaction fees.

Given the recent performance and broader market context, Ethereum appears to be the smarter buy right now. It boasts stronger numbers over the past 90 days, requires a smaller increase to regain its all-time high, and benefits from significantly higher daily trading volumes. That said, XRP could still be a suitable option for those willing to endure more volatility, as it has kept pace with Ethereum over the past two months.

In conclusion, while Ethereum currently seems like the better investment following its remarkable 71% quarterly growth, this could shift as we approach late October. If XRP continues to close the gap in its 90-day gain, or if Ethereum’s price drops below $2,600—about 4% below its current price—the competitive landscape could change.

sources.title: OpenAI takes on Microsoft with the launch of what feels a whole lot like ChatGPT’s own office suite
passages: OpenAI has been a close partner of Microsoft from the jump, but the AI lab is increasingly going after the company’s bread and butter, workplace software, with new features that closely resemble an office software suite like Microsoft’s.

Most notably, OpenAI launched a feature called Space, a shared workspace inside ChatGPT where co-workers can collaborate with the chatbot and with their own Dots, OpenAI’s newly launched AI agent personas (that can carry out tasks on a user’s behalf), on a range of work tasks.
Over the past year, both companies have released a slew of AI products as the software industry attempts to keep up with the shifting landscape.
Users can “write, research, generate charts, create images, or visualize information” in it, OpenAI says.
At its DevDay developer conference in San Francisco on Tuesday, OpenAI announced several new ChatGPT features designed for office workers.
OpenAI has also announced its answer to PowerPoint with what it calls collaborative slides.
These slides can be created by merely talking about them within ChatGPT.
Once the slides are generated, multiple workers and agents can work together within them and will have the ability to leave comments and edit them.
Slides isn’t available quite yet but will roll out to users in the coming weeks, an OpenAI representative said.
PitPro’s first tire-changing robot goes live in Canada Sean O'Kane

At its DevDay developer conference in San Francisco on Tuesday, OpenAI announced several new ChatGPT features designed for office workers. Most notably, OpenAI launched a feature called Space, a shared workspace inside ChatGPT where co-workers can collaborate with the chatbot and with their own Dots, OpenAI’s newly launched AI agent personas (that can carry out tasks on a user’s behalf), on a range of work tasks. “Your pages and files all live together in Space, like they would in a drive,” said CEO Sam Altman during Tuesday’s presentation. “But spaces feel alive.” Altman said users can give a page specific instructions, such as checking a team channel and updating the page with what it finds. OpenAI also launched Pages, a companion word processor that the company describes as “a new type of document, built for human and agent collaboration.” It appears to be OpenAI’s answer to Google Docs and Microsoft Word. These slides can be created by merely talking about them within ChatGPT. Once the slides are generated, multiple workers and agents can work together within them and will have the ability to leave comments and edit them. Slides isn’t available quite yet but will roll out to users in the coming weeks, an OpenAI representative said. As OpenAI edges into Microsoft’s territory, Microsoft and other software companies like Salesforce are busy trying to become more like OpenAI. Over the past year, both companies have released a slew of AI products as the software industry attempts to keep up with the shifting landscape. sources.title: Here’s why OpenAI is absent from Nvidia’s industry-wide effort to end rogue AI agents
passages: The new effort, dubbed Nvidia’s Open Agent Safety Platform, is Nvidia’s attempt to spread its homegrown, and largely open source, AI agent-security tech throughout the AI ecosystem as a direct response to the types of ongoing rogue AI agent incidents frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI have disclosed.
OpenShell is open source software that creates a sandbox specifically designed to keep agents from escaping.
Clearly, OpenAI sees AI safety as an opportunity for independence from its major investor Nvidia, as well as a chance to show its own leadership.
That is true even though it was OpenAI’s AI agents that scared the industry with the Hugging Face incident .
For instance, the company is developing its own safeguards for its research and products and is disclosing the worst incident it discovers .
Meanwhile, OpenAI has its own AI cybersecurity consortium for sharing information, called the Defense Factory .
When Nvidia announced on Monday a new consortium of more than 100 companies dedicated to solving rogue AI agents, there was one name notably missing: OpenAI.
It allows Nvidia to ensure that this solution always runs best on its own hardware.
While it is still curious that OpenAI didn’t simply become a supporter of the initiative like its archrival Anthropic did, the fact that the frontier AI lab is supporting the effort is good news.

“From what we know (take with a grain of salt, we need much more transparency!), if @OpenAI had been running this on their own agents that attacked us, they would have caught them before we did!” Delangue posted .
The hardware monitoring part relies on Nvidia Sentry, a proprietary feature that runs on special Nvidia processors called BlueField-4 data processing units.
Sentry continuously monitors agent behavior from these processors and can instantly shut agents down, Nvidia promises.

It also enforces agent behavior at a hardware layer, where agents can’t detect that they are being watched. (Some AI models and agents lie and pretend to be following the rules when they know they are being watched.)
And Nvidia is sharing reference designs for the whole software-and-hardware idea.
And, truth be told, some level of fear is good for business.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been calling rogue AIs an ordinary engineering problem that can be solved like any other tech issue.

extraction.body: When Nvidia announced on Monday a new consortium of more than 100 companies dedicated to solving rogue AI agents, there was one name notably missing: OpenAI. While OpenAI wasn’t the only Big Tech player that didn’t sign on — Amazon, Google, and Apple haven’t joined either — it was the most obvious missing player, especially because Anthropic is a supporter. However, despite OpenAI’s lack of a public pledge to the consortium, which presumably means that each company will use and sell some version of the technology and contribute features back to the project, an OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch that the company is supportive of Nvidia’s work. The new effort, dubbed Nvidia’s Open Agent Safety Platform, is Nvidia’s attempt to spread its homegrown, and largely open source, AI agent-security tech throughout the AI ecosystem as a direct response to the types of ongoing rogue AI agent incidents frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI have disclosed. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been calling rogue AIs an ordinary engineering problem that can be solved like any other tech issue. The Open Agent Safety Platform is Huang putting his money where his mouth is. OpenAI is working with Nvidia on agent security, including on one of the key bits of software that’s part of this platform: OpenShell. OpenShell is open source software that creates a sandbox specifically designed to keep agents from escaping. While it is still curious that OpenAI didn’t simply become a supporter of the initiative like its archrival Anthropic did, the fact that the frontier AI lab is supporting the effort is good news. That’s because OpenAI, in particular, could benefit from this tech, at least according to Hugging Face founder and CEO Clem Delangue (who just sold his company to Nvidia for $12.9 billion earlier this month ). “From what we know (take with a grain of salt, we need much more transparency!), if @OpenAI had been running this on their own agents that attacked us, they would have caught them before we did!” Delangue posted . Delangue said Hugging Face has already contributed a feature to the Open Agent Safety Platform that will detect and shut down AI agents that are using websites they are allowed to visit but are doing so in unauthorized ways. For instance, this feature will act if agents are bypassing their guardrails and coordinating an attack by writing notes to one another in an open source code hosting repository. That’s one of the ways OpenAI said its wayward swarm of agents coordinated its attack on Hugging Face. But there’s another reason why some of these big names, including OpenAI, might not want to publicly commit to Nvidia’s efforts. To use the full system, there is a hardware component that is not open source software, remains proprietary, and can only be deployed on Nvidia’s hardware. The Open Agent Safety Platform doesn’t just offer a sandbox. It also enforces agent behavior at a hardware layer, where agents can’t detect that they are being watched. (Some AI models and agents lie and pretend to be following the rules when they know they are being watched.) The hardware monitoring part relies on Nvidia Sentry, a proprietary feature that runs on special Nvidia processors called BlueField-4 data processing units. Sentry continuously monitors agent behavior from these processors and can instantly shut agents down, Nvidia promises. While a hardware solution is clearly a good idea, it means that the Open Agent Safety Platform isn’t exactly a pure open source play. It allows Nvidia to ensure that this solution always runs best on its own hardware. Indeed, Nvidia has said that, for those already running workloads on its latest hardware, implementing the Open Agent Safety Platform is an easy software update. Still, Nvidia competitors, including Arm and Intel, have signed on as Open Agent Safety Platform supporters because the sandbox, OpenShell, can be modified to work with other chips and hardware. And Nvidia is sharing reference designs for the whole software-and-hardware idea. All of which makes OpenAI’s absence even more noticeable. Clearly, OpenAI sees AI safety as an opportunity for independence from its major investor Nvidia, as well as a chance to show its own leadership. That is true even though it was OpenAI’s AI agents that scared the industry with the Hugging Face incident . For instance, the company is developing its own safeguards for its research and products and is disclosing the worst incident it discovers . Meanwhile, OpenAI has its own AI cybersecurity consortium for sharing information, called the Defense Factory . Those that signed on to support that idea include Anthropic, Amazon Web Services, and Google — many of the names that didn’t sign on to Nvidia’s technology-oriented approach. And, truth be told, some level of fear is good for business. OpenAI is busy crafting cybersecurity into an enterprise offering, with everything from its own cyber-oriented model, Daybreak, to a growing network of partners that enterprises can hire to implement AI security. extraction.body: When Nvidia announced on Monday a new consortium of more than 100 companies dedicated to solving rogue AI agents, there was one name notably missing: OpenAI. While OpenAI wasn’t the only Big Tech player that didn’t sign on — Amazon, Google, and Apple haven’t joined either — it was the most obvious missing player, especially because Anthropic is a supporter. However, despite OpenAI’s lack of a public pledge to the consortium, which presumably means that each company will use and sell some version of the technology and contribute features back to the project, an OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch that the company is supportive of Nvidia’s work. The new effort, dubbed Nvidia’s Open Agent Safety Platform, is Nvidia’s attempt to spread its homegrown, and largely open source, AI agent-security tech throughout the AI ecosystem as a direct response to the types of ongoing rogue AI agent incidents frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI have disclosed. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been calling rogue AIs an ordinary engineering problem that can be solved like any other tech issue. The Open Agent Safety Platform is Huang putting his money where his mouth is. OpenAI is working with Nvidia on agent security, including on one of the key bits of software that’s part of this platform: OpenShell. OpenShell is open source software that creates a sandbox specifically designed to keep agents from escaping. While it is still curious that OpenAI didn’t simply become a supporter of the initiative like its archrival Anthropic did, the fact that the frontier AI lab is supporting the effort is good news. That’s because OpenAI, in particular, could benefit from this tech, at least according to Hugging Face founder and CEO Clem Delangue (who just sold his company to Nvidia for $12.9 billion earlier this month ). “From what we know (take with a grain of salt, we need much more transparency!), if @OpenAI had been running this on their own agents that attacked us, they would have caught them before we did!” Delangue posted . Delangue said Hugging Face has already contributed a feature to the Open Agent Safety Platform that will detect and shut down AI agents that are using websites they are allowed to visit but are doing so in unauthorized ways. For instance, this feature will act if agents are bypassing their guardrails and coordinating an attack by writing notes to one another in an open source code hosting repository. That’s one of the ways OpenAI said its wayward swarm of agents coordinated its attack on Hugging Face. But there’s another reason why some of these big names, including OpenAI, might not want to publicly commit to Nvidia’s efforts. To use the full system, there is a hardware component that is not open source software, remains proprietary, and can only be deployed on Nvidia’s hardware. The Open Agent Safety Platform doesn’t just offer a sandbox. It also enforces agent behavior at a hardware layer, where agents can’t detect that they are being watched. (Some AI models and agents lie and pretend to be following the rules when they know they are being watched.) The hardware monitoring part relies on Nvidia Sentry, a proprietary feature that runs on special Nvidia processors called BlueField-4 data processing units. Sentry continuously monitors agent behavior from these processors and can instantly shut agents down, Nvidia promises. While a hardware solution is clearly a good idea, it means that the Open Agent Safety Platform isn’t exactly a pure open source play. It allows Nvidia to ensure that this solution always runs best on its own hardware. Indeed, Nvidia has said that, for those already running workloads on its latest hardware, implementing the Open Agent Safety Platform is an easy software update. Still, Nvidia competitors, including Arm and Intel, have signed on as Open Agent Safety Platform supporters because the sandbox, OpenShell, can be modified to work with other chips and hardware. And Nvidia is sharing reference designs for the whole software-and-hardware idea. All of which makes OpenAI’s absence even more noticeable. Clearly, OpenAI sees AI safety as an opportunity for independence from its major investor Nvidia, as well as a chance to show its own leadership. That is true even though it was OpenAI’s AI agents that scared the industry with the Hugging Face incident . For instance, the company is developing its own safeguards for its research and products and is disclosing the worst incident it discovers . Meanwhile, OpenAI has its own AI cybersecurity consortium for sharing information, called the Defense Factory . Those that signed on to support that idea include Anthropic, Amazon Web Services, and Google — many of the names that didn’t sign on to Nvidia’s technology-oriented approach. And, truth be told, some level of fear is good for business. OpenAI is busy crafting cybersecurity into an enterprise offering, with everything from its own cyber-oriented model, Daybreak, to a growing network of partners that enterprises can hire to implement AI security. extraction.body: Taxpayer money from U.S. Customs and Border Protection funded the pro-Trump television ads that have drawn bipartisan scrutiny just weeks before November's midterm election , The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday. President Donald Trump personally pushed for the ads and was involved in creating them, the Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter. The revelation puts a CBP, part of the Department of Homeland Security, behind a campaign that looks far different from its traditional public messaging. CBP routinely runs ads discouraging illegal immigration. These spots instead feature Trump heavily, tout his tax cuts , attack communism and recycle language from his 2024 campaign. One ad declares that "America will never be a communist country" as images of Trump fill the screen. Another revives his "final battle" message from the 2024 race and attacks the political establishment and news media. The ads have already aired thousands of times nationally and locally. CNBC previously reported that more than $1.2 million had been spent airing two of the spots, according to AdImpact, which tracks political advertising spending. Democrats and at least one Republican senator have questioned whether taxpayer dollars should be used for ads centered so heavily on Trump. Some Democrats in Congress are now calling for investigations into whether money appropriated for border protection is being used to promote the president's political message. "It appears DHS has dedicated $20 million to this outrageous scheme," Sens. Patty Murray , D-Wash., and Chris Murphy , D-Conn., wrote in a letter to DHS on Tuesday, saying the department tapped money provided to CBP through Republicans' " One Big Beautiful Bill Act ." Federal contracting records show CBP awarded $20 million to Maryland-based advertising firm LMD Agency on Sept. 20 for a "National Media Campaign." The one-year contract was fully funded at the time of the award. The award came one day after the Office of Management and Budget approved the release of $20 million to CBP under a "Commemorative Events" funding line. The public contract record does not specify what the "National Media Campaign" entails or establish that LMD worked on the Trump ads. LMD has previously performed advertising work for agencies within the Department of Homeland Security, federal procurement records show. LMD did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on whether its $20 million contract is connected to the ads, whether it is playing a role in the ad campaign or whether additional advertisements or media buys are planned. CBP did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the ads or the procurement contract. Blowback to the ads also spread to federal regulators Tuesday. Watchdog group Public Citizen filed a complaint with the Federal Communications Commission and Federal Trade Commission urging broadcasters to stop airing the ads, while separately asking the Government Accountability Office and Office of Special Counsel last Friday to investigate alleged violations of federal propaganda restrictions and the Hatch Act, which restricts the involvement of federal government employees in political campaigns. The White House defended the campaign Tuesday, calling the spots public service announcements. “These public service announcements are about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad,” a White House spokesperson told CNBC. “The ad is educational and unapologetically patriotic. President Donald Trump personally pushed for the ads and was involved in creating them, the Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter. The revelation puts a CBP, part of the Department of Homeland Security, behind a campaign that looks far different from its traditional public messaging. CBP routinely runs ads discouraging illegal immigration. These spots instead feature Trump heavily, tout his tax cuts , attack communism and recycle language from his 2024 campaign. One ad declares that "America will never be a communist country" as images of Trump fill the screen. Another revives his "final battle" message from the 2024 race and attacks the political establishment and news media. The ads have already aired thousands of times nationally and locally. CNBC previously reported that more than $1.2 million had been spent airing two of the spots, according to AdImpact, which tracks political advertising spending. Democrats and at least one Republican senator have questioned whether taxpayer dollars should be used for ads centered so heavily on Trump. Some Democrats in Congress are now calling for investigations into whether money appropriated for border protection is being used to promote the president's political message. "It appears DHS has dedicated $20 million to this outrageous scheme," Sens. Patty Murray , D-Wash., and Chris Murphy , D-Conn., wrote in a letter to DHS on Tuesday, saying the department tapped money provided to CBP through Republicans' " One Big Beautiful Bill Act ." Federal contracting records show CBP awarded $20 million to Maryland-based advertising firm LMD Agency on Sept. 20 for a "National Media Campaign." The one-year contract was fully funded at the time of the award. The award came one day after the Office of Management and Budget approved the release of $20 million to CBP under a "Commemorative Events" funding line. The public contract record does not specify what the "National Media Campaign" entails or establish that LMD worked on the Trump ads. LMD has previously performed advertising work for agencies within the Department of Homeland Security, federal procurement records show. LMD did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on whether its $20 million contract is connected to the ads, whether it is playing a role in the ad campaign or whether additional advertisements or media buys are planned. CBP did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the ads or the procurement contract. Blowback to the ads also spread to federal regulators Tuesday. Watchdog group Public Citizen filed a complaint with the Federal Communications Commission and Federal Trade Commission urging broadcasters to stop airing the ads, while separately asking the Government Accountability Office and Office of Special Counsel last Friday to investigate alleged violations of federal propaganda restrictions and the Hatch Act, which restricts the involvement of federal government employees in political campaigns. The White House defended the campaign Tuesday, calling the spots public service announcements. “These public service announcements are about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad,” a White House spokesperson told CNBC. “The ad is educational and unapologetically patriotic.
